articles.title: Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
articles.summary: The attack comes at a time of heightened tensions in the West Bank and four days before Israel's general election.

blocks.text: Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.
Unverified footage shared on social media shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.

The attack comes at a time of high tensions in the West Bank, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.

The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle. The military said they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but unexpectedly ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security, said he had instructed the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday. The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media.
Netanyahu added that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning.

articles.title: Detective raped by fellow officer David Carrick calls on Met chief to resign
articles.summary:
Linda Williams says police force’s handling of her attack in 2004 was ‘like being raped all over again’

A detective who was raped by the former Scotland Yard officer David Carrick has called…

blocks.text: A detective who was raped by the former Scotland Yard officer David Carrick has called for the head of the Metropolitan police to resign, saying the handling of her case was “like being raped all over again”.

Linda Williams, 60, who has waived her right to anonymity, was attacked by Carrick in 2004. She launched a legal case against the Met for failing to protect her against the serial rapist, and has now settled for an undisclosed six-figure sum without the force admitting liability.
Carrick, 51, who previously served as an armed officer in the Met, is one of the country’s worst sex offenders and is serving 37 life sentences after attacking more than a dozen women.
Williams, from Hertfordshire, has said the way she was treated by the force throughout her legal claim was “devastating” and that it drove her to contemplate suicide.

“The whole process has taken me right back to how I felt when I was raped by Carrick: controlled, abused and powerless,” she said. “If I was raped tomorrow, I wouldn’t report it. Both the criminal justice process and the civil process have been so traumatic.

“I say that as someone who was once a sexual offences officer, supporting victims myself. Despite that experience and my understanding of the system, I still wouldn’t report it, because of the complete lack of empathy and support I have experienced from the police.
“At no point did I feel they sincerely acknowledged that I had been through a horrific sexual attack and that the trauma of that had deeply scarred me, or their role in it all.”

Williams brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis the force failed to protect her from Carrick and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape. She said the Met’s legal team in the case questioned the severity of her PTSD diagnosis.

“They used the fact that I just got on with my life as best I could after the rape against me,” she said. “I was an exemplary officer and continued to perform well at work, and they relied on that to suggest I had shown no signs of psychological trauma.
“As far as I am concerned, it is Mark Rowley, the [Met] commissioner, saying these terrible things, as he was the defendant in the case.”
She said the Met need to set up a unit overseen by victims like herself who understood what it was like to be raped.
“For this to happen Rowley needs to go and we need a new commissioner,” she said.

Williams alleged it was the “Met’s fault” that she could not report the rape in 2004, and that “little had changed” in the culture since then. She added that the force was “like an episode of Life On Mars”, the 2000s TV drama set in a fictional 1970s police station.
She said: “I wouldn’t have had the back up of my colleagues in dangerous situations and ultimately, I doubt anything would have been done about Carrick.”

Williams reported the rape in 2021, and said she has had no relationships since the attack, 22 years ago. She said: “After the attack, I couldn’t face the thought of being with a man or even having somebody in my home. That makes for a lonely Christmas and no holidays.
after newsletter promotion
“It’s my choice, but the reason behind it wasn’t my choice. That’s down to the attack. Carrick stole the future that I wanted.”
Williams told the BBC the PTSD she had experienced after the attack was “90% down to the Met police, 10% to Carrick”.

In 2022 and 2023, Carrick pleaded guilty to 71 sexual offences, including 48 rapes against 12 other women over 17 years. In November last year, he was convicted of molesting a 12-year-old child in the late 1980s and repeatedly raping and abusing a female ex-partner.
A Met spokesperson said: “Serious flaws in the way we approached such investigations at the time meant we did not spot his pattern of abusive behaviour.

“As a result, we missed opportunities to pursue him through the misconduct process. We deeply regret this. We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer.

“Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable. Throughout subsequent legal proceedings, the Met has tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams’ welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible.

“The commissioner has previously met with DC Williams in person as well as spoken to her via email on multiple occasions. He has repeatedly acknowledged that she has shown courage in speaking out about her experience in an effort to drive forward necessary change and in now waiving her anonymity to continue to do so.
“He has contacted DC Williams to ask whether she would be willing to meet again and further discuss these issues in person.”

articles.title: MRT-3 privatization eyed by mid-2027 under P103.6-billion deal
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez says the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

blocks.text: TRAIN. Commuters crowd the MRT at the Araneta Cubao Station during the first day of the work week to avail of the month-long free train ride implemented by the government, on March 28, 2022.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
Transportation Secretary Giovanni 'Banoy' Lopez says the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

MANILA, Philippines – The Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) may be privatized by mid-2027, with the Department of Transportation (DOTr) set to bid out the train line under a P103.6-billion public-private partnership project this year.
The decision to privatize the train line comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s order to prioritize the modernization of MRT-3.
DOTr Secretary Giovanni “Banoy” Lopez said the government would retain control over fares of MRT-3 under the proposed arrangement.

“Through public-private partnership, we bring in the expertise and investment this line needs. Ang kailangan natin dito ‘yung may matagal nang experience sa pagpapatakbo ng riles para sa kapakinabangan ng mga komyuter. At lilinawin ko po, mananatili pa rin sa DOTr ang pagtatakda ng pamasahe,” Lopez said in a statement released on Friday, October 23.
(What we need here is an entity with extensive experience in operating railways for the benefit of commuters. And let me make this clear, the DOTr will still be responsible for setting fares.)

Under the arrangement, a private company will be responsible for operating, maintaining, and upgrading the railway under a concession agreement. The project includes replacing trains and upgrading the signaling system to improve the line’s capacity, reliability, and efficiency.

Payments to the private operator, or concessionaire, will be linked to its delivery of services and compliance with performance standards covering train availability, reliability, cleanliness, and maintenance. The agreement is intended to hold the operator accountable for the quality of service it provides to commuters.
The DOTr said about 100 local and international companies have already expressed interest in the MRT-3 project. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sri Lanka: Death of iconic elephant raises habitat concerns
articles.summary: The death of what was thought to be Sri Lanka’s largest elephant has drawn attention to human-elephant conflict in rural communities. The island country sees a high number of deadly encounters.

image.caption: The 11-foot bull elephant 'Kavantissa' died after being shot in the leg earlier in OctoberImage: newswire.lk

blocks.text: The recent death of an iconic male elephant in Sri Lanka has raised concerns over ongoing contact between humans and the giant animals who are quickly seeing their habitats reduced.

The elephant known as "Kavantissa" had been considered to be the tallest living male elephant in the Sri Lanka. Thought to be anywhere from 45 years old and measuring roughly 3.3 meters tall (11 feet), he roamed Sri Lanka's northwest near the village of Galgamuwa, and was widely admired for his majestic stature.

In late September, villagers noticed the 5.5 ton-tusker (5,500 kg) was limping, and a closer look reveled a gunshot wound on his right leg. Despite the intervention of veterinary surgeons, the elephant died on October 16.

Sri Lanka records the highest number of elephant deaths annually and the second highest number of human deaths globally from violent interactions between elephants and humans, which usually happen when crop raiding elephants encroach on farmlands.
According to official statistics, since 2019, 370 elephants and 125 humans have died on average in human-elephant conflict incidents.
The situation affects the natural habitats of elephants and the livelihoods of rural communities.
Home to about 10% of the global Asian elephant population and occupying about 2% of their total natural range, Sri Lanka has the highest density of Asian elephants in the world.

The Sri Lankan elephant is an endangered subspecies in the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, and protected under Sri Lankan law, with punishment by fines and jail terms for wildlife-related offences.

blocks.caption: Some villages use electric fences to keep elephants away from crops and peopleImage: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: A shrinking habitat for elephants
During the past few decades, forest cover in Sri Lanka has shrunk along with rapid population growth.
Statistics show the rural population of Sri Lanka increased from 8.25 million in 1960 to 17.8 million in 2020.
Agriculture remains the primary source of income for these rural communities. As a result, the land is cleared for agricultural activities.

According to Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC) statistics, in 2024 an estimated 7,451 wild elephants were recorded in Sri Lanka. About 70% of these wild elephants live outside protected areas.
Research shows elephants have a massive daily dietary requirement of about 150 kilograms (330 lbs.) of green matter, which drives them into farmland.

"Driven primarily by habitat loss, agricultural expansion, fragmentation of elephant corridors, and increasing competition for land and resources, human-elephant conflict continues to cause hundreds of elephant deaths and more than 100 human fatalities annually," said Ravi Corea, President of Sri Lanka Wildlife Conservation Society, a Sri Lankan non-profit conservation organization.
The conservationist told DW that rural communities are severely affected, and the agricultural losses caused by elephants can threaten a family's primary source of food and income.

"This distinguishes human-elephant conflict from many human-wildlife conflicts in economically developed countries, where wildlife encounters, although sometimes serious, generally do not threaten household subsistence to the same extent," he said.
Indian villages deter wild elephants with lemon trees
Elephants and humans clash
"Despite the efforts by the government to mitigate HEC, the numbers are rising demonstrating the continuing severity of the crisis," Corea added.
Elephants are shot, poisoned, or killed by improvised explosives hidden in food and train collisions, experts say.
In view of the escalation of human-elephant conflict, the Sri Lankan government in 2020 drafted a national action plan to mitigate the problem.

"The 2020 Action Plan provides a valuable foundation for reducing human–elephant conflict, but its recommendations must be strengthened through a comprehensive national conservation strategy with enforceable habitat protection at its core," Corea said.

"The ultimate measure of success must be not merely a reduction in human–elephant conflict, but the permanent protection of ecologically connected habitats, the survival of viable wild elephant populations and the ability of people and elephants to coexist sustainably for generations to come," he added.
Community-level initiatives protect people and elephants

Meanwhile, community-based programs by non-government organizations have proven effective and sustainable. These initiatives are complemented by elephant monitoring, scientific research, habitat assessments, community education, and the development of locally appropriate deterrents, Corea said

"Our flagship initiative Project Orange Elephant in Sri Lanka's Wasgamuwa region promotes the cultivation of citrus which elephants do not like to eat as a trophic deterrence. This reduces crop raiding while generating alternative income for farmers," Corea added, pointing to things like electric fencing protecting settlements and agricultural lands while encouraging local responsibility.

blocks.caption: Elephants do not like the taste of citrus fruits Image: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: Another issue is confrontations on elephant corridors, that in some cases have discouraged children from walking to school.
Elephant corridors are designated strips of land that connect larger forest and habitat patches, allowing elephants to move safely between them for food, water, breeding, and seasonal migration.

To address this, the "EleFriendly" bus service in Wasgamuwa, provides safe transportation for schoolchildren through elephant corridors and has reduced dangerous human-elephant encounters along its original route by over 90%.

blocks.caption: A bus takes students to school in order to avoid elephant paths Image: Ravi Corea

blocks.text: "An ethically just solution must protect human lives, livelihoods, and elephant populations simultaneously, said Kamal Shashendra, a Sri Lanka-based environmental ethics researcher.

He told DW that this required scientifically informed land-use planning, protection of elephant corridors, appropriate community-based fencing, effective early-warning systems, and fair compensation for affected families.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Friday called out corrupt government officials who extort from business owners by delaying permit issuance, among others, for their own gain.
Remulla made the statement during this meeting with the members of Cebu's lechon industry.

"Ang nangyayari ngayon is 'impunity of corruption.' Ang abuso from barangay captain, kagawad, tanod hanggang itaas. Grabe ang kikil. Pinahirapan nila ang negosyante. Hingi nang hingi. Iniipit. It comes to the point, kasosyo na sila ng mga negosyante. May porsyento na sila sa ginagawa niyo," Remulla said.

(What is happening is impunity of corruption. There's abuse of power starting with the barangay captain, council members, barangay watchmen, and up. The extortion is severe. They extort from businessmen and keep on asking for money. It comes to a point wherein these extortionists become business partners of the businessmen. They have a percentage of the profit.)

"Ang cost of doing business tumataas dahil maraming nang-iipit. At 'yan ang gusto natin baguhin. Maraming pressure sa amin. Protektahan 'to, huwag papatulan 'to. Huwag ikukulong 'yan, huwag idemanda 'yan. Hindi po. Kailangan gawin namin. Gagawin namin talaga," Remulla added.

(The cost of doing business is so high because there are lots of extortionists. And that is what we want to change. We face a lot of pressure. Protect this and that, don't send them to jail, don't file cases against certain people. No. We need to do our job and we will do our job.)
Ombudsman Remulla then said the government should enable legitimate business operations, instead of standing in their way.

"It shouldn't happen. Government should be there to assist business because you are the economy. The business sector's role is crucial in driving economic growth, generating employment and improving the purchasing power of Filipinos," Remulla said.

Remulla then cited the opening of the Investors' Window in the Ombudsman, which is a mechanism wherein business owners and investors may bring forward concerns involving government officials and transactions that impede their operations such as extortion, abuse of authority, unreasonable delays and other forms of misconduct in government.

"Kung ang Anti-Red Tape Authority report sa amin, 'yung permit hindi binibigay, susulatan natin 'yan. Sa susunod 'yan, 'pag hindi pa rin ginawa 'yan, suspend kaagad 'yan. Suspendihin natin kaagad 'yung concerned official. I can assure you that. Binigay sa amin ang power ng batas para gawin 'yan," Remulla said.
(If the permit to operate business is being withheld, then we will write them. If they still won't comply, we'll hand them suspension order. We have the power to do that.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Digital 2027 report: Global use of GenAI tools rises, web browser activity declines
articles.summary: 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up use AI tools each month, but only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up pay for subscriptions to an AI tool each month, the…

blocks.text: 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up use AI tools each month, but only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up pay for subscriptions to an AI tool each month, the study finds
MANILA, Philippines – Media intelligence company Meltwater and creative agency We Are Social released the Digital 2027 report this October, providing data on worldwide digital trends.

The more than 900-page report seeks to provide worldwide statistics on the various aspects of digital daily life, from the adoption of artificial intelligence tools like generative AI, to the use of web browsers and mobile phones. It is aided by a series of individual deep dives by author Simon Kemp into specific aspects of the main report.
In the local country headlines report, the Philippines is said to have a total population of 118 million people, a figure that increased by 936,000 from last year.

The report also showed 149 million cellular phone connections in the country, or 126% compared to the total population of the Philippines. The figure likely infers people having more than one phone on hand.

Meanwhile, 95.9 million individuals — or 81.3% of the population — were using the internet, while the report mentioned there were 94.7 million social media user identities in the country, which represent a decline of about 1.1 million user identities.

The report also mentioned 94.4% of internet users in the Philippines aged 16 and up used AI tools each month. However, only 5.5% of internet users in the country aged 16 and up paid for subscriptions to an AI tool each month.

Within the Philippine context, 71.17% of active AI users aged 16 and up use AI tools to find information, 37.6% of active AI users aged 16 and up use AI tools to seek advice on problems, 32.8% of active AI users aged 16 and up used AI tools for personalized recommendations.
Further, 27.5% of Philippine internet users aged 16 and up believe AI benefits society overall.
According to the report, 38.9% of the global population of 8.32 billion people — or around 3.24 billion — currently use generative AI tools each month.

This shows a growth of about 1.2 billion new users, though the report emphasizes a caveat of potential duplication —that a user may have more than one account for a generative AI service to decouple personal and work uses.

Meanwhile, social media user identities now number 5.81 billion or 69.9% of the world’s population, though a similar caveat applies here as some duplication due to decoupling personal and work social media identities may occur.

Citing two separate reports from GSMA Intelligence and Ericsson, there are now 5.86 billion unique mobile phone users worldwide as of the report’s release this month. Further information from Ericsson showed the 7.68 billion smartphones in use today account for nearly 90% of all active mobile phone handsets, and nearly 86% of total cellular mobile connections, with the caveat that some folks may have more than one smartphone.
The report said that across the world’s top 10,000 web domains, the total monthly web traffic declined by more than 10% since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
Combined traffic across the top 10,000 web domains fell by almost 50 billion visits per month between Q4 2022 and Q2 2026.

Further, there has been an 11.2% decline in the total time spent visiting the top 10,000 global domains over a two-year period, This fall is equivalent to more than 6.6 billion hours per month in that time frame.
Aside from the potential effects of AI use, the report suggests people are more readily using native mobile apps rather than using their browsers to get what they want from the internet.

That said, web users did load an average of just under 3 trillion pages per month across the world’s top 10,000 domains in the second quarter of 2026. The figure is up more than 2% compared to the same time period in 2024.
The full Digital 2027 report can be downloaded from this site. Meanwhile, Simon Kemp’s reports on some of the pertinent statistics are available here. – Rappler.com

The world’s second largest brewer sent a presentation to British hospitality customers earlier this month warning that GLP-1 use – led by Ozempic and Wegovy – can reduce the desire to drink alcohol, which could lead to “fullness and fewer serves” of pints in pubs and bars.
The document, revealed by Reuters, warned that the GLP-1 era could lead to the tradition of the multi-pint drinking session becoming a less frequent occurrence.

The Netherlands-headquartered company offered advice including promoting half pints, low- and zero-alcohol options and pairing drinks with small plates of food, or risk declines in customer visits and spending.
GLP-1 use has soared as consumers seek a quick, easy solution to rapid weight loss, with 10 million people turning to medication in the US last year, according to research by JP Morgan.

Heineken, the world’s second largest brewer after AB InBev, said the presentation was shared with customers as part of its regular engagement with UK businesses to help them understand how consumer habits are evolving.
“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” the company told Reuters.

Trends the brewer has identified in GLP-1 users include opting for smaller serves, lower alcohol drinks and more premium products, which Heineken said also aligns with broader changes in the market as the habits of younger generations change.
As well as its eponymous lager, Heineken also owns brands such as Amstel, the Mexican lager Sol, and Strongbow cider.

The Guinness maker, Diageo, has told investors that any impact from GLP-1 drugs becoming mainstream should be manageable, while Carlsberg told Reuters that data did not currently support the view that the use of weight-loss drugs affected beer consumption trends.
after newsletter promotion
However, surveys by research companies including Circana, NIQ and KAM have pointed to reduced drinking by GLP-1 users.
According to Heineken, there was almost £14bn in sales of beer in British pubs, bars and restaurants in the year to February, with less than £300m of that from no- and low-alcohol products.

articles.title: Greece joins countries putting age-limits on social media, banning access for kids under 15
articles.summary: Greece has passed legislation banning social media access for children under 15. New rules will come into effect on January 1, 2027, and are designed to protect children's mental health.

image.caption: Greece's lawmakers say 'uncontrolled internet use leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health' and claim the new law will give them back their childhood Image: Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: A bill to "ban the use of online social media services by minors" was passed by a majority vote of the Greek parliament Thursday and will go into effect on January 1, 2027.
The New Democracy party was the only bloc in parliament to support the measure; while opposition parties SYRIZA, Greek Solution, KKE, Niki and Freedom Course voted against it, and PASOK abstained.

Minister of Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Dimitris Papastergiou called the step, "necessary, effective, proportionate and EU-law-compliant," according to Greek newspaper Kathimerini, adding that social media platforms would have until the first of the year to, "determine whether the accounts they host and the services they provide are intended for adults or not."

Pointing to similar age limits on alcohol and tobacco sales to minors, Papastergiou said lawmakers had no time to wait for Brussels to pass "the perfect European law," saying, "let's send the message that the problem of uncontrolled internet use — which leads children to addiction at the expense of their mental health — cannot continue."
Why does Greece want to introduce social media age limits?
The move to put legal age limits on social media use began last year in Australia, with numerous countries around the world swiftly following suit.

Greece is one of seven EU countries seeking to introduce standards for age-verification on social media, which proponents argue will curb the "endless scrolling" that deprives kids of sleep, destroys their attention span and ability to concentrate and keeps them from playing outdoors and spending time with their friends.
Papastergiou defended the use of an app known as "Kid's Wallet" as a means to that end, saying that it had been established according to codes and technical specifications set by the EU.

The minister was emphatic that the app, "does not provide any personal data whatsoever about children or users, other than whether they are over or under 15 years of age — not even their date of birth."

"We owe our children their childhood," said Papastergiou. "That is what we are doing today. We have a duty to protect them. Given the current challenges, the social media bill delivers what society has been waiting for."
EU-wide social media ban for kids?

articles.title: Briton facing forced separation from baby son after Sweden orders his deportation
articles.summary: Exclusive: Photographer Simon Montgomery told ‘state’s interest in regulated immigration’ outweighs his family concerns

blocks.text: A British photographer is facing deportation from Sweden and forced separation from his 16-month-old son after authorities ruled in favour of the country’s immigration interests.

Simon Montgomery’s application to remain after the birth of his son last year was rejected on multiple grounds by the country’s migration agency, a decision that was then upheld by the migration court.

He is appealing to the higher migration court, arguing he has EU freedom of movement rights as his son is a German citizen through his mother. “I am not here because I want to be in Sweden, I am only in Sweden to be with my son,” he said.
The couple separated shortly after the child was born but Montgomery, who grew up without his father in his life, said he was determined to stick around and be there for his newborn.
The pair have legally recognised joint custody, with a parenting agreement that meant his time with his son increased as he got older and no longer needed night time breast-feeding.
He said he saw his son three days a week and took an active part in his care and daily routine with a “stable parenting plan” agreed via discussions with the municipal family law service.
He moved to Sweden after Brexit so was not entitled to any withdrawal agreement residency rights, but applied to stay on the basis he was the father of an EU citizen.

Montgomery said it was shocking that Sweden was prepared to separate a son from his father, even though the child had rights under EU law as well as international conventions. “Everything in Sweden is about the children’s right to both parents,” Montgomery said.
“But this seems to be ignoring all of that, when it comes around to immigration. Sometimes I feel like people don’t know what happens here. That’s why it’s so important to have these stories told.

“Everyone’s so friendly here; society works and things are nice. And when you tell them what’s happened, they just look shocked. They think you must have done something wrong and when I explain I have done nothing wrong they just don’t understand.” \
Montgomery said he was unable to leave the country to see elderly relatives in the UK for fear he would be blocked from returning to be with his son.

“It’s almost like torture in some ways, like having to make these decisions between staying to fulfil your parenting roles and not being able to visit my 98-year-old grandmother back in the UK and say my goodbyes.” he said.

His residency application, made when his son was six months old, was rejected last December by the migration agency on the grounds there was no evidence he had “actual care” for the child, who at that point still stayed overnight with his mother.
It also said he was free to maintain a relationship with his son from afar as he could enter the country visa-free and “still have the opportunity to visit the child in Sweden”.

He appealed against the decision but the court this month sided with the authorities, which assessed, according to the ruling, that the “state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs your interest in the protection of your private and family life in a proportionality assessment”.
after newsletter promotion

Montgomery said he was taken aback by the court’s suggestion he did not need to be in the country full time because he could visit his son by entering the country as a visitor. “Because I can come here visa-free, [they say] it shouldn’t interrupt my parenting ability. That’s crazy because I look after my son three days a week now … and overnights are about to start very soon.”

blocks.caption: Simon Montgomery: ‘Everyone’s so friendly here … when you tell them what’s happened, they just look shocked.’ Photograph: Simon Montgomery

blocks.text: According to court papers, the decision to reject an application for residency and a simultaneous decision that he should be deported was made “primarily on the grounds that he had not demonstrated that he met the conditions for the right of residence as a family member of an EEA citizen”.

His lawyer argued that if he were “forced to leave Sweden, this would undermine the process and create instability for his son”. They added: “His son is an infant and is in a critical attachment phase where it is in his best interest to have both parents physically present and actively involved.”
They argued that the boy’s father’s presence was “particularly important” because his former German partner did not have a family network to rely on if she was sick or at appointments.

“Deportation would constitute a disproportionate interference in their family life,” they said, arguing that the lower migration court had interpreted “actual care” – evidence of a child’s relationship with a parent – “too narrowly on the grounds that the son primarily lives with his mother”.
They alleged forcibly separating a son from his father would violate article 8 of the European convention of human rights.
Montgomery is appealing the case to the higher court but said he wanted to share the story so people understood how immigration law was being implemented.
Sweden’s migration agency has been approached for comment. The German government said it could not comment on the case.

articles.title: Reader Q&A: what’s next for France? Ask our Europe columnists
articles.summary: Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live taking questions from readers about the riots and protests in France at 3pm BST / 4pm CEST today. Send your questions by…
articles.byline: Rokhaya Diallo, Alexander Hurst, Michael Hubbard and Guardian moderators

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2d agoWelcome to the Conversation

blocks.text: Welcome to the Conversation

blocks.caption: The Hôtel de Ville in Limoges, central France, on fire during a weekend of unrest. Photograph: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: After weeks of protests and a weekend of riots in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured, the repercussions for France – for its society and its economy – continue. Allegations of police brutality surfaced, and the violent protests unnerved investors, resulting in a debt sell-off, with borrowing costs rising higher than for Greece. All of this ahead of a hotly contested presidential election that’s now just six months away.

The French government’s escalating financial problems were covered by the Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley who wrote: “France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.”

Columnist Paul Taylor commented that “Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel (Marine) Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy.”

And the Guardian’s editorial noted that “In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.”

What are your views on the riots, their causes and their aftermath? Are they paving a path to the presidency for Le Pen? In his final months in charge, can embattled incumbent Emmanuel Macron meaningfully address the situation in which France finds herself?
France-based Guardian Europe columnists Rokhaya Diallo and Alexander Hurst will be live here at 1500BST today to answer your questions on what happened, why, and where France goes from here.

Wadephul warns shipping disruptions could lead to famine
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that continuing disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea could potentially lead to famine in the global south.

"We're all feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping lanes, whether at the gas station or in the supermarket," he said ahead of a meeting with fellow foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday. "But elsewhere, there is a threat of famine when fertilizers don't arrive in the places where they are essential for basic production."

Wadephul was referring not only to the Iranian closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthi threats to the Bab al-Mandab strait, but also to Russian attacks on shipping in the Black Sea as part of Moscow's ongoing war against Ukraine, one of the world's leading producers of wheat.

"Together, we want to send a signal: we will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias [in Yemen] holding global trade hostage," Wadephul continued.

"The indiscriminatory attacks on free shipping and on neighboring countries must stop. For people across the region who are suffering from hunger, who no longer feel safe in their own homes, the continuing insecurity is not acceptable."

articles.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
articles.summary: One person has died after being swept away by waves in Taiwan's Liuqiu island, authorities say.

blocks.text: Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast.

Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday.
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate.

Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far.
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) .

After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island.
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan,

However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches.
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said.
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains.
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island.
Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather.
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual.
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company.
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines.
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan.
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane.
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea.

This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms.

The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No Palace announcement abolishing Grades 11 and 12
articles.summary: The Department of Education has already debunked the false information, calling it fake news

blocks.text: Claim: The Office of the President announced the official removal of Grades 11 and 12 from the country’s education system.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook user posted a supposed statement from the Office of the President, purportedly signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

It read: “Inanunsyo na ng DepEd [Department of Education] ang pinal na desisyon na tuluyan nang alisin ang Grade 11 at 12 sa ating sistema. Wala na ang Senior High School, kaya magbabago na ang nakasanayang antas ng pagtatapos ng mga mag-aaral.”

(The DepEd has announced its final decision to completely remove Grades 11 and 12 from our system. Senior High School is being phased out, which means the established level at which students complete their education will change.)
The statement continued, “Ang hakbang na ito ay bahagi ng pagbabago ng DepEd upang ituon ang pokus sa ibang antas ng edukasyon.”
(This step is part of the DepEd’s transformation to shift its focus toward other levels of education.)

The post’s author said in the caption, “Good news nga ito. Kung ito ay nalagdaan na, laking ginhawa sa mga magulang at sa mga bata. Sayang naman kasi ang dalawang taon para sa K-12 na ‘yan; ‘di naman nagagamit talaga.”

(This is indeed good news. If it has already been signed, it will be a huge relief for both parents and children. After all, those two years for K-12 are just a waste — they don’t really get put to any actual use.)
The post garnered 1,100 reactions, 352 comments, and 572 shares as of writing.
The facts: There is no official announcement abolishing Grades 11 and 12. The K to 12 program remains in effect as it is mandated by law under the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013.
The misleading post sourced the fake announcement from a TikTok video posted by “Department of the Philippines,” an account posing as a government social media page.

The Department of Education (DepEd) has already debunked the fake post. In an October 21 statement, the agency said, “Fake news ang kumakalat na post sa social media tungkol sa umano’y pagtanggal ng Grade 11 & 12.”
(The post circulating on social media regarding the alleged removal of Grades 11 and 12 is fake news.)
It further reminded the public not to follow pages falsely claiming to be affiliated with the government and to consult only DepEd’s official channels for verified information.
The Presidential Communications Office also denied the statement’s authenticity, according to multiple media reports.
Removing K to 12: There have been countless debates and multiple attempts to remove or revise the K to 12 curriculum.

In June 2025, Senator Jinggoy Estrada filed Senate Bill No. 3001 or the proposed Rationalized Basic Education Act, which sought to remove senior high school in the current learning system and revert back to the four-year secondary curriculum.
In July 2026, Senator Alan Peter Cayetano also voiced opposition to continuing K to 12 and proposed to scale back to K to 10.

Back in April, DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara, one of the primary authors of the law, expressed continued support for the K to 12 system amid calls for its abolition. He said that instead of removing it entirely, the department is focusing on “decongesting” the curriculum, such as prioritizing core subjects and addressing concerns over heavy workload.
Other fact checks: Rappler has previously debunked false claims about removing the K to 12 curriculum:

items: FACT CHECK: No DepEd announcement abolishing Grades 11 and 12
FACT CHECK: K to 12 program not abolished
FACT CHECK: No law passed abolishing K-12 program
FACT CHECK: Arroyo did not say the K to 12 program will be abolished

blocks.text: – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

TOKYO, Japan – Japan said on Friday, October 23, it will set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organizations scramble to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet.

Government and company websites across the world went offline this week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the widely used programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts, forcing website operators to rush to protect or temporarily shut down their systems.

blocks.caption: Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws

blocks.text: Highlighting the extent of the disruption, Japanese mobile carrier SoftBank said on Friday it was suspending its emergency alert system for mobile users. That means customers will not receive early warnings for earthquakes, tsunami alerts or disaster and evacuation information as the system undergoes maintenance to address a PHP vulnerability, SoftBank said.

“An attack can succeed by getting through just one hole … for that reason it’s important we shift our mindset and think from the perspective of the attacker,” Japanese industry minister Ryosei Akazawa said on Friday.
“Defenders also need to make use of AI and respond proactively, staying one step ahead.”

Emergency shutdowns this week from Tokyo to Helsinki of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services marked one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running.
Companies including brokerage Nomura, lender Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, airline ANA, and East Japan Railway (JR East) temporarily suspended some internet services as part of emergency measures.
Japan’s Ministry of Finance, National Tax Agency and Meteorological Agency also suspended some online services.

On Friday, JR East said some group services had resumed while others would be restored once confirmed safe. Nippon Paint said it had applied a security patch as a precaution and its website is back online.
Attackers are likely targeting Japanese businesses for their thorough records, which are no longer protected by a language barrier because of AI, said Eva Chen, CEO of Trend Micro.
Japan has been too comfortable with its existing infrastructure, which it felt was safe enough, she said.

Cybersecurity experts have said AI is helping attackers automate tasks ​from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.

The developers of PHP — a computing language like HTML and Python — released fixes on Wednesday for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI. They urged users to “update immediately.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: PCO execs submit courtesy resignations but Claire Castro to stay -Lino Cayetano
articles.summary: Officials of the Presidential Communications Office have tendered their courtesy resignations, but Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro is sure to keep her post, according to the new PCO chief,…
articles.byline: JEAN MANGALUZ, IVAN MAYRINA, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 4:30pm

Officials of the Presidential Communications Office have tendered their courtesy resignations, but Palace Press Officer Usec. Claire Castro is sure to keep her post, according to the new PCO chief, Sec. Lino Cayetano.
Cayetano called Castro "a treasure" and said he admired the undersecretary's "combative" style in protecting the administration's programs.

"I do not want to say that we are a package deal but Usec. Claire is a treasure in this government; I haven’t seen someone who can articulate so well what this government is doing," Cayetano told reporters, in a mix of Filipino and English.

"I think we’ll work closely together so we can help translate a lot of the issues, a lot of the programs, a lot of the policies of the government... Usec. Claire is a treasure, and I am excited to continue working with her,” he added.
Cayetano has replaced former PCO Secretary Dave Gomez, who missed getting confirmed by the bicameral Commission on Appointments.

Castro has been a staple in the Palace, responding to the administration’s critics and controversies. She was appointed to the post when former Secretary Jay Ruiz was named PCO chief and remained in her post when Gomez replaced Ruiz.
Asked if Cayetano agreed with Castro’s combative side, Cayetano said “yes”.

“In terms of being combative, of protecting what this administration is doing, to be able to explain to the Filipino people why we are doing certain things, I admire Usec. Claire when it comes to that,” Cayetano said.
However, Cayetano stressed that he also wanted to relay more information about the President’s programs and projects to help people.
Cayetano said he hoped that the media was also more critical on topics such as healthcare so that it could be discussed more.
“Please help us na mahimay yung mga storya at yung mga kwento na tingin namin na mahalaga sa sambayanang Pilipino,” Cayetano said.
(Please help us to break down the stories and narratives that we think are important for the Filipino nation.) —NB, GMA News

Remulla said November would mark one year since the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Dela Rosa over his alleged criminal responsibility for killings linked to the Duterte administration's war on drugs.

articles.title: Starlink access for Ukraine limited after Trump’s claims satellite service restored, officials say – Europe live
articles.summary:
The satellite service was still operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences

A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 22m agoDid Trump or Musk restrict Starshield access?
34m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: A quick update from what the Ukrainian and Russian officials are saying this morning on overnight attacks:
Ukraine says Russia targeted energy sites in six different regions. Currently more than 500,000 people are without power.
Russia’s defence ministry confirmed strikes on Vilkovo port in Odesa, a railcar depot in Poltava and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.
Did Trump or Musk restrict Starshield access?

blocks.caption: Jonathan Yerushalmy

blocks.text: Jonathan Yerushalmy
A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink.

The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials.

The US president said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning. What has Trump said?

Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.

Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”
Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.

The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.

He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.

However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”.

What about Musk? Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.
Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.

Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.

Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.
Amid the war of words, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.
Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our Europe live blog, where we’ll begin in Ukraine.

Local authorities reported explosions overnight in Lutsk, a city not far from the Polish border, and in the central Poltava and southern Sumy regions. Russia this morning has also claimed strikes on ships in the Black Sea.
Both sides engaged in heavy strikes yesterday with Russia bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles and Ukraine sending swarms of drones to Moscow.

Trump has declared that Starlink is once again running at full speed across Ukraine after the service was throttled last week -but Ukrainian and European officials say they haven’t seen that speed and functionality resume.

The satellite service was still only operating at a cap of 161km/hr, crippling key air defences and limiting mid-range strikes, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent after Trump’s comments. “Overall, nothing has changed anywhere,” the paper quoted the unnamed official saying.

Elsewhere we’re watching this continued wave of student-led protests across Europe. From Rome to Athens, Madrid and Paris, young people are venting their anger over the lack of resources in schools as well as wider housing and cost-of-living concerns. They’ve often been joined by their teachers in these ralies.

Fearing another weekend of street marches descending into violence and looting, French authorities have banned some protests over the coming days. President Emmanuel Macron, just returned from his mid-week tour to the Gulf states, is due to meet with student leaders around lunchtime in Paris.
It’s Frances Mao today in London, covering for Jakub, stay with me for all the developments.

articles.title: Severe flooding in eastern Spain, while UK hit by first named storm of winter
articles.summary:
Storm Adam brings heavy rain to Valencia, Alicante and Balearic Islands, as Storm Austen gusts strike England and Wales

Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week.…
articles.byline: Megan Davies, Claire Jones and Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Adam brought torrential rain to eastern Spain earlier this week. In Pego, Alicante, 632mm fell in 36 hours with 430mm of this falling in just six hours, while the Valencian town of Olivia received 600mm in 24 hours. As a result, 145 municipalities, approximately 850,000 people, across Valencia and Alicante were placed in a temporary lockdown on Monday due to the severe flooding.

At least five people have died and 500 have been rescued and 2,100 evacuated. The storm also affected the Balearic Islands, with more than 130 incidents recorded in Ibiza including standing water at the airport, which caused some flights to be diverted or suspended. Although the worst of the storm has passed and conditions improving across Valencia and Alicante, local disruption is expected to continue.

The first named storm of the winter for the UK is currently tracking through the Channel. Storm Austen is bringing damaging winds not only to south-west England and Wales, but also south-west Ireland and northern France. Gusts are expected to be around 50-60mph, but some exposed north-western coasts of France could experience winds of up to 80-90mph.

blocks.caption: A car is surrounded by fallen branches in Falmouth, England, after Storm Austen made landfall. Photograph: Hugh R Hastings/Getty Images

blocks.text: Following quickly on from Storm Austen is another deep low pressure system, Storm Boelo, which is expected to track across northern Scotland on Saturday into Sunday. Much of the UK and Ireland will see very unsettled conditions with further damaging winds and heavy and prolonged rain. Western Scotland will face the strongest gusts, but the rest of the UK and Ireland will see 40-55mph winds. Western parts of Ireland will experience 50-60mph winds with up to 70-80mph in exposed parts of north-west Ireland, similar to western Scotland. Again, heavy rain associated with Storm Boelo will reach 10-20mm with as much as 30-60mm in western parts of Ireland, Wales and south-west England. This, on top of the rainfall from Storm Austen, will increase the risk of flooding.

Super Typhoon Champi is headed towards China and Japan over the weekend after passing north-eastern Taiwan on Friday. While it has weakened since Wednesday, it is still a significant typhoon with the equivalent strength of a category 5 hurricane, producing 185mph gusts and sustained winds of 121 mph.Following torrential rain associated with the typhoon this week, up to 900mm of rain is forecast to fall in the mountainous regions of northern and eastern Taiwan from Tuesday to Saturday. As a result, there are school closures, cancelled flights and six-metre waves, with more impacts to come over the next few days.

articles.title: Government won’t put together ‘shopping list’ for public to stockpile for emergency – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Ministers have repeated several warnings in the last 18 months about the threat of hybrid attacks from overseas

Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has been meeting armed forces veterans and Royal British Legion Poppy Appeal collectors to mark the start of the year’s campaign.
Burnham welcomed them to Number 10 North’s office in central Manchester, contrary to the usual convention of making a donation to the cause on the steps of Number 10 in Downing Street.

Good morning from London, where we’re less than a week from Andy Burnham and John Healey’s first budget, and the Government has been telling people to build up 72 hours of supplies in case of a disaster. We’ll be bringing you updates throughout the day. I’m Harry Taylor.

The Government has said that will not be putting together a “shopping list” for the public to buy in anticipation of a disaster, despite launching a campaign on Thursday which told people to stock up on supplies.
Treasury minister James Murray has been on the broadcast round this morning where has been asked about the announcement yesterday that people should assemble three days of supplies.
It’s come after repeated warnings in the last 18 months about cyber-attacks from overseas that could affect key systems.
It’s also timely as 32 Government services were taken offline yesterday after millions of attempts to exploit a weakness in numerous’ websites coding.
However Murray told Times Radio this morning: “This is not about the Government sending out a shopping list to everyone in the country.

“This is about putting the right information there on the government website, having an information campaign so that people are aware about it and then people taking the right choices for themselves about what they need to make sure they have supplies of at home.”
Meanwhile it’s five days until Healey’s budget, and Murray was asked on BBC Radio 4 whether he would be reducing red tape for business.
He said cutting “pointless bureaucracy” was “at the heart of what the Chancellor is going to be thinking about”.
Healey said the Treasury would aim to cut £800m of red tape for businesses at the budget, including reduced reporting requirements.

articles.title: Why Quebec's strategic reserve of maple syrup is running dry
articles.summary: Quebec maple syrup producers say the province's strategic reserve will be "completely depleted" by the end of February. What's going on?

image.caption: Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec, the group that represents nearly 13,500 maple syrup producers in the province, says the strategic reserve it oversees will be 'completely depleted' by the end of February. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: It's roughly the size of 53 Olympic swimming pools, but the world's only strategic reserve of maple syrup — spread out across three Quebec warehouses — is running dry.

Producteurs et productrices acéricoles du Québec (PPAQ), the group that represents nearly 13,500 maple syrup producers in the province and oversees the reserve, said its stockpile will be "completely depleted" by the end of February.

According to PPAQ president Luc Goulet, that's largely because demand for Canadian maple syrup has soared around the world, including in the United States — the $1.2-billion industry's largest export market.
There has been a "sharp rise in exports," Goulet said in an interview with Radio-Canada's Midi-Info radio program this week.
"We have major challenges with the strategic reserve, which needs to be replenished. But we also have the challenge of developing our sector" to meet increased demand, he said.
So what exactly is going on, and should breakfast lovers be worried? Here's what we know.
Why more people are choosing Canadian maple syrup — instead of American
First, how does the reserve work?

Quebec's maple syrup producers set up the reserve in 2000 to try to stabilize supplies and prices, said Maurice Doyon, a professor at Laval University in Quebec City who specializes in agri-food economics.
The province produces 90 per cent of Canada's maple syrup and more than 70 per cent of the world’s supply.

items: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report

blocks.text: But the industry is heavily dependent on weather conditions: maple trees need regular springtime cycles of freezing and unfreezing to produce sap, which is transformed into syrup.
Is your maple syrup real or fake? It’s not that hard to tell
Before the reserve existed, Quebec producers would have to lower prices when supplies outpaced demand. Conversely, prices would go up when demand exceeded supply after bad harvests.
"The idea was to manage that a bit better," Doyon told CBC.
A quota system was also put in place in the early 2000s to regulate production levels.
Today, the reserve can hold as many roughly 60 million kilograms, or 218,000 barrels, of maple syrup. "When there's a bad harvest, [they] can dip into that reserve to supply the market," Doyon said.
So did Quebec have a bad harvest?
No. This time, the reserve is running dry because Quebec's authorized maple syrup processors — who buy, bottle, process and market the sticky stuff — appear to have bought out what was there.
The reserve held 39.4 million pounds (around 18 million kilograms) of maple syrup in February, the PPAQ said.

In an email to CBC News, the organization said while it expects the reserve to be depleted by the end of February "once all volumes under contract have been delivered to buyers," the overall supply remains similar to what it was a year ago.
"Inventories have simply shifted from the strategic reserve to buyers' warehouses. We estimate that buyers' inventories have increased by more than 35 million pounds [about 15.8 million kilograms]."
Cans of maple syrup sit at the Bistro La dent Sucre sugar shack in St. Eustache, Que., on April 6, 2021. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)
Why would processors buy from the reserve?

Doyon said processors don't have a strong incentive to dip into the reserve when it's full because they need to pay both for the syrup and to store what they don't immediately sell. But when the reserve is low, they are in competition with each other to secure their supply.
"It's initiated by the fact that the reserve is low," said Doyon, who likened buying up the reserve to taking out insurance.
"If disaster strikes — in other words, a bad harvest — they're going to be happy to have taken those precautions."
The Conseil de l'industrie de l'érable (CIE), which represents authorized processors in Quebec, said they "maintain inventories in their own warehouses to meet market needs throughout the year."
Asked how much maple syrup the processors have stored right now, the group told CBC it couldn't comment, citing confidential business practices.
"In a context where market growth is putting increased pressure on supply, our members must plan their needs flexibly to ensure business continuity and meet demand."
Why is there increased pressure on supply?
Both PPAQ and CIE say there has been a surge in global demand for maple syrup.
Canadian exports of maple products increased by 15.8 per cent in 2025 compared to the previous year, according to data provided by CIE. That followed a 9.3 per cent jump from 2023 to 2024.
Statistics Canada also said $844.2 million worth of Canadian maple products were exported last year — a 17.2 per cent increase from the previous year.
Inside the world’s only maple syrup reserve
What's fuelling demand internationally?

PPAQ's Goulet pointed to several factors, including uncertainty linked to U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs, which have not hit the maple industry yet, as well as success in promoting Canadian maple syrup abroad.
Sixty-five per cent of all Canadian exports in 2025 went to the U.S., the CIE said. The next largest market was Germany at seven per cent, followed by the U.K. at five per cent.

items: International demand for Canadian maple syrup surges amid U.S. trade war
Why more people are choosing Canadian maple syrup — instead of American

blocks.text: Growing demand for "natural sweeteners" also has been credited with making maple syrup more popular, according to experts.
Will Quebec run out of maple syrup?
The PPAQ says it's not time to panic.

It said the processors' inventories coupled with an increase in the number of taps being installed across Quebec mean "there are no concerns about market supply in 2027, even if the upcoming crop is not particularly strong."
"That said, we are hoping for an exceptional season so that we can replenish the reserve."
Barrels of pasteurized maple syrup are stored at a strategic reserve warehouse in Plessisville, Que., on March 6. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
But will 'an exceptional season' be possible?
We can't say for sure. Doyon said there are ultimately only two ways to get more maple syrup: get more sap out of the trees that are already tapped or tap more trees.
But both those things could be easier said than done, said Guillaume Moreau, another professor at Laval University who specializes in maple syrup production.
Tapping more trees is a challenge because maple syrup producers are competing with other interests — notably the hardwood lumber industry — to gain access to forests on public lands in Quebec.
Climate change also has created new challenges for producers, who have seen harvest periods gradually shift earlier in the year due to fluctuating temperatures, Moreau said.
"We're having trouble to know ahead of time whether it will be a bad year."
And with the reserve now sitting empty and climate change fuelling uncertainty, "we're ultimately at the mercy of that uncertainty," he told CBC.

After a record fiscal 2025, customs officers on track to search even more devices

Searches of electronic devices such as phones and laptops of travellers entering the United States are up more than 32 per cent this year and are on track to set a new record, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data obtained by CBC News.

The numbers show that during the first three quarters of its 2026 fiscal year, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, CBP officers searched 52,080 electronic devices. During the same period the previous year, CBP searched 39,251 devices.
In fact, CBP searched almost as many devices in the first three quarters of 2026 as it did during the entire 2025 fiscal year, when a record 55,424 devices were searched.

According to CBP, 47,517 were basic searches, which can be done by an officer without any reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing. Another 4,564 were advanced searches, which allow an officer who believes there is a reasonable suspicion of an activity that violates the law or a national security concern to analyze and/or copy the contents of an electronic device.

items: Canada updates travel advice to warn of U.S. border officers' power to search electronic devices

blocks.text: However, the customs agency won't reveal what percentage of the searches took place at the northern border with Canada or the southern border with Mexico. Nor would it provide a breakdown between searches at airports versus land borders or a breakdown by land border posts.

It also would not say how many travellers entered the U.S. during the first three quarters of 2026 or how many searches targeted U.S. citizens versus non-U.S. citizens — numbers it generally provides in its annual reports.

Jessica Turner, public affairs officer with CBP, said in 2025, the searches only affected a small fraction of the 419 million travellers who entered the U.S. and searches of electronic devices "remains exceedingly rare."

"CBP's border searches of electronic device numbers are consistent with increases since 2021, and year-over-year only 0.01 per cent of travellers have their devices searched," Turner wrote in an emailed response.
"These searches are conducted to detect digital contraband, terrorism-related content and information relevant to visitor admissibility, all of which play a critical role in national security."

However, Esha Bhandari, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Speech, Privacy and Technology Project, says the increase in searches of electronic devices by U.S. border officials requires more congressional oversight and accountability.

"It's hard to speculate on the reasons for the increase because the government doesn't explain it," she said. "But I think what we're seeing is a classic example of when the government has the power to do something, it will exercise that authority to the detriment of travellers' privacy."
Bhandari said the aggregate numbers provided by the U.S. government make it difficult to "really get a handle on what's going on."
However, she said the anecdotal evidence her group hears is "certainly troubling."

"They're often asked questions at the border about their political opinions or perhaps their writing or things related to their religious practice that might suggest that's the reason they've been singled out for a search," she said.

In January, CBP updated its guidelines governing searches of electronic devices at the border to spell out that it included devices like flash drives, SIM cards, GPS systems, unmanned aircraft systems, vehicle infotainment systems and smart watches. It also added smuggling narcotics, firearms or other goods and transnational theft of proprietary information and digital contraband to the list of crimes the searches are designed to detect.

But Bhandari says the new directives only changed "a few procedures at the margins." She believes the increase in searches may have more to do with advances in technology and the failure of federal courts to put limits on the government's authority to conduct them.

items: U.S. customs searched a record number of electronic devices last year
Canadians caught in crossfire as searches of devices rise at U.S. borders

blocks.text: Laura Dawson, executive director of the Future Borders Coalition, which focuses on cross-border issues, said the increase in searches is difficult to assess without knowing where they took place and the number of people who travelled to the U.S. during that period.
"These searches are taking place not just at land borders, but also at seaports, at airports and there's lots of people coming in and out. And we had World Cup this summer," she said.
"It could be a greater diversity of traveller coming in."
Dawson said she is also seeing more focus on border security and more co-operation between Canadian and U.S. border services in areas such as human smuggling and the Ryan Wedding case.

items: Ryan Wedding murder trial delayed to 2027 due to 'unusual and complex' case

blocks.text: "Having more scrutiny at the border is actually a positive in many ways," she said.

While Canadians may be alarmed by stories shared on social media of device searches at the border, Dawson points out that the practice is still rare. She said one in 9,000 border crossings result in a U.S. inspection and one in 14,000 crossings result in a search on the Canadian side of the border.

In recent years, Canadian officials have searched a much smaller percentage of devices at the border than their U.S. counterparts and the numbers have been dropping. Canada Border Services Agency officials say statistics on the number of electronic device searches carried out in 2026 are not yet available.

Award-winning reporter Elizabeth Thompson covers Parliament Hill & the federal government. A veteran of the Montreal Gazette, Sun Media & iPolitics, she works in the CBC's Parliamentary bureau, specializing in investigative reporting & data journalism. She's also a member of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to ElizabethThompson.26
