articles.title: A polarized Brazil heads to presidential vote Sunday with economy, corruption top of mind
articles.summary: Frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation driving voting choices as Brazil heads to presidential run-off on Sunday, Oct. 25.

image.caption: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left, is running for re-election against Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party. (REUTERS)

blocks.text: During a recent Bible study service in the Río de Janeiro neighbourhood of Vila Isabel, the congregation recited a prayer about God and being faithful.
Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, one of the congregants, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens.

"We have ... expectations that our country’s leadership would be concerned with meeting essential needs — such as health care and education —and that, at the very least, these areas would be properly cared for," she said.

Still undecided about who to vote for, Andrade said she was leaning toward Flávio Bolsonaro, the 45 year-old senator son of Jair Bolsonaro, the former Brazilian president convicted of plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Brazil's former president gets 27 years for plotting a coup in 2022 | Hanomansing Tonight
Andrade said Flávio Bolsonaro was a better candidate than his father.
"Bolsonaro … may waver between one extreme and the other at times, but I see a genuine interest on his part in finding balance," she said.
"I don't know if he'll succeed, but I'm not particularly concerned — his father engaged in corruption to the point of ending up in prison."
Regina da Silva Andrade, 38, centre, said that while she believed God was in charge of the universe, Brazil's elected officials had a duty to care for the country's citizens. (Douglas Engle/CBC)
Presidential race 'never this close,' journalist says

Flávio Bolsonaro — campaigning on tax cuts, a hard line on crime and family values — emerged from the first round of voting on Oct. 4 in Brazil's presidential election with about 2.2 million more votes than Lula, the 80-year-old incumbent.
Recent polls have shown the race between the two candidates tightening.
"It's really a toss of a coin," said Pedro Doria, editor of MEIO media group in Río de Janeiro.
Still, Doria said no presidential candidate who came in second after the first round of voting has ever won an election since 1989 — when the current electoral system was put in place.
"But it was never this close. Flávio's difference against Lula was 1.9 percentile points. This is basically nothing."

items: Lula and Bolsonaro head to run-off in Brazil's presidential election

blocks.text: Doria said that the Brazilian population is heavily polarized, and some voters are more motivated to vote against a candidate than in support of someone they believe in.
"A third of Lula's voters are not voting for Lula, they are voting against Bolsonaro," said Doria. "Half of Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's voters are voting against Lula, not for Flávio."

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's Centre for International Relations Research, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro. (Courtesy of Marsílea Gombata)

Marsílea Gombata, a researcher with the University of Sao Paulo's Centre for International Relations Research, said frustrations around corruption and feelings of personal financial stagnation have driven many voters to cast ballots for Bolsonaro despite the actions of his father and the candidate's own record of controversy.

Bolsonaro has in the past been tied to paramilitary groups — he praised them in a two decade-old speech while a state deputy, and his office once employed the mother and wife of the founder of a paramilitary group linked to the killing of a human rights activist.

items: See the Amazon rainforest wildfires that have politicians pointing fingers amid Brazil presidential elections

blocks.text: Bolsonaro's father's coup-plotting conviction — which included allegations there were plans to assassinate Lula — and subsequent 27-year sentence has had limited impact on Flávio Bolsonaro's support, said Gombata.
"We can see that it doesn't matter to people."

While Lula, who previously served two presidential terms between 2003 and 2011, strengthened and reintroduced social programs in his last term to help the poor such as Bolsa Familia, which provides conditional direct cash transfers to families, a large swath of the population has felt left out, said Gombata.
The lower middle class, where many work a second job in the gig economy, has felt "betrayed" by Lula's promises of prosperity that, they believe, never materialized for them.
"They were hoping for a better life, for their children, but it didn't happen and today life is more difficult," said Gombata.
Bolsonaro's promises of tax cuts for fuel, electricity and transport, as well as reductions in government spending appeals to this segment of the population, she said.
Paulo Coelho, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, 64, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro. (Douglas Engle/CBC)

The 2014 Operation Carwash investigation, which ensnared several top officials in Lula's Workers Party and Lula himself — until the Supreme Court overturned his corruption-related conviction in 2021 — still casts a long shadow, Gombata said.
"We are still living those consequences … the theme of corruption is a big one."
Both candidates facing corruption probes
Bolsonaro has been side-swiped during the election campaign by his own corruption allegations.

It recently emerged that Bolsonaro requested and received millions of dollars for a documentary about Jair Bolosonaro from a key player in a major bank fraud case. Flávio is also under investigation in relation to the case.
However, Lula has faced his own troubles. His son is under a separate influence peddling and corruption probe ordered by the Supreme Court, Reuters reported.
Paulo Coelho, 64, who runs the Cavacas Sporting Goods store in Río de Janeiro, said he’s voting on the economy Sunday and his ballot will go to Bolsonaro.
"Everyone is worried about slowing economic activity in Brazil," he said.
"Flávio Bolsonaro has an economic plan and vision that I am more aligned with."
The Brazil election's U.S. factor

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries a Bolsonaro government will sever the social safety nets that have kept many people from misery.
"I have three children, ages 15, 11 and five, and I don’t want to jeopardize their future," she said.
"There is a real risk to our population given the stances they've taken on social issues."

Aline Vieria, 38, who runs a community dance program for women, said she's voting for Lula because she worries that a Bolsonaro government will lead to a severing of social safety nets. (Douglas Engel/CBC)
Solange Marquez, vice-president of policy with the Canadian Council for the Americas, says Sunday's results could impact Brazil's relationship with the United States.

The close relationship between the Bolsonaro family — Flávio is one of three brothers — and the U.S. administration of Donald Trump could lead to an escalation of U.S. military involvement in South America through boots on the ground in Brazil in joint security operations against armed drug trafficking groups, said Marquez.
"I think [Flávio] Bolsonaro is eager to open the door to Donald Trump in exchange for a better economic, commercial relationship with Washington."
Trump threatens 50% tariff on Brazil over Bolsonaro trial
U.S. boots on Brazilian soil is something that worries retiree Carlos Vitor, 65, who voted twice for the elder Bolsonaro. This time, he says, he's voting for Lula.
"I’m afraid that the United States might invade Brazil because of the drug traffickers," he said.
Vitor said a Flávio win will magnify the deep divisions that currently exist within the country and possibly lead to violence.
"The left, they're going to fight. If Flávio wins, they're going to fight," he said.
"Will this place turn into a civil war? For sure."

articles.title: Yaga, Crave's witchy new show, is full of myth, legend and Canadian stars. Here's what to know before watching
articles.summary: There's big buzz around Yaga, the new Crave show premiering Friday and featuring Hudson Williams in his first major role since Heated Rivalry. But the entire cast of the witchy series is packed with…

image.caption: Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson Williams star in Yaga, the witchy new streaming series filmed on Vancouver Island. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

There's big buzz around Yaga, the new Crave show premiering Friday and featuring Hudson Williams in his first major role since Heated Rivalry. But the entire cast of the witchy series is packed with Canadian talent, including Carrie-Anne Moss and stars from Schitt's Creek and Letterkenny. We've got a primer featuring lore from the show and insight from its creator.
Heated Rivalry heartthrob is providing buzz, but the series is packed with powerful women, Canadian talent

There are two kinds of people who will be watching the premier of Yaga on Crave this weekend: Hudson Williams fans who've been waiting for his next major project after Heated Rivalry, and anyone who treats spooky season like a major religious holiday.
Don't worry, it's OK to identify as both.

The eight-episode half-hour drama is getting a lot of attention because of the aforementioned hockey romance heartthrob, but the entire cast reads like a who's who of Canadian talent: Carrie-Anne Moss from The Matrix, Noah Reid of Schitt's Creek, Clark Backo from Letterkenny, even Anne of Green Gables herself, Megan Follows.

The series promises a sexy mystery — with Williams playing two separate characters — set in the fictional town of Whittock (filmed on misty Vancouver Island), where one wealthy family is in control, but witches aren't afraid to exert power.
Or as cast member Sheila McCarthy put it, "It's sort of Dexter with witches."
The first two episodes drop on Friday, with subsequent episodes released weekly until the two-episode season finale on Nov. 27.

From left, Noah Reid, Ezra Franky, Sam Krochmal, Kat Sandler, Clark Backo, Carrie-Anne Moss, Sheila McCarthy, Hudson Williams and Megan Follows attend the premiere of Yaga at the Toronto International Film Festival. (Darren Eagles/2026 Getty Images)
Theatre roots
Before it became a streaming series, Yaga was a play that premiered at Toronto's Tarragon Theatre in September 2019.
The play, which was nominated for a Dora Award, was part folklore and part whodunit, featuring three actors playing 17 parts on a largely bare stage.
It was written and directed by Kat Sandler who now serves as writer and show runner for the streaming series.

"To get to expand the world with such a brilliant, beautiful, wonderful cast and all these creatives really makes the story, I think, sing," she told CBC News on the TIFF red carpet at the Yaga premiere. "It feels really right as television."

items: TIFF's at a turning point — but how will the film festival's new focus on dealmaking affect fans?

blocks.text: Fun fact: Noah Reid, who plays private detective Charlie Rapp in the Crave series, said he was supposed to be part of that original theatre performance, but couldn't do it because it conflicted with Schitt's Creek.
Viewers may not recognize much of lovable Patrick from Schitt's Creek in his Yaga character, though.
"We have joked with some of the producers that this is like my dark era and I'm enjoying it," he said.
Kat Sandler wrote and directed Yaga when it was play in Toronto, and serves as the show runner for the new streaming series on Crave. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDb)

In the play, the character now played by Hudson Williams was just one person. But Sandler said they had decided to split that role into two parts well before Williams skyrocketed to international fame on Heated Rivalry.
"We needed more suspects and a fuller town … and it just was a really amazing kismet that he was available and wanted to come and play in the woods with us," she said.
Baba Yaga: the folklore
The female character Baba Yaga comes from Slavic folklore. She's the classic crone who lives alone in the woods in a hut that stands on giant chicken feet.
Sometimes she's an evil witch who eats children. Other times, she's a wise sage helping a hero on his journey.

The tale of Baba Yaga is included in the 1992 best-seller Women Who Run With the Wolves. In that telling, the Baba Yaga character is about facing darkness, aging and death — and transforming into a source of mature feminine power.
Carrie-Anne Moss seduces Hudson Williams in Yaga

That book is also partly responsible for Carrie-Anne Moss's involvement with Yaga. It's one of her favourite books, and she had just been re-reading it when she received a heartfelt letter from Sandler asking her to be part of the show.
She took it as a sign.
"I take those kinds of things quite literally," Moss told Eli Glasner in an interview for The National. "Things like that have always guided my life."
Women who run the show

The story of Yaga is about powerful women in front of the camera — and behind it. For Clark Backo, who plays Sergeant Carson, a local police officer reluctantly paired with Rapp, that shouldn't seem exceptional.
"It's my everyday life. I just finally get to reflect that on TV," she said. "I wish I could say it was more of a big deal, but I am surrounded by powerful women. My mom's a powerful woman."

items: From The Matrix to Yaga, Carrie-Anne Moss still believes rejection can open the right door

blocks.text: As showrunner, Sandler had high praise for the acclaimed Canadian cast, who she described as really collaborative, generous and kind.

Up-and-coming actor Sam Krochmal said he was struck by how humble and egoless the more seasoned professionals were. "I think there was this unspoken buy-in that everyone was really excited and really understood and saw Kat's vision."
Also lining up behind that vision: Alanis Morissette, who covered Donovan's Season of the Witch for the show and shared it on Instagram with the hashtag #witchesunite.
So how is Sandler feeling ahead of Yaga?
"I'm feeling unhinged, I'm feeling powerful, I'm feeling feminine. I'm feeling sexy and I'm feeling like it's about time we had this show here."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.
With files from Griffin Jaeger and Eli Glasner

articles.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North again
articles.summary: South Korea is attempting to mutually determine the land border with North Korea amid military incidents and escalating tensions.

image.caption: The DMZ is the four-kilometer-wide strip of land that has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday proposed military talks with North Korea in an attempt to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels.
The ministry said it had proposed talks last November to resolve differences over the line, and reduce the risk of accidental deaths, but Pyongyang had not responded.
Why is South Korea proposing talks with the north?

The latest proposal, announced by Deputy Minister for National Defense Policy Kim Hong-cheol, follows a landmine blast in the demiliterized zone (DMZ) in September that injured three South Korean soldiers.

North Korean troops have been building tactical roads, fences and been laying mines in the DMZ in the recent years. South Korea's Kim said the North's troops have repeatedly crossed the line in the process.
Seoul's military also concluded that North Korea had buried mines south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) which caused the recent blast. Pyongyang has rejected those findings.
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs
Avoiding future incidents on the Korean peninsula

Miliatry tensions between the two Koreas has been escalating. Just days ago, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong announced that Pyongyang had moved new troops into "firing position" along the border.
She later said the North would also place loudspeakers on standby along the border, a repeated move of aggression aimed at harassing South Korean soldiers and villages along the border.
Jin Yong-sung, chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, also ordered the military to "respond with firm resolve" should North Korea use Seoul's actions as a pretext for aggressive action.

It is difficult to predict "what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed," the South's Defense Ministry said on Friday, adding that they hoped for a positive response from their rival neighbor.
It also proposed the option of "three-way talks involving the United Nations Command would also be possible."

articles.title: Retail sales in Great Britain fall as struggling households cut back
articles.summary: Latest negative economic update comes as John Healey is due to announce budget next week

blocks.text: Retail sales in Great Britain fell more steeply than expected last month, the latest negative economic update before the chancellor, John Healey, announces his budget next week.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold fell 0.4% month on month in September, much steeper than economists’ consensus expectations of a 0.1% fall.

The drop in sales, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter wear because of unseasonably warm weather last month, comes as figures show that consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate since the Covid pandemic.

While retail sales dropped across almost all sectors of the industry, the volume of motor fuel sold soared 2.2% month on month in September despite prices at the pump soaring to record highs, returning to levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East.
In value terms the 6.1% increase in fuel sales is the biggest month-on-month increase since 10.9% was recorded in March, the month immediately after the start of the US-Iran conflict.
Stripping out the boost from fuel, retail sales slumped 0.7% month on month in September, much worse than the 0.1% fall forecast by the City.

“October’s sharp fall in consumer confidence and the dip in retail sales volumes in September show that times are getting tougher for households just as the all-important festive period for retailers is just around the corner,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics. “This supports our view that both real consumer spending and real GDP will grind to a halt in [this year’s fourth quarter and the first quarter next year]. And this fall in consumer confidence is also the kind of thing that makes the prime minister less likely to call an early election soon.”
Non-store retailing, predominantly online sales, fell 2.2% month on month, the biggest percentage fall across the retail sector.

Textile, clothing and footwear stores recorded a 0.9% fall, household goods retailers were hit by a 0.5% sales slump, while supermarkets dipped 0.4%, partly because of poor sales of clothing ranges due to the weather.
The only sector to record an increase in sales last month – apart from automotive fuel – was department stores, where the volume of goods bought rose 0.2% compared with September.
after newsletter promotion
The fall in monthly sales follows a bumper August, with the ONS revising figures up from a 0.5% monthly rise to 0.7%, helping quarterly sales increase to 0.7% year on year.

“Retail sales grew in the latest quarter with growth led by motor fuel, which, despite recent price increases at the pump, have now returned to monthly sales levels last seen before the start of the conflict in the Middle East,” said Hannah Finselbach, a senior statistician at the ONS. “Food and drink sales also contributed to growth in the quarter, partly helped by the warm weather and the World Cup, although they fell back slightly in September.”

articles.title: Will the Senate consider a P2-B budget cut for 2027?
articles.summary: 'If we are asking other government agencies to exercise fiscal discipline and justify every peso of their budget, then the Senate should lead by example,' says Senate finance committee chair JV…

blocks.text: SENATE PRESIDENT. Senate President Win Gatchalian opens the second regular session of the 20th Congress on July 27, 2026.
Angie de Silva/Rappler

'If we are asking other government agencies to exercise fiscal discipline and justify every peso of their budget, then the Senate should lead by example,' says Senate finance committee chair JV Ejercito

At the hearing of the Senate‘s proposed budget for 2027 on Thursday, October 22, Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr. presented “permutations” of the upper chamber’s budget for next year: P7.7 billion, as provided under the proposed National Expenditure Program (NEP), to as low as P2 billion less that amount, or P5.7 billion.

Bantug said that the various permutations of the Senate budget he presented “will enable the Senate to sustain its constitutional mandate, to legislate effectively, provide accessible and transparent public service, modernize institutional system, maintain responsible management of public resources, while sustaining personnel requirements, essential operating needs, and the delivery of legislative and public-facing services.”

After Bantug’s presentation, Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito said: “In the Senate, we are practicing what we preach. We are one of the very few agencies that has a lower budget for 2027…because of the very limited fiscal space. We practice austerity.”
He was apparently referring to the P7.7-billion Senate budget for 2027 under the proposed NEP, which is 10% lower than its 2026 budget.

Less than 20 minutes into the hearing, Ejercito recommended the proposed budgets of the Senate, Senate Electoral Tribunal (P325.1 million), and the Commission on Appointments (P1.1 billion) for plenary consideration.
After the hearing on Thursday, the question left on many people’s minds is, will the Senate indeed practice austerity and give itself a budget cut?

When asked if the various permutations of the Senate budget presented at the Thursday hearing would still be considered during the plenary deliberations even after the P7.7-billion budget was approved at the committee level, Ejercito said on Friday, October 23: “Yes, that’s correct. The P7.7 billion budget was approved at the committee level for plenary consideration. However, it is not yet final.”
“The possible P2-billion reduction is still on the table and will be subject to further discussions during the plenary deliberations,” Ejercito said.
He reiterated that the Senate wants to “lead by example.”

“If we are asking other government agencies to exercise fiscal discipline and justify every peso of their budget, then the Senate should lead by example. We have to hold ourselves to the same standards,” he added.

Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, chairperson of the Senate committee on accounts, shared the same view. While responding to questions on the Supreme Court decision deeming certain provisions of the 2024 and 2025 national budgets unconstitutional, Lacson said on Friday that the eyed Senate budget cut is intended to set an example for the House of Representatives, particularly in the wake of the SC ruling.

“We will reduce about P2 billion just to set the trend for the House to follow. The House added P5 billion but the Senate is considering reducing its proposed budget from the NEP by P2 billion,” Lacson said.

Should the upper chamber decide to do so, it won’t be the first for this budget season. The Department of Budget and Management has moved to slash its own 2027 budget request by P2.7 billion. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DILG offers P50-M reward for arrest of 'armed and dangerous' Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: The Department of the Interior and Local Government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who according to Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic"…

blocks.text: The Department of the Interior and Local Government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who according to Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla is now considered "armed and dangerous."

Remulla bared the bounty on Friday, two days after he said Dela Rosa is under the protection of a group in Mindanao, with whom the government is initiating negotiations. He said an operation to get the former Philippine National Police chief could result in 10,000 deaths.

“We have given him all the courtesy that can be afforded as a senator of the Republic of the Philippines, but he showed nothing but cowardice by going into and remaining in hiding. Senator Bato mistook my gesture of negotiation as a sign of weakness," Remulla said in a news conference.
GMA News Online is reaching out to Dela Rosa's camp and will publish his side as soon as it is available.
'Co-perpetrator'

Dela Rosa, who has a pending warrant of arrest from the International Criminal Court for charges of crimes against humanity, was placed under the protective custody of the Senate when Senator Alan Peter Cayetano was Senate President on May 11. He last attended the Senate session on May 13.
He is charged before the ICC as a co-perpetrator with former President Rodrigo Duterte for cases of murder and attempted murder tied to the war on drugs of the latter's administration.
Both Duterte and Dela Rosa have denied the allegations against them.
Dela Rosa left the Senate before dawn on May 14, hours after a shooting incident in the chamber's premises.
Cayetano has since been replaced by Senator Sherwin Gatchalian as Senate President.

"It's time for the gloves to come off. It’s time to give justice to his victims. As of today, Senator Bato will be considered armed and dangerous. We are placing a bounty of P50 million for his capture,” Remulla said.
'No mercy'
If he chose not to turn himself in to authorities, Remulla said in a text message that law enforcement would show “no mercy.”
According to Remulla, a task force has already been formed to track down and arrest the former police general.
Dela Rosa was given 10 days to surrender.
PNP chief Police Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said the police force is prepared for whatever outcome the senator’s arrest might bring, whether peaceful or armed.
“The Philippine National Police is always ready for that, whether peaceful or it will come to an armed confrontation. Of course, we would like to have a peaceful confrontation,” Nartatez said.

“Pag sinabing madugo, it is our assumption kasi nga meron kang senator at maraming nagco-coddle, and the way we look at the area… these are secluded areas and diyan nangyayari ‘yung armed conflict before and so sinsabi natin na assumption that is madugo,” he added.

(When we say bloody, it is an assumption because you are dealing with a senator and many are coddling him. The way we look at the area... these are secluded areas where armed conflict has occurred before, which is why we assume it could turn bloody.)
'Option to surrender'
Nartatez explained that making such an assumption is necessary to craft a solid contingency plan.
He clarified that law enforcement agencies are not negotiating with Dela Rosa, but are merely giving him the option to surrender.
“Hindi naman tayo nakikipag-negotiate. We are giving him the option to surrender. Yon ang pinakamaganda, di ba, mag-surrender?” Nartatez said.
(We are not negotiating. We are giving him the option to surrender. That is the best outcome, isn't it—for him to surrender?)
'Hiding places'

At present, Nartatez said authorities have already searched and are continuously monitoring areas believed to be the senator's hiding spots, including several locations in Western Mindanao, Eastern Mindanao, Bicol, Central Luzon, Metro Manila, and Southern Tagalog.
Nartatez did not identify specific locations, but noted that PNP intelligence operatives had scoured potential hideouts across these regions.
The PNP chief warned that any group proven to have coddled and hidden Dela Rosa will face the full consequences of the law. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Senate to cut own 2027 budget by P2 billion -- Lacson
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson said Friday the Senate intends to reduce about P2 billion from its own proposed budget for fiscal year 2027 "to set an example" for the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 3:19pm
Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson said Friday the Senate intends to reduce about P2 billion from its own proposed budget for fiscal year 2027 "to set an example" for the House of Representatives.
Lacson, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Accounts, said this in light of the Supreme Court decision declaring the 2024, 2025, and portions of 2026 national budgets unconstitutional.

"Nagkasundo kami nina Senate President (and I agreed) the other day… we will reduce our budget, 'yung Senate budget, by about P2 billion pesos from the [National Expenditure Program]," he said in an ambush interview.
"Magbabawas kami just to set the example or set the trend for the House to follow because ang House, nagdagdag sila ng P5 billion," he added.
(We will cut our own budget just to set an example or establish a trend for the House to follow because the House added P5 billion in its proposed budget.)
Under the 2027 NEP, the Senate originally sought a P7.7-billion budget for next year.
Lacson assured that the planned budget cuts would not affect the services of the upper chamber.
"Wala naman, kasi mayroon pang unused eh na puwede pang gamitin," he added.
(Nothing will be affected because we still have an unused budget that we could still utilize.)
He also said the release of the SC decision was timely, considering that reforms in the budgeting process are currently needed.

In a landmark decision, the SC struck down the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 after Congress added appropriations beyond what the President had recommended in the National Expenditure Program.

Specifically, the 2024 budget was voided due to a P449.5-billion increase in unprogrammed appropriations, while the 2025 budget was struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
The High Court likewise deemed as unconstitutional Special Provisions 1(a) and (b) of Chapter XLIII in the 2026 GAA, which authorized unprogrammed appropriations.
Recall budget bill?
Lacson also expressed belief that recalling the House's version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) is not the solution to the SC decision.

"Ang effect niyan, magre-reenact tayo, which is worse… Hindi 'yan ang solution. The solution is for the Senate to really scrutinize and cut all the fat doon sa ipinadala na GAB ng House," he explained.

(If the House recalls its budget bill, it would result in a reenacted budget, which is worse… That is not the solution. The solution is for the Senate to really scrutinize and cut all the fat from the GAB transmitted by the House.)
Lacson said House members who have concerns regarding the proposed 2027 budget should instead reach out to their own colleagues who will be members of the bicameral conference committee.
Members of the Makabayan bloc earlier urged the recall of the House-approved P7.2-trillion proposed national budget for 2027, following the release of the SC decision.
Both Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian and Senate finance panel chairperson JV Ejercito have expressed apprehensions regarding the petition to recall the House budget bill. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Germany sit out FIFA Under-15 World Cup as Russia return
articles.summary: Germany is one a handful of FIFA's 211 nations to refuse an invitation to play at the inaugural under-15 World Cup. The tournament will also mark Russia's return to the FIFA fold.

image.caption: The U15 World Cup has been met with some criticism, and not just because of Russia's participationImage: Patrick Reichardt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the under-15 boys World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards. It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before.

For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young.

"At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read.

"More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group.

"In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market."
Rejection continuation of German caution, Moukoko an exception

The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development. While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga, players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old.
That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process.
Youssoufa Moukoko: Bundesliga's youngest-ever player

But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup. Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen.

Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But it is a part of the game often poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023.

"We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football."
Germany not alone in declining invitation to tournament

Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation. The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine, whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February that: "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help."

Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only.

"Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present.
"This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow."
FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment.

blocks.caption: Some believe Arsène Wenger (left) is the man to replace Gianni Infantino as the head of FIFAImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other.

For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds.

FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers."

But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022, it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics.

Jire Carreon/Rappler
The complaint comes weeks after Vice President Sara Duterte jokingly said in a press conference that she would file a libel suit against GMA Network over the Gracioso report

items: Davao City Representative Paolo Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against GMA Network officials and journalists over bribery claims involving him and Vice President Sara Duterte.
The complaint, based on an affidavit by former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., alleges that he delivered large sums of money to both Duterte and the Vice President during her tenure as mayor.
Vice President Duterte denied the allegations in a press conference and jokingly suggested filing her own libel complaint against GMA Network.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against officials and journalists of GMA Network over the latter’s report about bribery claims against him and Vice President Sara Duterte.
Representative Duterte filed the complaint with the Davao City prosecutor’s office on Friday, October 23, against the following:

items: National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag
Former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
GMA chairman Felipe Gozon
GMA president Gilberto Duavit Jr.
GMA anchors Mel Tiangco, Vicky Morales, Emil Sumangil
GMA senior reporter Darlene Cay
GMA executive producer Marvin Parado
GMA director Joel San Luis

blocks.text: “GMA Network has yet to receive a copy of the complaint. We will review the matter and comment accordingly upon receipt,” GMA Network said in a statement.

The legal action is still at the complaint level. Prosecutors will assess first if the complaint has sufficient evidence to become a case. If the prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction is found, the prosecutors will indict the respondents and file a case with the court.

In his eight-page affidavit, Gracioso claimed that he delivered millions of pesos to the Vice President when she was still the mayor of Davao City. He alleged that there were similar incidents like this, almost 10 times, from 2018 to 2020.
He also claimed there that he allegedly delivered money to Representative Duterte.

blocks.caption: The Gracioso affidavit: Ex-cop claims he delivered millions to Sara Duterte

blocks.text: GMA Network was the first to publish a report about Gracioso’s affidavit.

Days later, on October 6, the Vice President held a press conference where she denied the allegations. She also said there that Gracioso was motivated by anger and money. In the same press conference, Vice President Duterte jokingly said that she would file a libel complaint against the network.

“Puwede ko ba i-libel ang GMA News nito? Hindi man lang sila nag-check ba? Nagturo. Libel ko itong GMA. Magkano? P200 million para pumera naman ako dito. Imagine, nagturo ng bahay namin. Hindi man lang chineck kung totoong bahay namin ‘yon,” the Vice President jokingly said.

(Can I file a libel complaint against GMA News? Did they not check? I will file a libel complaint against GMA. How much? P200 million so I can get money from this? Imagine, they pointed a supposed house. They did not even check if that is really our house.)
The Gracioso affidavit is the latest allegation hurled at the Vice President, who’s currently in the middle of an impeachment trial at the Senate.

In late 2025, self-confessed bagman Ramil Madriaga, through affidavits, tagged the Vice President to the Philippine offshore gaming operators and confidential funds issue. Vice President Duterte filed two separate perjury complaints against Madriaga, but the Taguig City prosecutor’s office already junked the first complaint. – Rappler.com

articles.title: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
articles.summary:
Case filed in 2022 by patient unable to afford medicine leads to cap on drug prices for millions who face ruin if diagnosed

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer…

blocks.text: The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.

From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.

Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.

blocks.caption: Sarojam Radhakrishan initiated the court action after being unable to pay for her cancer drugs. Photograph: Facebook

blocks.text: The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.

A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.

“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.

Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.

As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.

Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.

Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.

“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.

As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.

“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.

Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.

The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

articles.title: China towing away BRP Sierra Madre is 'act of war' against PH -- Teodoro
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said that if China forcefully towed away the sunken warship BRP Sierra Madre, it would be an act of war against the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 2:53pm
Defense Secretary Gilberto "Gibo" Teodoro said that if China forcefully towed away the sunken warship BRP Sierra Madre, it would be an act of war against the Philippines.

A report from a Chinese news outlet claimed that Beijing was mulling sanctions against Manila, including the towing of the BRP Sierra Madre—a World War II-era warship that was deliberately run aground in 1999 in Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea and continues to serve as an outpost for the country.

"'Yung Sierra Madre BRP, barko ng Republika ng Pilipinas ano at kung iyan ay tinangka, or, may mangyari diyan at sa kadahilanan ng ginamitan ng puwersa, eh, iyan ay act of war against the Republic of the Philippines," Teodoro said.

(The Sierra Madre BRP, it is a ship of the Republic of the Philippines, and if there is an attempt, or if something happened to it by force, that is an act of war against the Republic of the Philippines.)
Teodoro made it clear that an "act of war" is different from a "state of war," as only the President and Congress can declare war.
The Defense Secretary said that because the BRP Sierra Madre is a warship, any offensive act against it is an act of war.
"Any threat against BRP Sierra Madre will be taken very seriously because it will be an act against a military vessel of the Republic of the Philippines," Teodoro said.
Asked if the Philippines will envoke its Mutual Defense Treaty with the United States if China boarded the BRP Sierra Madre, Teodoro said that that "the possibility is open".
However, it would be presidential decision if it happened, Teodoro said.
Diplomatic ties between Manila and Beijing were strained anew after Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan recently said China would easily win if it used force in the West Philippine Sea.
Several Filipino officials called for Quan’s expulsion, urging President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. to declare the envoy persona non grata.
Teodoro said that while the threats have become more overt now, they have always been present.

"It just goes to show you that whatever supposedly goodwill that they are doing is a weapon and they are weaponizing it. And it also serves as a lesson for us to make our economy more resilient and to build up our industries and to firm up our country," Teodoro said.
"We are constantly being threatened, subtly, and now more overtly," he added.

Tensions between China and the Philippines have increased due to the territorial row in the West Philippine Sea. Despite the Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling in favor of the Philippines in 2016, China has continuously disregarded the verdict and claimed most of the South China Sea for itself. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Claire Castro to retain post as all PCO execs file courtesy resignations
articles.summary: Acting Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano will not accept the courtesy resignation of Palace Press Officer Claire Castro, he said on Friday, October 23.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 2:44pm
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro on October 20, 2026
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Acting Communications Secretary Lino Cayetano will not accept the courtesy resignation of Palace Press Officer Claire Castro.

Cayetano confirmed this in an interview with reporters on Friday, October 23, where he also said all undersecretaries and assistant secretaries of the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) were asked to file courtesy resignations.

Cayetano gave no timeline for acting on the other resignations. He told reporters that evaluating his team would be an ongoing process rather than a one-time reshuffle, with some decisions coming within days and others months later.

“Usec. Claire, I don’t want to say we’re a package deal, but Usec. Claire is a treasure in this government,” Cayetano said in mixed English and Filipino. “I haven’t seen someone articulate [that] well what this government is doing.”

Without giving further details, Cayetano said the PCO currently has an "innovation" that he wants Castro to be a part of. "In this age of digitalization, we want an analog office. I think the PCO also needs to focus on being on the ground," he said.
Cayetano was all praise for Castro's combative style of responding to issues and affirmed he would like both of them to continue working closely.
"In terms of being combative (sic) and protecting what this administration is doing, to explain [why we do what we do], I admire Usec. Claire," he added.

"For me, that's the strength of Usec. Claire. That's her personality. We will balance that out, that if there is a need to explain a policy, we will invite the relevant department or Cabinet secretary [during briefings]," Cayetano said.

Cayetano became the PCO’s head after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced during a press interview in Singapore on October 11 that he was replacing Dave Gomez, whose appointment had been bypassed by the Commission on Appointments.

He took his oath in Malacañang on October 13, becoming the sixth official to lead the PCO under the Marcos administration, after Trixie Cruz-Angeles, Cheloy Velicaria-Garafil, Cesar Chavez, Jay Ruiz and Gomez.
A former Taguig City mayor and television director, he had been general manager of state-run PTV-4, a PCO-attached corporation, since June.
This is the third leadership transition Castro has been a part of since she entered the PCO.
Asked whose resignations he would accept, Cayetano said: “That will be a process as long as I am here.”

articles.title: Taiwan braces as El Nino-supercharged Typhoon Champi approaches island
articles.summary: One person has died and thousands have been evacuated as Taiwan prepares for a possible direct hit. Though no longer a "super" typhoon, Champi is still packing winds of nearly 200 kmh and will bring…

image.caption: One person was killed after being swept away by waves reaching heights of up to 10 meters (33 feet) while thousands have been evacuated to higher groundImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: Taiwan is bracing for potential impact as Typhoon Champi bears down on the island after weakening slightly, with nearly all businesses, shops and schools closed.
Over 1,300 people have been forced to evacuate to higher ground, and hundreds of flights have been cancelled across the region according to the Ministry of Transportation.
At least one person has already been killed after being swept out to sea and dozens more have been injured.
What do we know about Typhoon Champi?

On Friday, locals were still busy installing sandbags and metal barriers in front of doors and windows to defend against flooding, while authorities positioned inflatable boats and amphibious vehicles around the island to aid in rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: Shops and houses have been boarded up in preparation for Champi's arrivalImage: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP

blocks.text: In the capital Taipei, public transport was still operating, but at reduced capacity.
Taiwan's Central Weather Administration (CWA) says Champi is currently about 220 kilometers (137 miles) east of the island's southern shore.

The storm is projected to move past Taiwan's northeastern shore before turning north to China and eventually moving east into southern Japan. But forecasters say that any deviation from its current course could mean a direct hit for Taiwan.
Why are there so many big storms in the Pacific this year?

The storm is expected to bring torrential rain, massive waves and sustained high winds to Taiwan throughout Friday and Saturday. Military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts throughout.

"As it approaches Taiwan's northeastern tip, the typhoon may slow down. If it slows down, its impact will last longer," CWA Administrator Lu Kuo-chen told reporters, adding, "People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow."
Forecasters say the storm's radius is currently about 320 kilometers, wide enough to blanket most of the island.

blocks.caption: Though no longer a 'super typhoon' Champi has maintained high winds and has a footprint big enough to cover all of TaiwanImage: CSU/CIRA/JMA/JAXA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Fueled by this year's exceptionally strong El Nino season — a cyclical weather phenomenon that sees water temperatures in the tropical Pacific rise, in turn turbocharging storms, or inversely droughts — Champi attained "super typhoon" status as it built strength during its approach, with winds clocking 298 kmh (185 mph).
Though it has weakened, the CWA says Champi is still packing wind gusts of about 190 kmh as it approaches from the southwest.

This year's El Nino phase, which the United Nations on Wednesday described as "heading off the charts," is expected to peak in December. It's impact however, could last years, with the UN urging nations in the Pacific to prepare for the worst.

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian: Recalling 2027 budget 'unnecessary;' Senate to do corrections
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Friday that it is not necessary for the House of Representatives to recall its version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, as the upper chamber will…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 2:32pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said Friday that it is not necessary for the House of Representatives to recall its version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill, as the upper chamber will already do the corrections pursuant to the recent Supreme Court decision.

This came after members of the Makabayan Bloc urged the recall of the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed national budget for 2027, in light of the SC decision declaring the 2024, 2025, and portions of 2026 national budget unconstitutional.

“Not necessary naman dahil papasok na kami sa consolidation ng budget dito, so we can do the correction ourselves. So that hindi made-delay ‘yung budget process, dito na namin iko-correct,” Gatchalian said in an ambush interview.

(It’s not really necessary, since we are about to begin the budget consolidation process and we can handle the corrections ourselves. We’ll make the necessary corrections here so that the budget process isn’t delayed.)

“And looking at ‘yung Supreme Court decision, on the 2026 budget, onti lang naman ‘yung maapektuhan. So, hindi ko nakikita [na] malaking correction ang gagawin dito sa 2027 budget. Of course, we'll take note of the other issues, but, kaya na namin i-correct,” he added.

(And regarding the Supreme Court decision, specifically on the 2026 budget, only a small portion will be affected. Therefore, I don’t see any major corrections necessary for the 2027 budget. Of course, we will take note of the other issues, but we are capable of making the corrections ourselves.)

In a landmark decision, the SC struck down the General Appropriations Acts (GAAs) for 2024 and 2025 after Congress added appropriations beyond what the President had recommended in the National Expenditure Program.

Specifically, the 2024 budget was voided due to a P449.5-billion increase in unprogrammed appropriations, while the 2025 budget was struck down because of the additional P17.99 billion for the Special Road Fund of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
The High Court likewise deemed as unconstitutional Special Provisions 1(a) and (b) of Chapter XLIII in the 2026 GAA, which authorized unprogrammed appropriations.
Senate to comply

Gatchalian said the Senate will comply with the SC decision without prejudice to the motion for reconsideration that will be filed by the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), to ensure that the 2027 budget will not be unconstitutional.
“We will make sure. First, we will comply with the Supreme Court ruling,” he said.

“Of course, hindi na lalampas rin dahil isa sa pinakamahalagang decision ng Supreme Court,. ‘wag ka lumampas doon sa proposal ng Presidente. So, 2026, hindi naman lumampas and we will make sure 2027 hindi rin,” he added.

(Of course, we will ensure that the 2027 budget won’t go beyond the President’s proposal because that’s one of the most significant rulings of the Supreme Court. It did not exceed in 2026, and we will make sure that it won’t for 2027 either.)
The Senate President likewise assured that the 2027 budget will not be an “election budget” that can be used for the 2028 national elections.

“The 2027 budget will be a budget that will be responsive to the needs and the requirements of the country…to boost our economy, to respond to inflation, and to respond to El Niño,” Gatchalian said. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Jordon Steele-John’s position remains in limbo as Greens prepare for moment in spotlight
articles.summary:
David Shoebridge’s newly-minted leadership under pressure over handling of misconduct allegations as Senate estimates looms

More than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon…

blocks.text: More than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon Steele-John had behaved inappropriately towards women made headlines, his position in the party remains in limbo and its new leader’s handling of the issue in question.

David Shoebridge’s first major challenge at the helm of the federal Greens came earlier this month when the Nine newspapers reported a three-page letter had been sent to him urging an independent investigation into Steele-John.
It referred to second-hand allegations that the Western Australian senator had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
As a progressive party that prides itself on taking such matters seriously and fairly, it made sense that Shoebridge announced the 32-year-old’s leave amid an independent probe into the claims.

But the process quickly became more complicated. Days later, a defiant Steele-John rejected the allegations against him, denied he agreed to take leave from parliament, and accused an internal faction within the WA Greens of playing “nasty political games” in its decision to release the letter to the media.
Steele-John said he made a public statement because he didn’t want his silence on the letter’s claims to be perceived as guilt.
While Shoebridge insists Steele-John agreed to take leave, he acknowledges he alone does not have the power to force the senator to do so.
Only if two-thirds of the party room - or more than seven members - decided to expel him in a secret ballot, would Steele-John have no option but to comply.
Such a move would be nuclear. Even if the WA Greens’ independent investigation clears him of any wrongdoing, Steele-John’s standing in the party room would be shattered.
The week ahead under scrutiny
On Monday, Shoebridge’s ability to deal with the matter will be on show.

Senate estimates is a time for members of the upper house to have their moment in the spotlight. For the Greens, it’s a chance to extricate answers about government policies from carefully trained bureaucrats to drive home a political point.

With the NDIS undergoing major changes between now and the decade’s end, the Greens will have to decide whether their disability spokesperson, Steele-John, who is championed and well-liked within the disability community, should be allowed to attend. Perhaps, virtually.

For many supporters within and outside the Greens, the optics of allowing a federal party member accused of sexual misconduct – even though a complainant has not directly come forward to make those allegations – to continue public duties will be a tough pill to swallow. Particularly as the “manosphere” phenomenon and backlash against the MeToo movement gain momentum in mainstream society.
The question over whether the allegations were politically-motivated by adversaries of Steele-John, looking to gain advantage in the state’s pre-selection, is a part of the equation.

But the fact remains that the rumours have persisted over the senator’s time in office. Even if they are malicious, as Steele-John contends, the simpler option would still be to stand aside and settle them while they are investigated.
The decision over whether to force Steele-John to take leave will be as much about Shoebridge’s leadership as it is about the party’s processes.
The party room, and its membership more broadly, prides itself on being a movement based on consensus decision-making.

Shoebridge will need the support of the party room to take the expulsion route. How he handles this issue will also set the tone for the rest of his leadership and, depending on his actions, could prompt an ugly battle with Steele-John.
It’s a quagmire – politically, legally and ethically.
There are unlikely to be any winners.

articles.title: Philippines reports highest disaster impact among 140 markets in global poll
articles.summary: Four in five Filipino adults said they had personally been affected by a disaster linked to a natural hazard.

blocks.text: Climate and Environment
October 23, 2026 | 2:18pm

This aerial view taken on July 7, 2025, shows wooden boats anchored beside cramped houses on Isla Pugad in Hagonoy town, Bulacan province, north of Manila. Sea levels across the Philippines as a whole are rising three times faster than the global average of 3.6 millimeters per year, and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has said this could accelerate to 13 millimeters annually.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — Four in five Filipino adults said they had been personally affected by disasters linked to natural hazards in the past five years, the highest share among 140 countries and territories surveyed in a global poll.
The Philippines' 80% rate was the highest recorded in the Lloyd's Register Foundation's 2026 World Risk Poll, which examined people's experiences of disasters, early warning systems and resilience.
Gallup conducted the survey across 140 countries and territories throughout 2025. The report defines disasters as the result of hazards having significant consequences for people.
In the Philippines, tropical storms emerged as the hazard with the greatest reported impact, cited by 52% of adults.
But experiences varied considerably across the country.
The Visayas recorded the highest reported impact from tropical storms at 67%, followed by provinces in Luzon outside Metro Manila at 59%.
In Metro Manila, 44% reported being affected by tropical storms, while 39% cited floods.
Mindanao stood out for earthquakes, with 44% of respondents in the region reporting being affected by them.
Philippines as most affected
Globally, 20% of adults surveyed said they had personally been affected by a disaster related to a natural hazard within the past five years.
The impact was substantially higher in poorer countries. Nearly one in three adults, or 31%, in low-income countries reported being affected, according to the poll.
Of the 10 countries with the highest self-reported disaster impacts, nine were classified as low-income or lower-middle-income economies, alongside Hong Kong. Eight were in sub-Saharan Africa.
The Philippines nevertheless ranked above all of them at 80%.
While those in lower-income countries tended to report greater disaster impacts, they also have fewer of the resources associated with preparedness and resilience.
Among adults in low-income countries, 42% said they could protect themselves in a future disaster, while 29% had a household plan for coping with one.

The poll also found higher levels of concern about weather-related hazards in low-income countries, with 52% saying they were very worried about serious harm from severe weather such as floods and storms.
How the Philippines was surveyed

Gallup interviewed 1,000 people in the Philippines from October 2 to December 5, 2025, through face-to-face interviews using handheld data collection. Respondents were asked about disasters that had personally affected them in the preceding five years, meaning the results reflect experiences through the time of the survey in late 2025.
Interviews were conducted in Filipino, Iluko, Cebuano, Hiligaynon, Waray and Bicol.
Gallup reported a maximum margin of error of 3.6 percentage points for the Philippine sample at the 95% confidence level.

The findings come as the Philippines faces renewed climate risks heading into 2027. DOST has warned that drought conditions could emerge in parts of the country from October and persist into March 2027, while a strong to very strong El Niño is expected to continue through the first half of next year. — Alyana Uy

articles.title: ‘We’ve lost a basic sense of politeness’: UK readers reveal daily reality of public transport
articles.summary:
Regular users detail their frustrations – and question whether Andy Burnham’s crackdown on antisocial behaviour will actually work

Andy Burnham has announced a campaign against nuisance…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has announced a campaign against nuisance behaviour on public transport, including “headphone dodgers” who play loud music.
“We’ve all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone,” Burnham said in a statement. “It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey.”
Six people share their views on Burnham’s new campaign and recount their experiences of antisocial behaviour on public transport.
‘It saddens me that we have lost a basic sense of politeness’

I live in London and commute daily on the tube. Even yesterday, sitting next to me was a guy playing videos out loud, which is the most common issue. I’m interested in what has caused a sudden change to our social contract that allows people the psychological safety to completely disregard others. It’s not top of the list of worst behaviour; it’s in the same bracket as leaning on poles so no one can hold them, leaving your bag on the only seat left, leaning your arm on the fold up chair, or man-spreading. It mostly saddens me that we have lost a basic sense of politeness.

I’m not sure Andy Burnham’s announcement will do anything. If you’re already playing very loud videos in public, presumably you don’t care very much about what you should be doing. You never really see police or “safety officers”, so who would enforce it? I’m glad they aren’t making the tube workers or bus drivers try to enforce it though; it would make their days hell. Claire, 41, London
‘Almost every bus or train journey has someone blaring music’

I get the train five nights a week to work and nine times out of 10, there is somebody taking phone calls on speakerphone, blasting videos or music, even in the so-called quiet carriage. Everyone’s too scared to ask them to move to a different carriage or turn it down, so it’s a regular occurrence. It makes my journey a nightmare. No one enforces anything. I doubt this new law will change this. It should include phone calls too and people putting calls on loudspeaker. It doesn’t go far enough. Margaret, 49, Weston-super-Mare
‘Commuters shouldn’t have to put up with it’

I think this is a great step to protect public spaces as shared spaces, and to show people the boundaries between acceptable and unacceptable behaviour. The last time I asked somebody who was playing reels aloud to use their headphones I was called “a piece of shit” and decided not to ask anybody that again. But commuters shouldn’t have to put up with it. Of course, the question is whether and how this will be enforced consistently. Ben Ellis, 38, Edinburgh
‘I’m sick of being the bad guy who points it out’

I’ve always challenged this behaviour by asking people if they have headphones. If they say no, I ask if they can turn the sound off. Most of the time this is OK, but I have had repeated incidents where people refuse. I’m stubborn and confident, so I’ll explain that it is not normal or socially acceptable to subject other people to jarring video scrolling. Only once in this situation did a train guard ask someone playing football at full volume to turn it off. And I can’t blame them. You’d be arguing with idiots for 90% of your shift if you did.

I’m sick of being the bad guy who points it out. It seems like people of all ages have forgotten basic decency and consideration. I had a run-in with a teenage kid who was watching TikTok or something, and he said, “What do you mean? If you were watching Netflix on your phone, wouldn’t you have the volume on?” So there’s a range of understanding of what people think is appropriate behaviour in a public place. John, 43, Sheffield

One of the bigger issues that never gets addressed is football fans on public transport. I’m a football fan myself, but fans on trains can be extremely offensive, oppressive, aggressive and difficult for people to deal with. One time that springs to mind was a bunch of fans on a two-carriage train. They were drinking, singing loud, offensive songs regardless of the fact that there were kids on the train, banging on the ceiling of the carriage, making a hell of a racket. There were no police or staff. There was a bunch of people waiting at the railway station at the other end, but it’s too late at that point.

It’s become almost like an accepted thing that if you go in on a train, this is what you have to put up with. I’m glad to see that [Burnham] recognises that behaviour on public transport is an issue that needs to be addressed. Do I think this will address it? Not at all. How do you get to someone on a train? Will this be app based? Only instant reporting and action will work, but how does that square with a public transport network with significant coverage gaps? Mike Hughes, 63, Tyldesley, Greater Manchester
‘It’ll end up like the law against hogging the middle lane on the motorway’

The Manchester Metrolink has no [regular] conductors, so antisocial behaviour goes unchecked. It happens to the extent that it deters me from travelling on buses and trams. Trains aren’t quite as bad, because if someone’s really annoying, one can leave one’s seat to go and seek out the train manager and tell them what seat the offender is sitting in. This is impossible on the Manchester trams, so what possible incentive do habitual offenders have to desist? I suppose, over time, the campaign might lead to gradual social change – so even just raising and highlighting the issues might result in attitudinal change. My main concern is that it’s going to be nigh on useless having a fining policy unless transport is policed. It’ll end up like the law against hogging the middle lane on the motorway. How many people have been pulled up and fined for that? How many people still do it? Linda, Manchester

articles.summary: Coordinates for farm-to-market roads allegedly point to the Celebes Sea or waters near Brunei

blocks.text: HEARING. Senators and officials of the Department of Agriculture (DA) review the proposed 2027 budget of the DA and its attached agencies and corporations, on October 21, 2026. Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the DA is set to receive ₱198.4 billion, an 8 percent decrease from its ₱215.7-billion budget in 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit
Coordinates for farm-to-market roads allegedly point to the Celebes Sea or waters near Brunei

items: The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) raised concerns about the proposed 2027 budget for the Department of Agriculture, specifically regarding farm-to-market roads and irrigation projects that lack proper documentation.

PBC highlighted issues such as erroneous coordinates for several projects, with some pointing to bodies of water instead of their intended locations, and alleged that many projects are overpriced compared to standard costs.
The Department of Agriculture acknowledged PBC's concerns and welcomed their involvement in verifying the progress of existing projects to enhance transparency and accountability in public spending.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The civil society group People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) raised several red flags during the Senate finance committee hearing on the proposed budget of the Department of Agriculture (DA) for 2027.

At the center of the group’s report are farm-to-market (FMR) and irrigation projects. Following the flood control scandal, the DA launched a portal for FMR projects to monitor the standard and completion of farm-to-market roads worth millions of pesos.
Here are the issues that the PBC raised during the hearing:

The group flagged P15 billion worth of FMR and irrigation projects that do not have publicly-posted project attachments. They alleged these projects are insertions made in the House of Representatives.
Kenneth Isaiah Abante, co-convenor of the PBC, said the House inserted 355 FMR projects not originally included in the National Expenditure Program and the DA’s proposal.
“We are not sure if these are connected to the national highway network or connected to their resorts,” Abante said.
In addition, Abante alleged that the House also inserted 319 irrigation projects worth P9.4 billion without proper documents.

Coordinates of some FMR projects are erroneous as well, according to citizen-led mapping of 18,000 projects in the House’s general appropriations bill. (READ: House passes P7.2-trillion 2027 budget amid pork barrel concerns)

A P23-million FMR project in Nueva Ecija had coordinates that point to the sea near Benham Rise, said Abante. A project that is supposed to be in Cebu appeared in Celebes Sea. Coordinates of a P55-million project appeared in the waters near Brunei.

The group also flagged costings that it alleged were way over the market price. The standard cost per kilometer of a farm-to-market road is P15 million, but some projects allegedly showed costs of P6 million to P19 million per meter.
“If we take the budget as is, there will likely be overpriced projects in the DA,” said Abante.

The group also said instruments for solar irrigation pump systems were likely overpriced. Abante questioned the P50 million to P200 million price tags for solar panel systems, noting that individual 600- to 700-watt panels cost around P7,000.

The cost of solar materials has risen amid the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has fueled fears of power outages and higher electricity bills. (READ: ‘Solar rush’: Surge in solar demand overwhelms local industry)

blocks.caption: MARKET. People buy basic commodities at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.

blocks.text: Watchdogs and civil society groups like the People’s Budget Coalition are given the floor to present recommendations and red flags in the proposed 2027 budget.
This is part of an effort to make the budget process more transparent and participative after the public uproar over the flood control scandal.
The DA accepted PBC’s offer to mobilize their volunteers in verifying the progress of existing FMR projects.

“We welcome initiatives that empower citizens to hold public spending accountable and ensure that funds go where they are intended and deliver real benefits to the people, from agricultural workers to ordinary residents whose lives are improved by these infrastructure projects,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said.
The DA took over FMR projects from the Department of Public Works and Highways after the latter faced public scrutiny over allegations of massive corruption. – Rappler.com
