articles.title: Teodoro: Use of force vs BRP Sierra Madre an 'act of war'
articles.summary: The Philippines' defense chief issued a warning over actions against the BRP Sierra Madre, saying it would be an act of war.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 1:55pm

This file photo taken on April 23, 2023 shows the grounded Philippine navy ship BRP Sierra Madre where marines are stationed to assert Manila's territorial claims at Second Thomas Shoal in the Spratly Islands in the disputed South China Sea.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — Following a report that China was mulling the removal of a grounded Philippine warship, Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro Jr. warned that any use of force against the BRP Sierra Madre would be an act of war against the Philippines.

"Any threats against BRP Sierra Madre will be taken very seriously, because it will be an act against a military vessel of the Republic of the Philippines," Teodoro said in an interview with reporters Friday, October 23.

Chinese Commercial News, a Chinese-language broadsheet in the Philippines with ties to Beijing, earlier reported that China was considering pulling the Philippines' naval outpost from Ayungin Shoal as retaliation for Manila's "recent actions."

Asked whether the military would update its rules of engagement for troops aboard the ship to prevent it from being boarded by another nation's troops, Teodoro declined to discuss "operational matters." He instead restated the vessel's status.

"The BRP Sierra Madre is a ship of the Republic of the Philippines. If anything is attempted against it, or anything happens to it through the use of force, that is an act of war against the Republic of the Philippines," he said in mixed Filipino and English.
The defense chief was careful to clarify that any action taken by China toward the aging warship would be an "act of war" but not a "state of war."

Under the 1987 Constitution, only Congress, by a two-thirds vote of both chambers voting separately, can declare the existence of a state of war. Acts of war refer to hostile action done by a foreign state against another.
The 10 countermeasures. The report, published this week by Chinese Commercial News, said Beijing was losing patience with Manila and was considering 10 countermeasures.
The Binondo-based newspaper said Chinese authorities had not confirmed the measures and that it was unclear whether they had entered Beijing's formal decision-making process.

The options being weighed purportedly include towing the Sierra Madre away, blocking resupply missions to its crew, sanctioning Filipino politicians seen as hostile to China, and cutting oil and fertilizer supplies to the Philippines.
The Philippine Navy deliberately ran the World War II-era ship aground at Ayungin in 1999 to assert Manila's sovereign rights.

The shoal lies about 200 kilometers from Palawan, within the country's exclusive economic zone. It was a frequent flashpoint for confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels until both sides reached an "arrangement" in 2024 to de-escalate tensions.
The report by Chinese Commercial News surfaced amid a widening diplomatic row between Beijing and Manila.

The Department of Foreign Affairs summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over his October 19 remarks that China could easily win a military conflict. Lawmakers have since filed resolutions urging the president to declare him persona non grata.
'No one has the right'
Teodoro also rejected Chinese claims that Manila sought Beijing's approval for Wednesday's rotation and resupply mission to the BRP Sierra Madre.

The China Coast Guard said the Philippines delivered supplies to the ship with Chinese approval, and that it verified the Philippine vessel and monitored the whole operation, according to the state-run news outlet Global Times.
The newspaper later published a video it said showed a Philippine boat cooperating with a coast guard inspection.
"No one has the right to ask the Republic of the Philippines to ask for permission for a resupply of Sierra Madre. So that is false," Teodoro said.
"We have no obligation to say what is on board, or what the cargo is, of a ship of the Republic of the Philippines," he said in Filipino.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, Rear Adm. Roy Vincent Trinidad, confirmed Thursday that the military did not ask China for permission prior to the conduct of the resupply mission.

blocks.text: The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is "back" in Ukraine, US President Donald Trump said on Thursday.
His announcement comes after the Wall Street Journal reported that the US president asked tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore the service vital to Ukraine's defense against Russia's invasion.

"I guess the bottom line, he put it back," Trump said, referring to Musk.
Kyiv is yet to confirm if the throttling has been lifted.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense of late after Trump called for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced after he criticized a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.
Meanwhile, Kyiv has questioned Washington's support over intelligence sharing and speculation that the White House may have ordered the restrictions on Starshield.
The unsolved mystery of who throttled Starshield

Earlier this week the Journal reported that Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network. The move rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, it added.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?

The report, citing two unnamed sources, said Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public. One person claimed that Musk spoke with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, before imposing the speed cap.

In response to that report, Musk had said that "any limits to speed or usage" of Starshied, operated by his company SpaceX, were "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Both Trump and then Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the Pentagon had not directed any changes.
Ukraine has not recieved a clear official explanation of who ordered the restrictions or why, a senior European official familiar with the matter told AP on Thursday.
US Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal on Thursday said he had opened an inquiry into the matter.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No reports link Sandro Marcos, Romualdez to Laos drug bust
articles.summary: Remulla rejected claims linking Sandro Marcos to the intercepted drug shipment; there are also no PNP or PDEA statements about the two officials' alleged involvement

blocks.text: Claim: A Filipino suspect in the drug shipment intercepted in Laos, who was reportedly a former employee of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, identified presidential son and Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative Sandro Marcos as the alleged mastermind behind the operation.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post by “Nimfa Ambasan Oranio,” published on October 16, bears the claim.
Its caption reads, “Agoy paano yan kumanta na ang Pilipino na nahulihan ng dr*ga sa Thailand.”
(Oh no, what now, the Filipino caught with drugs in Thailand has already spoken.)

The accompanying graphic asks, “Mastermind si Sandro Narcos?” (Is Sandro ‘Narcos’ the mastermind?) and claims that the Filipino arrested in Laos and Thailand was a Romualdez employee who pointed to the presidential son as the alleged mastermind of the attempted trafficking of 521 kilograms of shabu from Laos.
As of writing, the post has received 645 reactions, 278 comments, and 902 shares.

The facts: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla rejected claims linking Marcos to the drug shipment. In an interview on October 19, he said there was “no grain of truth” to the allegations and that investigators found no evidence connecting the presidential son to the operation or its alleged financier, former Bangsamoro Transition Authority parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang.

The Filipino arrested in the Laos case was identified as Fahad Mulok Dibarosan. Laotian authorities detained him on October 1 at Luang Prabang International Airport after intercepting 521 kilograms of suspected shabu aboard a chartered Learjet bound for the Philippines. As of October 21, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) had sent a letter to Lao authorities as part of their probe.

There is no credible report or official statement showing that Dibarosan named Marcos as the mastermind or that he worked for Romualdez. The post offers only an unverified social media comment to support the alleged employment link.
There are also no statements from the Philippine National Police or the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) about the alleged involvement of Marcos or Romualdez.

The misleading post also conflates the Laos drug seizure with a separate incident in Thailand. In early October, Thai authorities intercepted about 1,178 kilograms of suspected shabu aboard a fishing vessel in the Gulf of Thailand en route to the Philippines, but PDEA chief Isagani Nerez later said that there was no evidence indicating that the shipment was bound for the country.

The Laos shipment probe: On October 16, Remulla identified 11 persons of interest in the drug seizure investigation, including Rimbang, whom he named as the alleged financier; former commercial pilot Rioklyn “Boyet” Toledo, who allegedly procured the aircraft; and Police Executive Master Sergeant Aileen Mendoza, who allegedly arranged arrival permits and hangar access in Manila.
The Criminal Investigation and Detection Group has issued 40 subpoenas as part of its investigation into the case. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
articles.summary: Names are central to our identity, so what happens when that name is a source of ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

image.caption: From childhood bullying to workplace discrimination, awkward names can influence how people are perceived and treatedImage: Dreamstime Demidovic/Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.
"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."
The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name — or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?
"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."
Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.
This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.
How do names shape first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."
"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.
What do Nigerians think of bullying?
'Weirdness': Why people react negatively to some names

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.
Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.
Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.
Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.
"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.
Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.
"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."
Pain, now 41, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.
"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"
Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.
How humor helps — and harms — as a coping mechanism
As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.
Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."
"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."
Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.
"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"
How an embarassing name can also offer a sense of belonging
"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.
Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point," she said.
But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.
"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."
But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.
"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.
Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.
"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message" and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.
Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong
Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."
But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.
Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.
For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.
"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."

articles.title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
articles.summary: The quake hit a mountainous, sparsely-populated area in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region.

blocks.text: The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas.
Local media said more than 12,400 people have been relocated after the earthquake.
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas.

The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km.
Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes.
Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape from the tremor.

Speaking to Tibet Daily, Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu said she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, "her legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home.
Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us".
Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet.
Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks have been registered since the quake occurred.

China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media.
Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude around 4,800 metres and prone to aftershocks.
The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations.
Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (£5.6m, $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet.
Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark, although these have not been independently verified.
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity.
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China.

Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing.
Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly.
In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police, and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet.
The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area.
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China.
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

articles.title: Visayas, Mindanao grids under red, yellow alert on Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 -- NGCP
articles.summary: The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said the Visayas grid will be placed under Red Alert on Friday afternoon, while the Mindanao grid will be under Yellow Alert due to the…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 1:06pm

The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said the Visayas grid will be placed under Red Alert on Friday afternoon, while the Mindanao grid will be under Yellow Alert due to the unavailability of coal plants and outages affecting multiple plants.

For the Visayas Grid, the Red Alert will be effective from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. It will later be put under Yellow Alert from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m., and then once more at 6 p.m. to 8 p.m., according to a Facebook post from the NGCP.
The available capacity is 2,407 megawatts (MW) against a peak demand of 2,558 MV.

The NGCP said eight plants are on forced outage on October, two plants since September, three plants since September, three plants since August, one plant since June, three plants since May, three plants since 2025, one plant since 2024, two plants since 2023, and one plant since 2021.
Meanwhile, 19 plants are running on derated capacities, leading to 606.6 MW being unavailable to the grid.
According to the NGCP, a factor that contributed to the red and yellow alert declaration was the unavailability of Visayas' large coal plants PEDC 3 and KSPC 1.
There were also limited power imports from Mindanao due to the planned outages of GNPK 4, TSI 2, and unplanned outages of TSI 1 and Pulangi 4 U2.

In a separate Facebook post, the Mindanao grid's Yellow Alert will be in effect from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. due to the planned outages of GNPK 4, and TSI 2, and unplanned outages of TSI 1, and Pulangi 4 U2.
There is an available capacity of 2,847 MW against a peak demand of 2,661 MW.

The NGCP said 11 plants have been on forced outage in October, one since September, two plants since August, two plants since July, one plant since June, two plants since January, one plant since 2025, and one plant since 2024.
Three plants running on derated capacities, for a total of 474.9 MW unavailable to the grid.

According to the NGCP, a red alert is raised when power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the transmission grid's regulating requirement. Meanwhile, a yellow alert is raised when the operating margin is unable to meet the transmission grid's contingency requirement. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Pulong Duterte files libel, cyberlibel vs. GMA Network, Matibag over cash delivery claims report
articles.summary: Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte on Friday filed a libel and cyberlibel complaint against National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag, and dismissed…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 1:01pm

Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte on Friday filed a libel and cyberlibel complaint against National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag, and dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. over the claims of cash delivery to their family.
GMA Network executives and journalists were also included in the complaint.

“Tungkol ito doon sa pinalabas nilang pre-recorded video noong September 25 sa GMA News 24 Oras na pinapalabas doon na, allegedly, nagbigay daw ng maletang cash itong si Gracioso,” Atty. Peter Paul Danao, Duterte's lawyer, said in an ambush interview.
(This concerns the pre-recorded video they aired on September 25 on GMA News’ 24 Oras, which allegedly showed Gracioso handing over a suitcase full of cash.)
“Tinatanggi naman ni Congressman Paolo na kilala niya itong si Gracioso at wala siyang tinatanggap na maleta na cash sa kanya,” he added.
(Congressman Paolo, for his part, denies knowing Gracioso and says he did not receive any suitcase full of cash from him.)
In a statement, GMA Network said it has yet to receive a copy of the complaint.
“We will review the matter and comment accordingly upon receipt,” it said.
According to Danao, Duterte sought P10 million for moral damages and P10 million for exemplary damages.
GMA News Online has asked the NBI for comment and will publish it once available.
To recall, Gracioso alleged that he delivered cash to Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte, and former President Rodrigo Duterte on former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco’s instructions.
The Vice President earlier denied the allegations and filed her affidavit with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
Rep. Duterte, meanwhile, dubbed Gracioso's allegations as "pure fiction."
“I do not personally know him. I did not receive any money or maleta ng pera from him, whether in a bar in Davao or elsewhere,” he said.
“Mr. Gracioso’s allegations are pure fiction. It is a fairy-tale lie,” he added.
Similarly, Velasco’s camp previously said the allegations against him had “no basis.” —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worse
articles.summary:
High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment can be added to the federal treasurer’s wall of worries

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.

Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.
In other words, things are getting worse, not better.
Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.

Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.
The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.
Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month.
That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November.
Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles.
Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.

Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.

With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.
High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.
It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.
“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.

“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.
after newsletter promotion

“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”
The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.
Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.
But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.
His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”

Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.
Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.
That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?
This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.

articles.title: Nigeria and Kenya Ebola patients may have crossed paths at Uganda airport, officials say
articles.summary: Officials say they both travelled through Entebbe International Airport on 3 October.
articles.byline: Makuochi Okafor, Simi Jolaoso, Wycliffe Muia

blocks.text: Health officials are investigating whether Ebola patients in Nigeria and Kenya may have crossed paths at Uganda's main airport earlier this month.

Both travelled through Entebbe airport on 3 October, and investigators are examining whether they could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said on Thursday.
Dr Wessam Mankoula, the agency's head of emergency preparedness and response, said this was "one of the possible scenarios", but stressed that no link had been established.
Nigeria is battling its first Ebola case in more than a decade, while Kenya has confirmed nine infections, including one death.
The Nigerian patient, a 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman who lives in Abuja, is receiving treatment in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

She is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Nigeria, Switzerland's foreign ministry confirmed to Reuters news agency. Her husband, who accompanied her on a trip to Uganda, is also in isolation but has not developed symptoms.
The woman returned to Nigeria on 3 October after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, travelling through Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, where she had a two-hour stopover.
She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive for Ebola on 20 October.
Health officials are now trying to establish where she contracted the virus and whether her movements overlapped with those of the Kenyan patient.

The Kenyan man had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on 3 October. He later died, becoming Kenya's first recorded Ebola death in the current outbreak.
Although both patients passed through Entebbe airport on the same day, health officials have not established whether they met, used the same facilities or had any other contact.
"One of the issues we are currently investigating has been some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
Investigators are also examining whether the two infections could have a common source.
The WHO said it was too early to determine where the Nigerian woman became infected.
"The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together," said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.
He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.
Nigeria's Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said it was carrying out genomic sequencing, which could help investigators understand whether the infection is related to other cases.
"The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority," said Dr Pavel Ursu, the WHO's representative in Nigeria.
Ugandan health officials previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo for business, where the current Ebola outbreak began.
However, the WHO, Africa CDC and Nigeria's health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she had visited the country.
Uganda has maintained that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says the woman's travel through the country does not necessarily mean she contracted the virus there.
Meanwhile, Africa CDC said Nigeria had identified additional people who may have been exposed to the woman, beyond the 44 contacts initially reported.

"Most of those contacts, they are from the healthcare workers in different facilities where this case has been receiving treatment. We have also some few family members," Mankoula told journalists on Thursday.
He said Nigerian authorities were working to identify and quarantine those considered at high risk, but declined to give an updated figure before the government released its findings.
"The position of the country [is] to bring those high-risk contact and put them on quarantine," he added.
Dr Ursu said the woman was receiving a high standard of clinical care and that her condition was stable.
In Kenya, the first group of people quarantined after possible exposure to Ebola will begin returning home on Sunday after completing 21 days of monitoring without developing symptoms.
Health Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said all nine confirmed infections were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission.
"We are not out of the woods," he warned, urging the public to remain vigilant but not panic.
He said the remaining eight patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between the DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.
Dr Otim warned that the long and porous border between the two countries made it difficult to screen everyone entering or leaving, as many people used unofficial crossing points.
The WHO's regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for "regional vigilance" and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like flu.
The virus can cause fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before they develop symptoms.
Health authorities say tracing contacts quickly, isolating suspected cases and providing early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

articles.title: Magnitude-7 earthquake hits China’s Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes
articles.summary:
Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, officials say, while at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region,…

blocks.text: A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued after the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units and about 3,000 tents and folding beds as well as torches and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191km (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18km.
The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10km, according to its website.
Videos posted by China’s national broadcaster CCTV said showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.
More than 300 police officers had been dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilised almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported.
Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that had forced local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows were expected in the quake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, CCTV said.
China’s leader, Xi Jinping, called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.
Nagqu is more than 300km north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.
Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.
A huge tremor in Sichuan province in 2008 left approximately 90,000 people dead or missing, including about 5,000 schoolchildren.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: UK consumer confidence falls at fastest rate since Covid as cost of living bites
articles.summary:
Economic fallout from war in Middle East adds to pressures on consumers and on chancellor before budget

Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid…

blocks.text: Consumer confidence in the UK has fallen at the fastest rate outside the Covid pandemic since the 2016 Brexit vote as the escalating economic damage from the war in the Middle East hits Britain.

With less than a week before John Healey’s first budget, the latest barometer from the data company GfK indicated confidence plunged by 11 percentage points in October to -24 amid pressure on consumers from the rising cost of living.

Highlighting the challenge for Andy Burnham and his chancellor before the statement on Wednesday, GfK said its consumer confidence index last fell by this much in a single month in July 2016, following the shock leave result in the EU referendum.

The index – which has been closely tracked by the government and the Bank of England for early warning signs from the economy since the early 1970s – recorded its largest ever fall, of 25 points, in March 2020 just after the start of the first UK lockdown.

The latest snapshot represents a marked change from the summer, when GfK said a “Burnham bounce”, along with a strong World Cup run by the men’s England football team and sunny weather, lifted the mood of consumers in its long-running monthly survey.

Neil Bellamy, consumer insights director at GfK, said: “Relentless cost-of-living pressures, against an international backdrop of unresolved regional conflicts that are themselves contributing to domestic inflation now at 3.5%, appear to have swept aside the nascent optimism we saw following the appointment of a new UK prime minister this summer.”

It comes as consumers face a fresh squeeze on living standards triggered by the unfolding war in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have surged close to record highs and energy bills have increased in advance of a difficult winter for households already feeling the pinch from years of price increases.
Over the past five years analysis by the Trades Union Congress shows that UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills.

With less than a week before his tax and spending speech to the Commons, the chancellor is under pressure to take action to support households amid warnings that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.

Healey has pledged to use his statement to announce “breathing space” measures to ease the pressure. However, he has also warned that the government has limited resources to intervene as the Middle East conflict pushes the UK’s borrowing costs to the highest level in decades.
Official figures released on Wednesday show headline inflation rose by more than expected to 3.5% last month, while the government deficit was a worse-than-forecast £24.5bn.

In a double blow for the chancellor, the twin pieces of bad news underscore the fact that consumers are facing a renewed cost of living squeeze, just as Healey is also under increased financial pressure.
According to the latest figures from GfK, consumers became less confident about the strength of their own personal finances, as well as the general outlook for the British economy at large.

The major purchase index fell by 14 points to -22 in October, suggesting that consumers could be bracing to cut back on spending over the winter months to make room in their finances for higher energy bills.
Separate figures from the CBI show investment intentions among manufacturing businesses were subdued as cost pressures remained high in the three months to October.
Manufacturing output is expected to stabilise in the next three months, according to the lobby group’s latest Industrial Trends Survey. However, cost pressures for businesses remained elevated.

Cameron Martin, senior economist at the CBI, said: “If the government wants to meaningfully tackle the cost of living, it must give manufacturers the breathing space to invest and drive the productivity growth needed to sustain rising real wages.
“Next week’s budget must deliver this by cutting business electricity costs, reducing labour costs and reforming business rates to support rather than hinder investment and growth.”
The Treasury has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Nationals leader Matt Canavan eyes move to lower house as pollster warns of One Nation wipeout
articles.summary:
Michelle Landry announces she will not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia at the next election

  • Get our

blocks.text: Matt Canavan could attempt a switch to the House of Representatives after a colleague announced her looming retirement, as a leading pollster said the Nationals leader had a “zero per cent” chance of holding his Senate seat if the One Nation polling surge remains unchanged.
Veteran National MP Michelle Landry on Friday announced she would not recontest her Queensland seat of Capricornia, around Rockhampton, at the next election.
Responding to speculation that Pauline Hanson could attempt her own switch to run in that seat, Landry said One Nation was “not very pleasant” and criticised the party’s “obnoxious” cartoon videos.
“I think they need to pull their heads in,” Landry said of One Nation.

There has been heavy speculation Canavan will run in Capricornia. Canavan earlier this month said he would do “whatever it takes” to hold Capricornia, telling Sky News: “if I’m required, if it is required to keep a seat, to hold one more seat in the lower house somewhere. I will do it.”

On Friday, at a press conference with Landry, Canavan shrugged off questions but did not rule it out. Landry denied she was pushed to resign from Capricornia to make way for another Nationals member, and declined to speculate on who could run as her replacement.

The Coalition leader, Angus Taylor, also declined to speculate about a Canavan lower house switch when asked at a separate press conference, only praising the Nationals leader as an “extraordinary colleague”.

Kos Samaras, director at polling group Redbridge, said Canavan faced losing his Senate spot in 2028, pointing to current polling showing a One Nation surge which he claimed could see Hanson’s party win upper house seats currently held by the Coalition.

Senators up for re-election in Queensland at the next poll include two LNP members in James McGrath and Canavan, two Labor, one Greens, and Hanson herself. But One Nation’s surge means the party could win one or more additional Senate seats, most likely at the expense of the second person on the LNP ticket – Canavan.
“He goes from a 0% chance of being elected as a senator, to potentially winning [in Capricornia],” Samaras said.
“That will also be difficult, because of One Nation, but he [Canavan] is in a better position going downstairs.”
Last month’s Guardian Essential poll showed One Nation with a 25% primary vote nationwide, with Labor at 29% and the Coalition at an all-time low 22%.
Landry took a parting shot at One Nation, and the prospects if Hanson were to attempt a run in Capricornia, in her press conference.
“I’ve had a lot of dealings with One Nation over the years, and I can tell you, most of it hasn’t been very pleasant.
“When I look at people that move into an area to run for a political position, it doesn’t usually end well,” Landry said.

Samaras pointed to Redbridge polling showing what he called “a complete wipeout” of the Coalition at the hands of One Nation, specifically a large analysis from May showing Hanson’s party winning up to 59 seats nationally – largely from the Liberals and Nationals.
“On current polling, they’ll win nearly every seat the LNP holds in Queensland,” Samaras said, including Senate spots.
“If there’s a state in this country that’s good for One Nation, it’s Queensland.”
However, Samaras noted large “volatility” in polling nationwide, noting that the Queensland’s state LNP government was polling well.
“Things can change,” he said.

articles.title: Ex-Bangsamoro solon Rimbang denies bankrolling P3.5-billion Laos shabu shipment
articles.summary: Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Rimbang has denied financing the recently foiled attempt to ship P3.5 billion worth of "shabu (meth)" from Laos into the Philippines.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 11:39am
Edrieza Rimbang, former Bangsamoro parliament member, denies allegations of having planned the recently foiled attempt to fly in drugs from Laos to the Philippines.
Office of the 1st MP Sultan Edrieza Rimbang Al-Hadj, MPA
MANILA, Philippines — Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Rimbang has denied financing the recently foiled attempt to ship P3.5 billion worth of "shabu (meth)" from Laos into the Philippines.
In a nine-minute video posted on Facebook on Thursday, October 22, Rimbang denied having connived with any individual to arrange for drug shipments to enter the Philippines.
"What they are saying, that we are involved in that Laos [shipment], is not true," he said in Filipino.

He also dismissed claims that he bankrolled the operation, pointing to his defeat in last month's Bangsamoro parliamentary elections, which he blamed on a lack of funds. "Now they are saying I financed drugs. Where would I get the money?" he said.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla named Rimbang on October 16 as one of 11 persons of interest in the case, saying he was "believed to be the financier of the entire operation."
Remulla claimed Rimbang chartered the private jet that carried the 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine intercepted in Laos.

The flight had first been scheduled to land at a general aviation hangar at Ninoy Aquino International Airport on September 26, but its date was moved three times, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines.
The flight manifest had deceptively declared the aircraft's cargo as vape products.

Rimbang was among four persons of interest who did not appear before the PNP Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, along with Abdulkarim Macalatas, whom Remulla identified as the intended consignee, Abdullah Rimbang Macarimbang and Aldren Samante.
Rimbang did not say in the video whether he would honor the subpoena. He did reject social media posts claiming he had fled abroad. "I did not leave. I did not leave our country," he said.
Nartatez said on October 16 that Rimbang was believed to be in the Philippines.
Rimbang was appointed to the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, the region's interim parliament, by former President Rodrigo Duterte in 2019.
He ran for the Lanao del Sur 3rd district seat in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao's first parliamentary elections on September 14 but lost to Abdul Rauf Adiong of the SIAP party.
In the video, Rimbang said he owed his appointment to the Duterte family and suggested his political ties explained why he had been named.
"Let's not link me to Laos just because I am pro-Duterte," he said.

Remulla has said investigators found no evidence connecting the Duterte family to the shipment, though he noted that Rimbang and the family had long been political allies who ran under the same party.

articles.title: Mother sought advice from Alan Jones after broadcaster’s alleged indecent assault of her son, court hears
articles.summary:
Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching

The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster…

blocks.text: The mother of the youngest alleged victim of Alan Jones continued to seek advice from the broadcaster after the teenager was allegedly indecently assaulted at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm, a Sydney court has heard.

The divorced mother told the Downing Centre court she had developed a pattern of not trusting herself and she continued her correspondence with Jones because: “I knew he knew about everything; he had an opinion about everything.
“I was in a web of dependency with Mr Jones,” the witness said on her last day in the witness box on Friday.
She previously said she corresponded with Jones after he allegedly kissed the 17-year-old and put his tongue inside his mouth out of fear Jones would withdraw his financial support.
During cross examination, defence barrister Claire O’Neill suggested the mother continued to correspond with Jones not because she was scared but because she wanted more money out of him.
O’Neill asked: “You did not continue to communicate with Mr Jones because you were scared of his influence over your finances, did you?”
The witness replied: “I absolutely was.”
Her son, complainant A, is one of five men who allege Jones, 85, sexually touched or indecently assaulted them between 2003 and 2020. All five have now completed their evidence.
Jones has pleaded not guilty to 21 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching.

Under cross-examination by the defence, the witness agreed she wrote to Jones about her son’s late university application, a superannuation payment, outstanding legal fees and attaining a Sydney Cricket Ground membership for her son.
She was shown an email in which she provided Jones with an update on her son’s university application. The defence asked: “You wanted to lay the groundwork for having Mr Jones pay the [legal] bill?
The mother said the suggestion was “absolute rubbish” and she was “proud of him” for finishing year 12 under difficult circumstances and wanted to convey that in the email.
She agreed she sent Jones information about the cost of repairs to her Land Rover but denied she was asking him to pay the bill.
“You have told lies in this court about why you continued to have contact with Jones?” O’Neill asked.
The witness replied: “Absolutely disagree, that’s rubbish.”
O’Neill: “You were taking advantage of Mr Jones’s generosity for as long as you could?”
Witness: “Absolute rubbish.”
When she was asked why she shared personal information with Jones about the deterioration of her relationship with her son she became emotional.
“My son, who was a child, suffered trauma and didn’t share it with anyone and it had an effect on his relationship with me and a lot of other people.”
Asked by prosecutor Georgina Wright what that trauma was, she replied: “I was referring to what happened to him at Fitzroy Falls”.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Serbia: Tens of thousands rally ahead of elections
articles.summary: After two years of student-led protests, Serbia will soon vote in what observers describe as a referendum-like snap election pitting strongman Aleksandar Vucic against the student movement.

image.caption: The crowds at the rally were optimistic that they would be free of populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in a matter of daysImage: Uros Arsic/REUTERS

blocks.text: Over a hundred thousand of Serbians took to the streets in support of Serbia's protesting youth movement on Thursday, in what was the final campaign rally ahead of a pivotal election challenge to the Balkan nation's populist strongman, Aleksandar Vucic.

Crowds poured into Belgrade's central square from all directions and filled up several blocks around the area. Independent crowd-monitoring group Archive of Public Gatherings estimated about 150,000 people were at the rally.

blocks.caption: Protesters filled Belgrade's Slavija square and its surrounding streetsImage: Marko Djurica/REUTERS

blocks.text: The optimistic crowds chanted "victory" ahead of Sunday's crunch vote which comes after two years of student-led protests against Vucic. It was triggered by a 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station which killed 16 people.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, has since snowballed from demands for an independent investigation into the incident, into calls for early elections.
The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election
What happened at the protest?
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is the veteran leader's biggest threat.
Thousands supporting it flocked to Belgrade's streets on Thursday.

"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told the French AFP news agency as she arrived for the students' rally.
"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible," she said.

blocks.caption: The Students List's election ticket is polling neck and neck with Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive PartyImage: DW

blocks.text: "We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours," university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd who chanted "Victory, victory!"
"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!"
How has Vucic responded?
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade now, either as prime minister or president of the Balkan country.
As pressure from the protests mounted, he announced a snap election last month. He has resigned as president, but many argue it is a tactical move so that he could run for prime minister.
This is now the biggest electoral challenge his party, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), has faced since it was elected into power in 2012.
The leader, meanwhile, has regularly accused the students movement of being a foreign-funded coup.

"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," Vucic said to a sports hall full of supporters on Thursday. "Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!"
Serbia's student revolt: Will it bring about change?
Worries of post-result unrest
Days before the vote, Serbian civil societies warned that conditions for "free and fair election" were lacking.

"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said, arguing it was supported by documented findings.

Analysts warn that a close election result could lead to post-election instability, if both sides declare victory. Vucic, who controls the Serbian police, has said he would quash any unrest after the vote.

While several minor parties are also in the race for premiership, observers say that there is a referendum-like atmosphere between Vucic and the students' movement which could sideline other parties in the 250-member parliament.

articles.title: Duterte ICC trial: Prosecutors seek to admit three witness accounts
articles.summary: One witness discusses 13 killings charged under Count 3, including a death during a police “One Time Big Time” operation.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 10:35am
ICC proceedings tied to former president Rodrigo Duterte's so-called drug war scrutinize command responsibility, police operations and the families' long-running calls for justice.
Philstar.com illustration

MANILA, Philippines — International Criminal Court prosecutors have asked judges to admit the recorded statements of three witnesses who they say can describe the policy to "neutralize" alleged drug suspects under former president Rodrigo Duterte.

One witness speaks about 13 of the killings charged against Duterte, including one during a police "One Time Big Time" operation, according to the redacted version of the court filing dated October 21 and signed by Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.
The three witnesses, all women, were already on the prosecution's witness list. The defense has known since August 31 that prosecutors planned to present them under this procedure.

Prosecutors are asking the court to allow transcripts of their earlier interviews with investigators to be admitted as evidence in place of most of their direct examination, saying this would save court time.

Under Rule 68(3) of the court's rules, each witness must still appear in court, confirm her statement is accurate and consent to its use. Duterte's lawyers can cross-examine them, and the judges and lawyers for victims can still question them.
All three accounts relate to Count 3, which covers killings in barangay "clearance" operations against alleged small-time drug users and pushers from about July 2016 to September 2018.

When the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed the charges against Duterte on April 23, Count 3 covered 45 victims, 43 of whom were killed. Count 1 covers 19 killings in Davao City from 2013 to 2016, when Duterte was mayor, and Count 2 covers 14 killings of alleged "high-value targets" in 2016 and 2017.
Pattern of killings
The identities of the three witnesses were withheld in the public document.
The statement of one witness, who is labelled in the filing as "P-0008," comes from two interviews with prosecution investigators.
In several of the 13 killings she discusses, she allegedly described events before the victims died. Names, dates and places are redacted in the public filing.

The filing does not say where or when the "One Time Big Time" operation took place. Police in the Philippines are known to have used the term for simultaneous, large-scale anti-drug sweeps, where deadly shootouts also occur.
Prosecutors said P-0008's evidence shows the "modus operandi and pattern of violence" police used against alleged criminals.
Another witness, labelled "P-1164," spoke about three charged killings by police.
Meanwhile, "P-1303" gives evidence about an individual who was shot dead by police, but her relationship to him is redacted in the filing. Prosecutors said her account relates to one charged killing.
Prosecutors said the three accounts are internally consistent and match evidence expected from other witnesses, including "P-0003," who is due to testify in person.
They said the evidence also helps prove that the killings were part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians, a requirement for crimes against humanity.
The prosecutors said the three witnesses will show there was a policy to "neutralise" alleged criminals through violence, including murder.
All three women were told their interviews were voluntary and were informed of their rights, and each confirmed she answered of her own free will, the filing said.

articles.title: Airbnb scraps guest checkout chores such as cleaning
articles.summary: Under new rules, guests will no longer have to do tasks that cleaners would normally handle. Hosts can now only make "reasonable" requests, such as leaving dirty dishes in the sink and sorting trash…

image.caption: Asking guests to do cleaning tasks can negatively impact their stay, Airbnb warns hostsImage: Jonas Been Henriksen/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chores such as washing dishes, stripping beds and taking out the trash at the end of your Airbnb stay will soon be a thing of the past.
Under new rules unveiled this week, the short-term rental platform says hosts should only make "reasonable" requests of guests.

Airbnb said hosts are generally not allowed to "ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes."

blocks.caption: 'Unreasonable' demands like changing the sheets are being scrappedImage: Sviatlana Barysenka/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why did Airbnb introduce the new rules?
Checkout chores have been a contentious issue for guests, especially in cases where they are also charged cleaning fees.
Airbnb has previously admitted that such fees can create confusion between guests and hosts.
"Guests expect checkout to be relatively simple, and most want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said in a message to hosts on the platform.
"Asking them to do things a cleaner should handle can negatively affect their stay and your reviews."

blocks.caption: Guests will still be expected to leave dirty dishes in the sink or dishwasherImage: Thomas Trutschel/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: The new rules come amid growing protests against housing shortages in many European cities, with protesters arguing that short-term rentals such as Airbnb have pushed them out of their own cities.
In September, the European Commission proposed more restrictions on Airbnb and other short-term rental companies in tourist hubs.
What else do the new Airbnb rules for hosts say?
Guests can still be asked to leave dirty dishes in the sink, to gather used towels and separate trash and recyclables, for example.
Hosts can also require guests to put trash in animal-proof containers areas where bears are active or ask them to "limit shower time due to local drought-related water restrictions."
But hosts will no longer be allowed to ban guests from using amenities listed in the property description, such as air conditioners, nor will they be allowed to fine guests.
Instead, hosts must seek compensation for any damage from insurance that the platform provides.
The new policy applies to bookings starting on November 20.

articles.title: Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcast
articles.summary: Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips, heads to Roraima to hear what’s at stake for the rainforest and the communities that live there in the Brazilian presidential runoff…
articles.byline: Presented by Helen Pidd with Tom Phillips; produced by Ivor Manley, Eli Block and Ross Burns; executive producer Sami Kent

blocks.text: For the Amazon and the communities who live there, the stakes in Sunday’s Brazilian presidential election runoff could scarcely be higher.

Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips heads to Roraima, the country’s most northern state, to hear from voters, preachers and politicians in a region that heavily backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round.

He finds them all hopeful that the far-right candidate will bring back the mining that his father Jair so heartily encouraged when in power in an administration that oversaw the felling of 11m acres (4.5m hectares) of rainforest.
Tom also meets Indigenous activists determined to fight back even if the Bolsonaros take power again.
Helen Pidd asks what it will all mean, not only for Brazil but also for the climate crisis more broadly.

articles.title: Ex-Bangsamoro MP Rimbang denies involvement in P3.5B Laos drug shipment
articles.summary: Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang on Friday denied involvement in the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of illegal drugs from Laos to the Philippines.

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 9:55am
Former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang on Friday denied involvement in the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of illegal drugs from Laos to the Philippines.
“Wala po itong katotohanan (there is no truth to this),” Rimbang said in a video posted on his social media page.

“‘Yung sinasabi po nila na [nag] import po tayo nung sa Laos, hindi po totoo ‘yun. Wala po akong nakausap na any government dito sa Pilipinas o mga tao dito sa Pilipinas para magpunta sa Laos o magdala dito ng kahit anong bagay na makakasira sa ating bansa,” he added.

(What they are saying about us importing that from Laos is not true. I have not spoken to any government or any people here in the Philippines about going to Laos or bringing anything here that could harm our country.)
Last week, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla tagged Rimbang as the Mindanao politician allegedly involved in the smuggling. He said Rimbang was believed to be the financier of the entire operation.
According to Remulla, Rimbang is married to Princess Rohaniah Rimbang, the sister of the wife of alias "Fahad" who was arrested at an airport in Laos.
Rimbang appealed to the government to refrain from disclosing his family’s names and pictures on social media.
He said that his family and children’s lives have been affected.
“Nakikiusap ako sa ating gobyerno na 'wag po natin ilagay sa social media ‘yung mga pangalan namin, ‘yung mga mukha namin na wala namang ebidensya, wala naman tayong ginawang masama,” he said.
(I am appealing to our government not to post our names and faces on social media when there is no evidence and we have done nothing wrong.)
“Pinanganak ako na wala akong naging kaso sa gobyerno, lalo sa droga. Hindi ako nakipagkuntsaba sa mga ilegal na gawain kasi ayaw ko masira ang pangalan ko,” he added.
(I was born without ever having a case against me with the government, especially involving drugs. I never colluded in illegal activities because I don’t want to tarnish my name.)
The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) has issued subpoenas to 11 persons of interest. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Flu cases rise on west coast earlier than usual as US health experts encourage vaccine
articles.summary:
California flu test rate at 9.65%, higher than normal 1% rate for early October, amid mutation of H1N1 influenza A strain

Flu cases on the west coast are on the rise months earlier than…

blocks.text: Flu cases on the west coast are on the rise months earlier than normal, prompting US health experts to stress the importance of the annual vaccine.
Flu activity typically ramps up in December, hitting its peak in February. But this season has kicked into action earlier this year, with higher positive cases than normal recorded.
Several experts have credited the early seasonal start to a new mutation of the influenza A strain H1N1, which was behind the 2009 swine flu pandemic.
This strain has accounted for 242 of 300 influenza viruses reported by public health laboratories to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to date (CDC).

In California, during the past two flu seasons, influenza test positivity hovered slightly above 1% in early October. As of 10 October, that rate is 9.65%, according to data from the state’s department of health.
As of 11 October, Utah has recorded 242 influenza A cases, up from 10 cases this time last year, according to Germ Watch, an Intermountain Health database.
Parts of central Oregon have also seen an influenza A surge.
Influenza vaccines can reduce severe illness and hospitalization, according to the American Medical Association, which recommends flu shots for all people 6 months and older.
The 2026-27 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, ​target H1N1, H3N2 – the dominant strain last flu season – and one influenza B virus.
Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year’s vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.
However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, “it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early”, Hensley said via ​email.
Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.
Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: ‘I’ve killed someone’: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to friend and asked for help moving bodies, court told
articles.summary:
Friend tells jury Lamarre-Condon told him in early 2024 ‘I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly confessed to killing two men, telling his friend it was an “out-of-body experience”, before attempting to play it off as a joke, a court has been told.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, is accused of fatally shooting couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Lamarre-Condon’s friend, whose identity is suppressed, told the New South Wales supreme court on Friday that the officer arrived at his workplace the day Baird and Davies were killed.
Lamarre-Condon told him, “I’ve done something”, and when the friend asked for an explanation, the policeman said “I’ve killed someone”, the jury was told.
“I said ‘Are you fucking kidding me?’, he said, ‘I wish I was’,” the friend told the court. “He said it just felt like an out-of-body experience and it just wasn’t him.”
The friend said when he asked how Lamarre-Condon did it, the officer said with a gun.
He then made a gesture with his fingers indicating a firearm and said “pew pew”, the friend told the court.
When asked for more details, Lamarre-Condon allegedly said: “I shot the first one through the head and the second one through the door.”
Lamarre-Condon then said the second person wasn’t meant to be shot but he “couldn’t leave any witnesses”, the friend told the jury.
The officer asked his friend to leave work to help clean up and move the bodies, the court heard.
The friend then returned to his workplace and explained the situation to his team lead, who told him to tell Lamarre-Condon he had a meeting he couldn’t miss.
Lamarre-Condon later messaged the friend and asked “I should get an Oscar, hey?” before going on video call and saying “Got you”.
When the friend got upset, Lamarre-Condon said, “it’s not a fucking joke, you’re mentally fucking with me”, the court was told.
The policeman responded: “OK it is real but I just didn’t want you to tell anyone.”
Earlier on Friday, the friend revealed he had travelled overseas in late 2023 for a trip with Lamarre-Condon.
He said that while overseas, Lamarre-Condon told the friend: “I need to find a spot … to purchase a silencer.”
The officer explained he was going hunting on a mate’s farm, the jury was told.
The two found what they believed to be a gun store, but it had either closed down or there had been a fake ad, the friend said.
after newsletter promotion
The friend returned to Australia before Lamarre-Condon and soon after received a photo from the officer showing multiple airsoft guns.
The witness on Friday said he asked if Lamarre-Condon had found what he was looking for and the officer said: “No, it was an airsoft gun shop, no suppressor there.”
Back in Sydney, Lamarre-Condon drove his friend to a national park and took a police service weapon out of a paper bag, the jury was told.
Lamarre-Condon gave his friend a police-issued radio and asked him to listen for any reports of police movement towards them after the officer shot the firearm.

“I said, ‘You can’t really shoot your police-issued firearm.’ He then told me that they were training bullets he had taken previously from a police shoot they do once a year,” the friend told the court.
He said Lamarre-Condon then fired the weapon and asked his friend how loud it was.
He tried again, shooting a bullet into the bushland before asking “does this make any difference on the sound?”, the jury heard.
“He’s asked me whether it would be louder or would you hear this in a house?” the friend said on Friday. “I proceeded to say ‘You could hear that anywhere, it was super loud’.”
On their way home, Lamarre-Condon then allegedly said, “you can’t tell anyone about this”, the court heard.
The defence team claims Baird and Davies were accidentally shot when the accused acted in “self-defence”.
Lamarre-Condon then “panicked considerably”, cleaning up the scene and disposing of the bodies, defence lawyer John Stratton SC said.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
