articles.title: The haunting call of Canada's common loon is becoming less common amid widespread declines, study suggests
articles.summary: A new study published Thursday in the journal FACETS reveals severe declines in loon chick populations across North America over the past three decades or more.

image.caption: A common loon baby rests on its parent's back on a lake in northwestern Ontario in July 2026. A new study published Thursday in the journal FACETS reveals severe declines in loon chick populations across North America over the past three decades or more. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A new study published Thursday in the journal FACETS reveals severe declines in loon chick populations across North America over the past three decades or more.
Prairies, Atlantic provinces among North American regions seeing steepest drops
It's a haunting sound synonymous with nightfall in the summer when an eerie calm spreads over glassy wetlands and cottage country lake surfaces across Canada.

But the trembling call of the common loon may be getting less common amid "substantial" North American declines, new research suggests — with Prairie and Atlantic populations suffering among the steepest losses.
"The most alarming thing is the extent of this decline," said Matthew Fuirst, an ecologist with Birds Canada and one of the authors of a study published Thursday in the journal FACETS.

Canada is home to 94 per cent of the global common loon population, with an estimated 254,000 breeding couples (half a million individuals) that migrate north to make the next generation every spring.

The iconic species, a minted representation of which many Canadians routinely carry around in their pockets and purses, has faced threats before — from DDT to lead-based fishing tackle and mercury poisoning.
From the CBC archives: Lost loons (1971)
Now, the latest team of nearly two dozen collaborators from Canada and the U.S. cite climate change among a list of possible drivers for declines in loon chicks.

The study analyzes loon breeding data from 3,421 lakes the past three or so decades, half of which came from thousands of volunteer observations as part of the long-running citizen science effort, the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey.
There were "significant declines" in how many chicks were observed in that time in a majority of regions.
Loon chick productivity rate was a benchmark measure defined by researchers as observations of six-week-old young across nearly 46,000 observations of loon pairs.
The study suggests a 40 per cent average drop in loon chick productivity in 10 of 12 study areas — including in B.C. and Ontario — over the past three or so decades.

Loon chick productivity sank even more starkly by 65 per cent across Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba since the early 1990s. Meanwhile, Canada's East Coast saw a 74 per cent reduction, according to researchers.
Quebec and the state of Maine were the only regions where chick productivity seemed more or less stable.
A common loon range map that appeared in the new FACETS journal article documenting loon declines in North America. (FACETS journal)

The team notes that while the loon chick population isn't the only measure of how healthy or stable the population is, the long-term declines could "signal looming population declines" in the Prairies, Ontario, Atlantic Canada and in New York, Massachusetts and New Hampshire.
The researchers looked at nearly 46,000 instances of loon pairs observed on a given lake and where eggs or chicks were recorded, but no six-week-old chicks were seen.

"This study design is very strong, and frankly, I consider the results that they are presenting here as being alarming," said Nicola Koper, dean of the faculty of environment at University of Northern British Columbia, who was not part of the study.
Koper is co-author of Best Places to Bird in the Prairies and she was professor of conservation biology for nearly two decades at the University of Manitoba before moving on to UNBC.
She said the losses are dramatic on their own, but the fact they've happened over only three decades is startling.

"Some [readers] will be 30 years old, and so if they think back to whether they feel like they saw more loons with babies when they were younger, the chances are that that's accurate, that they have themselves observed this change," said Koper.
Climate change behind declines
The research team says the cause of the declines may vary depending on the region and that unknown is something they're digging into now, said Fuirst.
But in all cases the losses are propelled by human activity.

items: Fewer loons on your lake? It may be due to climate change

blocks.text: "Human development and the development of shorelines, the environmental contaminants from climate change is another threat we're experiencing, " said Fuirst.
"As climate change influences weather patterns, the rain which is acidic makes the lake more acidic and thus reducing the amount of fish that are available for those loons."
A common loon baby rests on its parent's back in northwestern Ontario in July 2026. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
Warmer temperatures associated with climate change have also brought more rain and storm events to loon habitat.
That could be destroying low-lying loon nests or drowning eggs during flood events when waters rise or are disturbed from violent wave action, said Koper.
Recent research from the U.S. Midwest has also made a connection between poor loon health and lower water clarity, which can arise from sediment running into lakes as a result of more frequent rains.
That makes it harder for loons to see and hunt their minnow, crayfish and other prey in the water, said Fuirst.
"It's this domino effect of climate change basically down to water quality," he said.

The study pooled together Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba data into a single Prairie category because there wasn't enough data to analyze loon numbers confidently in each of those regions on their own.

items: For the birds: Manitobans pick loon to grace specialty licence plate

blocks.text: Koper said that may be more a reflection of how many of the many lakes in the Prairies are inaccessible to volunteers or otherwise unpopulated.
Fuirst said anglers should opt for lead-free, less-toxic tackle options, boaters should avoid disturbing loons and cottagers should ensure shorelines remain as natural as possible.
"The everyday person can take several actions to help steward lakes and the loons that they rely on," he said.

Koper encourages people concerned by the findings to take action and get involved in citizen science projects like the Canadian Lakes Loon Survey and "advocate with ... politicians about the importance of climate change and how it's impacting our wildlife and our lives."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bryce Hoye is a multi-platform journalist with a background in wildlife biology. He has worked for CBC Manitoba for over a decade with stints producing at CBC's Quirks & Quarks and Front Burner. He was a 2024-25 Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. He is also Prairie rep for outCBC. He has won a national Radio Television Digital News Association award for a 2017 feature on the history of the fur trade, and a 2023 Prairie region award for an audio documentary about a Chinese-Canadian father passing down his love for hockey to the next generation of Asian Canadians.

articles.title: Department of Justice opens criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski
articles.summary:
Ex-Trump adviser and former top aide for homeland security alleged to have profited off government role

Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and ⁠top aide at the…

blocks.text: Corey Lewandowski, a former political adviser to Donald Trump and ⁠top aide at the Department ⁠of Homeland Security, ​is under criminal investigation over allegations he profited off his role in the US government, three US officials and a fourth person familiar with the matter told Reuters ⁠on Thursday.

The investigation began with a criminal referral to the justice department from the internal watchdog at DHS, according to the four people. The DHS inspector general’s office has been investigating ⁠Lewandowski’s involvement in the handling of certain government contracts, according to one of the people, a DHS official.

A lawyer ​for Lewandowski, Adam Trigg, did not immediately respond to ‌a request for comment. The ‌investigation was first reported in the Wall Street Journal, which quoted Lewandowski’s lawyer as saying that his client denies ‌all allegations of wrongdoing.
The DoJ has not yet issued subpoenas or other legal demands in the criminal investigation, according to one of the people. All four of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The justice department under Trump has investigated several prominent critics of the president, including the former FBI director James Comey and the New York attorney general Letitia James, but investigations of people close to Trump have been rare. The department has also moved ‌to dismiss several existing cases involving Trump allies, including supporters charged in connection with the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
Asked about media reports on the investigation, Trump told reporters ​that he did not know the specifics of the investigation, but said: “I want my people to be honest.”
“And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DoJ go and do whatever they have to do,” Trump added.

Lewandowski served as a top aide to the former homeland security secretary Kristi Noem during her tenure leading DHS. Trump fired Noem in March after ⁠months of controversy, including the fatal shootings of two US citizens by federal officers ​in Minneapolis and lawmakers’ questions over a $220m advertising contract promoting Noem that was ​awarded without a standard bidding process.

Lewandowski had signed some DHS contracts despite having questionable legal authority ​as a special government ‌employee, according to the ​DHS official. Certain grants ​and contracts, including those involving the Federal Emergency Management Agency, were put on hold at Lewandowski’s direction, according to two of the people, both of whom are DHS officials.
Lewandowski previously served as a campaign manager during Trump’s first presidential run in 2016 and advised his 2024 campaign.

articles.title: Execution staff warned of possibility some of Christa Pike's veins had 'blown': attorney
articles.summary: Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike's arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or…

image.caption: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike is seen in a 2023 booking photograph. Pike survived an attempted execution on Sept. 30, including two doses of pentobarbital that were administered to her. Pike's attorney has said in a court document that execution team members failed multiple times to establish workin

blocks.text: World·New

Tennessee execution team members failed multiple times to establish working IV lines in Christa Pike's arms before her attempted execution and warned that some of her veins may have ruptured, or "blown," before she was injected with the lethal drug, her attorney wrote in a court document filed Thursday.
Defence says IV team went through about 10 needles, tried several IV sites

The IV team went through about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, attorney Randy Spivey wrote in the document, which provides the most detailed account of the execution attempt so far. They even struggled to push saline through the last IV site they established, Spivey wrote.

Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
No protocol for those who survive 2nd injection
State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn't result in death, but it doesn't spell out what to do if a person survives the second injection.

After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She ultimately regained consciousness and returned to prison after being discharged.

items: Emergency medical help for Christa Pike was delayed due to confusion, 911 tapes reveal
Christa Pike discharged from hospital after surviving execution attempt, attorney says

blocks.text: The failed execution has brought renewed scrutiny to how Tennessee carries out death sentences. The court document was part of a separate legal proceeding in which people on the state's death row are challenging Tennessee's lethal injection procedures.

"Our predictions about the likelihood of botched executions have come true — and will continue to come true — without substantial change," said Kit Thomas, an attorney representing people on death row in the case.
'Wincing and grimacing'

The execution team began trying to place the two IVs required by Tennessee's execution protocols at 6:34 p.m., Spivey wrote, and when they struggled Pike helped, advising them to look in her upper arm for a viable vein.
They managed to set an IV in Pike's right arm within about six minutes, but it took them nearly an hour to complete the same process in her left arm.
Pike was "wincing and grimacing" as the IV team members moved the needles around inside her left arm, Spivey wrote, and the team members repeatedly expressed doubts after inserting the needles.

One team member said a vein "might be blowing" at 6:57 p.m. while examining an IV in Pike's left arm, but two others said they couldn't tell, Spivey wrote. "One of them said something like, ‘it's either blood or blown, I need to know,'" Spivey wrote.
The team tried again with a different spot in her left arm, and the needle appeared to be severely bent when they pulled it out, the attorney said.
"I think it's blown," the attorney recalled one of the IV team members saying at 7:07 p.m.
After more attempts, the team decided at 7:13 p.m. that they had successfully placed an IV in Pike's left arm, and they taped her hands down and hooked her up to a heart monitor.
Complained of pain
A series of phone calls were made to the execution chamber starting about five minutes later.

Spivey said it appeared the execution team members responsible for pushing the pentobarbital into the lines — a process that happens in an adjoining room — were asking the IV team for repeated checks of Pike's left arm.
Emergency vehicles are seen arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tenn., on Sept. 30, after the execution of Christa Pike was halted. (AP Photo/George Walker IV)
It's not clear exactly when the pentobarbital was pushed into the IV lines, but at 7:34 p.m., Pike said her arm was hurting.

"I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns," she said, according to her attorney. She continued to talk to her spiritual adviser for the next 10 minutes before she began making an "agitated snoring sound," Spivey wrote.

Over the next 30 minutes Pike strained, flinched, moved her head and seemed to struggle to breathe, Spivey said, and when he asked to use a phone he was led on a circuitous, seven-minute route through the facility instead of being allowed to use the phone in the execution witness room.

Spivey called fellow attorneys at 8:22 p.m. and asked them to stop the execution because a third dose of pentobarbital isn't authorized under the state's protocol. He then went back to the witness room and told the deputy attorney general that Pike needed immediate medical care.

Spivey was told an ambulance was on the way at 8:50 p.m., and 20 minutes later he was told that medical staff were providing life-saving measures, he wrote. An ambulance was seen arriving at the hospital at 9:14 p.m.

articles.title: Signal No. 2 still up over Batanes, parts of Babuyan Islands as 'Rosal' keeps strength
articles.summary: Signal No. 2 remains in Batanes and parts of the Babuyan Islands as Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) maintains strength over the sea northeast of Batanes, PAGASA said Friday.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 8:34am
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) taken as of 4:30 a.m. of Oct. 23, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 2 remains in effect over Batanes and the northeastern portion of the Babuyan Islands as Typhoon Rosal (international name: Champi) maintained its strength while moving northwestward over the sea east-northeast of Batanes, the state weather bureau PAGASA said Friday.
In its 5 a.m. bulletin on Friday, October 23, PAGASA said Rosal was packing maximum sustained winds of 155 kilometers per hour near the center and gusts of up to 190 kph.
The typhoon was last spotted 275 kilometers east-northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, moving northwestward at 15 kph.
Strong to typhoon-force winds extend up to 900 kilometers from the center.
Warning signals
PAGASA raised the following tropical cyclone wind signals:
Signal No. 2
Luzon

items: Batanes
Northeastern portion of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan, Panuitan, Calayan and Camiguin islands)

blocks.text: Residents in these areas may experience gale-force winds ranging from 62 to 88 kph within the next 24 hours, posing minor to moderate threats to life and property.
Signal No. 1

items: Rest of the Babuyan Islands
Mainland Cagayan
Northeastern portion of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, San Pablo and Palanan)
Ilocos Norte
Apayao

blocks.text: Residents in these areas may experience strong winds ranging from 39 to 61 kph within the next 36 hours, posing minimal to minor threats to life and property.
The northeast monsoon and Rosal's outer circulation will also bring strong to gale-force gusts over the following areas:

items: Friday, October 23: Most of Luzon and the Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Camiguin, Davao Occidental and Davao Oriental.
Saturday, October 24: Batanes, Babuyan Islands, Ilocos Norte, Polillo Islands, Bicol Region, Romblon, Capiz, Iloilo and Negros Occidental.
Sunday, October 25: Batanes and Babuyan Islands.

blocks.text: Sea conditions
A gale warning is in effect over the seaboards of Northern Luzon and the eastern seaboards of Central and Southern Luzon.
Very rough to very high seas, with waves reaching up to 12 meters, are expected along the northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes.

Waves may reach up to 9 meters along the remaining seaboards of Batanes and up to 8 meters along the northern and eastern seaboards of the Babuyan Islands and the northeastern seaboard of mainland Cagayan.

Seas may reach up to 6 meters along the remaining seaboards of the Babuyan Islands and mainland Cagayan, the seaboard of northern Isabela and the northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte. Waves may reach up to 5.5 meters along the remaining seaboard of Isabela and up to 5 meters along the remaining seaboard of Ilocos Norte.

Waves may reach up to 4.5 meters along the seaboards of northern Ilocos Sur and northern Aurora, the northern seaboards of Camarines Sur and Camarines Norte, and the northern and eastern seaboards of the Polillo Islands and Catanduanes.

PAGASA warned that sea travel is risky for all types of vessels in areas where very rough to very high seas are expected. Mariners were advised to remain in port or seek shelter in a safe harbor until winds and waves subside.
Operators of small vessels, including motorbancas, were also advised against venturing out to sea under rough conditions, especially if their vessels are ill-equipped or they lack experience.
Track, intensity
Rosal is expected to continue moving generally northwestward until Saturday, October 24, before moving northward and then north-northeastward between Saturday and Sunday, October 25.
On its forecast track, the typhoon is expected to exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by early Saturday.

PAGASA said Rosal is forecast to weaken gradually within the next 24 hours before weakening rapidly. It may be downgraded into a severe tropical storm by Saturday morning and further weaken into a tropical storm by Saturday evening.

articles.title: What is PHP, and how did a flaw in its code lead several websites to go dark this week?
articles.summary: PHP is an open-source computer language that powers an estimated 70 per cent of the internet. While websites being taken offline caused alarm, that was done to implement a fix — which cybersecurity…

image.caption: PHP is an open-source computer language that's widely used across the internet. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

blocks.text: A vulnerability in a critical piece of the internet's infrastructure was exposed this week, sending website operators worldwide scrambling to implement a fix.

The problem resided in part of the PHP coding language — a commonly used software that's "the backbone of the internet," according to Isaac Privett, a senior penetration tester at Toronto-based cybersecurity firm Packetlabs.
And the vulnerability had been there for years, potentially allowing bad actors to access sites, make changes to them and harvest data.

items: Canadian government sites among those offline after flaw identified in widely used computer language

blocks.text: The issue prompted many to take their websites offline while they implemented a fix, causing some websites — including government ones in Canada — to go dark.
Here's what you need to know about the PHP language, how it came to light and how serious the vulnerability is.
What is PHP?

PHP is an open-source computer language — meaning anyone can download and use it for free — that's widely used across the internet. The tech is managed by the non-profit PHP Foundation, with a team of volunteer board members and a handful of developers.

When you visit a website, a lot of pieces of information, such as images, links and what colour a site should appear in, all need to be assembled and displayed correctly to end users, explains technology analyst Carmi Levy. That's the job PHP does, Levy says, pulling those elements together and bringing websites to life.

"PHP is silently working in the background to make sure that websites make it from disjointed data sitting on a server somewhere to a live website that you can interact with on the browser, on the device that is sitting in front of you," said Levy, who's based in London, Ont.

Wiz, one of the cybersecurity firms that helped identify the issue, estimates that about 70 per cent of websites are powered by PHP, while web technology tracker W3Techs puts the figure at 75 per cent.
A programmer works with PHP code at RK Solutions software development company in Guernica, Spain, on Thursday. (Vincent West/Reuters)

That widespread use makes the tech a "foundational" piece of technology for the internet to function, Levy said, and that's why a vulnerability with it can have potentially wide-reaching consequences.
What's the problem, and how was it discovered?

A group of researchers from two cybersecurity companies — Calif and Wiz — released blog posts Wednesday, saying they had found two vulnerabilities in PHP. The researchers had been working as part of an OpenAI program to detect potential vulnerabilities across the internet, including within PHP.

Ryan Austin, a cybersecurity researcher at Calif.io who helped identify the problems, says he was aware of a 2004 security issue with PHP and sent OpenAI's GPT‑5.6 Sol to look in the same part of PHP's code for other potential bugs.
"And then a few days later, we managed to find something pretty serious," Austin said.
The PHP Foundation explained in a Wednesday release that both issues sit in "parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling."
Austin explains that when PHP encounters an error, it leaves behind memory details that can be corrupted and potentially give hackers a way into sites.
Tech analyst Carmi Levy says the fact that PHP is used so widely across the internet is part of what makes a vulnerability with it so concerning. (Submitted by Carmi Levy)

Once inside, hackers would be able to make changes to the websites — potentially installing malware or removing content from the sites — or to read sensitive data such as passwords, according to Levy.

Wiz said the vulnerabilities had existed for more than a decade. PHP Foundation acknowledged that a researcher had theorized this possible exploit in 2024, but no concrete way to enact it was found at the time.
PHP Foundation said the delay in implementing a solution was a "structural failure" caused by a lack of resources and the security team's decision process.
How serious is it?
Levy likens it to if one of the most popular makers of locks for doors discovered a master key was widely available to use.
"So someone could literally walk up to your front door, put that master key in, and they could gain access to your home," Levy said.

He explains security incidents are scored on a scale from zero to 10 using something called the Common Vulnerability Scoring System. These ones ranked as a 9.2, which Levy says means they're quite serious.
Websites around world taken down after flawed code opens them up to hackers
"One vulnerability in a technology that almost everybody uses means there's a potential global impact here," Levy said.
From Austin's perspective, it's "probably one of the worst vulnerabilities that I've ever seen."
How is it being fixed?
Cybersecurity experts say the good news is that a solution exists.
PHP Foundation released patches for the vulnerability on Wednesday and urged those who use it in their websites to implement the fix as soon as possible.
Government cybersecurity agencies and government leaders around the world, including in Canada, echoed that call.

Many websites, including government ones from Canada, France and Japan, went dark while the potential security issue was remedied. Provincial sites for Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island were down for the day, for example, but both appeared to be running again on Thursday.
The U.S. National Security Agency's cyber unit called for any organizations that couldn't patch the issue immediately to take their websites offline until the fix could be put in place.

While websites going down caused some panic, Levy says the story has a silver lining. Those sites were taken down temporarily out of an abundance of caution after researchers identified a vulnerability before hackers did, and Levy says that shows the system for flagging these kinds of things is working.
The Newfoundland and Labrador government site was offline on Wednesday after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. (CBC)

Some sites experienced hack attempts after the vulnerability was made public, but those didn't appear to work. Cloudflare's CEO, for example, said on social media that the Cloudflare network experienced tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw within 45 minutes of the announcement being made and "hundreds of thousands" within two hours.
On Wednesday, PHP Foundation told CBC News in an email they hadn't seen any evidence of hackers being able to successfully exploit the vulnerability.
Do I need to take action?

Cybersecurity experts say because the issue affects the back end of websites, the onus is mostly on those who run them — like businesses or other organizations — to make sure they're implementing the fix.
That's fairly straightforward for website operators to do in most cases — somewhat like updating a personal computer, according to Privett from Packetlabs.
"You just have to upgrade to the newest version of PHP, and that seems to handle 99 per cent of your problems," Privett said.
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter

But because the vulnerability and the fix have been made public for quite some time now, Privett says website owners will need to be on watch for indicators of possible breaches that could have happened before they were able to put the patches in place.
"It's always a good idea that after you patch, just to look for indicators of compromise in case that someone got in your system using that bug," Privett said.
Privett also encourages consumers who have their own websites or apps to double check whether they use PHP to make sure that they're protected.

And for all consumers, Levy says they can protect themselves from any potential kind of data breach by maximizing their own personal digital safety protocols. Practicing good password hygiene — by changing passwords often and not reusing them — and activating two-factor authentication, for example, help ensure that even if hackers were to access your data on a breached website, they wouldn't be as effective at using that information against you.

articles.title: ICC prosecutors seek admission of 3 more recorded testimonies vs Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: The prosecution panel in the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court to admit the recorded testimonies of three more…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 8:25am

The prosecution panel in the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has asked the International Criminal Court to admit the recorded testimonies of three more witnesses.
In a 12-page application, the Office of the Prosecutor said granting the request will expedite the proceedings by reducing the length of the witnesses' direct examination.
It added that the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-0008, P-1164, and P-1303 are relevant, reliable, and probative.

"The Three Witnesses’ evidence further goes to the proof of the contextual elements of crimes against humanity and to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines," it said.

It further said that "the introduction into evidence of the Prior Recorded Testimonies is not prejudicial to or inconsistent with the rights of the Accused, as the witnesses will be available for cross-examination by the Defence and any further questioning by the Chamber, the parties, and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims."
The prosecution said it obtained the recorded testimonies of the three witnesses during the investigation, when they were interviewed.
It added that the three were informed of the voluntary nature of their interviews and of their rights.
"At the conclusion of the interviews, the witnesses confirmed that they answered the questions of their own free will and had no complaints about the way the interview was conducted," it said.
The document was signed by acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang.
Duterte is detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands. His trial is scheduled for November 30.
The drug war saw at least 6,000 people dead, with rights groups believing that the number could be as high as 30,000. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Attack on actor Tiger Shroff is dark reminder of Bollywood's gangster past
articles.summary: The attack on Shroff has revived memories of the 1990s, when gangsters wielded influence over the industry.

blocks.text: On Sunday evening, Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff went to play football in Juhu, a leafy, affluent Mumbai neighbourhood where film stars live, fans congregate and celebrity sightings are a part of life. But as the 36-year-old was leaving the ground in his BMW, shots rang out. His driver was wounded, as was a vlogger who had come to film the actor.
Shroff, whose films usually include elaborate action sequences and choreographed escapes, had just survived an actual shooting attempt.
Four days later, the case still dominates headlines in India, with each new revelation spawning fresh theories, competing claims and a growing list of alleged conspiracies.
Police have detained or arrested 10 suspects, with investigators tracing alleged weapon deliveries through several states and examining payments made to the alleged attackers.

The attempted shooting has also brought the name of Lawrence Bishnoi, one of India's most notorious gangsters, back into the headlines. Soon after the attack, a screenshot of a social media post purportedly made by an alleged associate of the Bishnoi gang circulated online, claiming responsibility. A separate audio recording emerged in which a man identifying himself as Anil Pandit repeated the claim and said Shroff had been targeted over his alleged links to actor Salman Khan, who Bishnoi has been threatening for years.
Mumbai police have not verified the claims or established that the Bishnoi gang was behind the attempted shooting. Investigators are still trying to determine who ordered the attack and why.

The targeting of Shroff follows a series of threats and attacks involving prominent Bollywood figures, including gunfire outside Khan's home in 2024 and filmmaker Rohit Shetty's house earlier this year. Together, the incidents have revived fears about the reach of organised crime into the film industry, stirring memories of a darker era in Mumbai's history.

During the 1990s and early 2000s, the city's underworld exerted formidable influence over the film industry, financing productions, demanding protection money and sometimes using violence to enforce its demands. It took years of police operations, and the gradual arrival of institutional financing, to loosen that grip.
Now, as fresh allegations and theories emerge almost daily, a question that once seemed to belong to Mumbai's past has returned: is the underworld trying to control Bollywood again?
Those who confronted organised crime in Mumbai at its peak say the answer is not as straightforward as the attempt to shoot Shroff might suggest.

D Sivanandhan, who took charge of Mumbai's Crime Branch in 1998, remembers a time when a phone call from Dubai, where some of the most notorious gang leaders were based, could decide the fate of a film - who starred in it, financed it or profited from its distribution.

In an industry dependent on private money, the line between investor and extortionist could be perilously thin. And the threats were real. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar was shot dead outside a Mumbai temple. Three years later, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan survived an assassination attempt.

Sivanandhan investigated the financing of Chori Chori Chupke Chupke, a Salman Khan film whose producer and his assistant were each sentenced to six years in prison under Maharashtra's organised crime law for underworld links. The film's financier received a one-year sentence for withholding information about those links. Police seized the film's negatives, and its release eventually happened under court supervision.

Gangsters were not always imposing themselves on a reluctant industry. Some filmmakers willingly sought their money, Sivanandhan recalled, in arrangements that could benefit both sides and proved difficult for police to dismantle.

But Sivanandhan is reluctant to see the latest violence as a return of the mafia he once fought. The men he pursued - Dawood Ibrahim, Chhota Shakeel, Arun Gawli and others - belonged to criminal networks rooted in Mumbai, even when their leaders operated from abroad.
"This is not the Mumbai mafia which we know in the last 60 years," he said. "This is something else."

That something else has become inseparable from the name Lawrence Bishnoi. A gangster with roots in northern India who has been in jail for years, Bishnoi has acquired an aura of folkloric menace: a prisoner said to command gunmen across continents, his name invoked in threats and claims of responsibility that spread almost instantaneously online.

Bishnoi has publicly threatened Khan over a 1998 poaching case involving blackbucks, a species of antelope revered by the Bishnoi community. In April 2024, gunmen fired five rounds outside Khan's Mumbai home. Six months later, Baba Siddique, a politician close to Khan and other actors, was murdered. Mumbai police have linked both attacks to the Bishnoi gang, though they have not established any personal involvement by Lawrence Bishnoi in Siddique's killing.

Some allegations against his network are backed by police investigations; others remain untested. But the distinction between what the gang has demonstrably done and what is claimed in its name can become blurred in the public imagination, doing little to diminish Bishnoi's notoriety.

Rakesh Maria, a former Mumbai police commissioner, has cited Bishnoi as an example of a new generation of gangsters who are more technologically adept and internationally connected than their predecessors. "The old underworld was visible and territorial, but the new one is dispersed, fluid, making it harder to pin down," Maria told The Print, external last year. "They no longer need to reside in the city to command it."
The relationship between gangsters and Bollywood has changed in another way, too, in who gets to shape their image.

In the 1990s, Bollywood itself helped turn Mumbai's feared underworld figures into objects of fascination. Films such as Satya (1998) and Company (2002) brought a gritty, visceral realism to their world, while Manoj Bajpayee's portrayal of gangster Bhiku Mhatre in Satya became, in the words of film scholar Ashvin Immanuel Devasundaram, "mythologised and talismanic".
The fear and fascination of that era were "seared into the collective consciousness", Devasundaram told the BBC.

Each new attack brings those memories back, he added. But today's gangsters no longer need cinema to build their mythology. Social media allows them to shape their own image, circulating threats, claims of responsibility and carefully staged photographs to audiences far beyond Mumbai.

After the latest shooting, police reportedly stepped up security outside the homes of Khan and Rohit Shetty. The All Indian Cine Workers Association demanded greater protection, asking: "Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?"
There is little evidence so far that criminal networks have regained their former influence over Bollywood's finances and decisions. But the latest attacks have exposed a different vulnerability.
Gangsters may no longer need to control an industry to unsettle it. A single shooting attempt, amplified across millions of phone screens, can spread fear far beyond its intended target.
Sivanandhan, who spent years confronting Mumbai's gangsters, knows the limits of even the tightest security.
"There is always a crack in the armour," he said.

articles.title: 'They destroyed my life': 2 Sask. men imprisoned for exploiting woman from Bangladesh
articles.summary: A Bangladeshi woman who was trafficked and exploited by two men in Saskatchewan — and repeatedly raped by one of them — says she now lives in fear and struggles to trust anyone.

image.caption: Sohel Haider, left, and Mohammed Masum pay for parking in front of Saskatoon provincial court on Wednesday, June 3, 2026. They are now both in custody serving sentences for human trafficking. (Hannah Spray/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
A Bangladeshi woman who was trafficked and exploited by two men in Saskatchewan — and repeatedly raped by one of them — says she now lives in fear and struggles to trust anyone.
Mohammed Masum, Sohel Haider sentenced for human trafficking
"I can't forget them. They stopped my dream. They destroyed my life. They ruined my honour, my future, my family, my career," the woman wrote in her victim impact statement.
Mohammed (M.D.) Masum, 45, and Sohel Haider, 56, were convicted earlier this year of human trafficking and returned to Saskatoon provincial court on Thursday for their sentencing.

Masum was also found guilty of three counts of sexual assault, for actions that the judge classified "in clearer and simpler layman's language" as rapes. The victim's identity is protected by a court-ordered publication ban.

Even though her name has not been published, she said in her victim impact statement that the gossip in her home community in Bangladesh has affected her family's honour and ruined her siblings' futures.

The woman said she used to be independent and self-sufficient, but now depends on others for support and struggles with that. She questions her decision to come to Canada, where she felt like a product being sold to a customer.

items: 2 Sask. restaurant operators convicted of trafficking woman from Bangladesh

blocks.text: The charges covered a period between Aug. 1, 2022, and March 31, 2023. The woman came to Saskatchewan after being told she would have a job in a restaurant that would help her stay in the country as a temporary foreign worker.

She worked first at a restaurant Haider operated in Gull Lake, then she was sent to Tisdale to work in a restaurant operated by Masum. They did not have the proper work permits for her, but said they were working on it. She was not properly paid and was forced to work long hours, six days a week.
When she finally received a work permit, it was for a different restaurant in Elrose. Shortly after arriving there, the woman fled with the help of some people who had become concerned about her.
Trust violated, Crown argues
Human trafficking carries a mandatory minimum sentence of four years in prison.

Crown prosecutor Leslie Dunning argued that Masum's crimes — one count of human trafficking and three counts of sexual assault — called for a total sentence of 15 years in prison, and Haider should be sentenced to five and a half years for the human trafficking.
Dunning argued both offenders were in positions of trust and authority over the woman, and they violated that trust by controlling "virtually every aspect of her life" after she came to Saskatchewan.
In addition, Masum exploited the woman "for his own sexual gratification" in a series of sexual assaults, including some that involved physical violence, Dunning argued.
Masum's lawyer Zachary Carter argued for a total sentence of seven to nine years, suggesting that is still a "substantial" sentence.

Haider's lawyer Chris Gratton argued for the mandatory minimum of four years, arguing there was an absence of aggravating factors that would push the sentence higher than the minimum, which is itself a significant sentence.
Restitution ordered
Judge Miguel Martinez delivered his sentencing decision late Thursday afternoon.
He agreed with Gratton that Haider should serve the mandatory minimum sentence of four years.
For Masum, the judge imposed a total sentence of 14 years.
He also ordered both men to pay restitution to the victim for wages owed to her. Haider was ordered to pay $5,885.16 and Masum was ordered to pay $12,268.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media
articles.summary: A powerful magnitude 7 earthquake has struck Tibet in southwestern China, official media reported. Chinese state TV said it's the strongest quake to hit the remote Himalayan region in five years.

image.caption: Earthquakes are relatively common in China [FILE: Nov 14, 2017]Image: Ivan Damanik/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A strong earthquake struck Tibet in southwestern China on Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring 32 others, Chinese state media reported.
Hundreds of homes in the remote Himalayan region collapsed due to the magnitude 7.0 quake, Xinhua reported.
The earthquake is the strongest to hit the region in the past five years, broadcaster CCTV said, and the most powerful to hit China since January 2024.
How severe was the earthquake in Tibet?
At least 339 residential buildings have collapsed, local government officials said, according to state media. Twenty livestock sheds were also destroyed.
Of the dozens injured, 11 were in a serious condition, the local media office said.
Disaster relief efforts were ongoing as officials assess the scale of the damage, the state news agency added.
Xinhua reported that power and communication lines to the area were also disrupted.
What do we know about the area where the earthquake struck?
The earthquake's epicenter is around 190 kilometers (120 miles) northeast of Nagqu, a city around 300 kilometers north of the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.
The mountainous area is sparsely populated.
The quake struck at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.
How often do earthquakes hit China?
Earthquakes are relatively common in China.
In January 2025, a quake near Mount Everest in Tibet's Tingri region killed at least 126 people.
In 2010, at least 2,698 people were killed when a magnitude 7.1 quake hit Qinghai province, which neighbors Tibet.

articles.title: Surveillance and 'constant paranoia': Western diplomats tell BBC of life in war-time Moscow
articles.summary: Officials compare working in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine to the Cold War era.

blocks.text: "Being the ambassador to Russia was probably the hardest assignment of my career," Lynne Tracy, who represented the US in Moscow from 2023 and 2025, tells the BBC.
US, UK and European diplomats once played a crucial role in Russia, defusing tensions even at the worst moments of the Cold War.

But now, deemed "unfriendly" by President Vladimir Putin's government, Western ambassadors are under constant surveillance, isolated and increasingly cut off from the country they were sent to understand, as the war in Ukraine grinds on through its fifth year.
The BBC has spoken to five diplomats who have served in Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion.

They compare current pressure levels to the Cold War era - when Western embassies were monitored through physical surveillance, listening devices hidden inside gifts, and "spy dust" - a near invisible chemical agent used to track officials.

Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from countries in Europe and the US after the war began in 2022. Moscow responded in kind, declaring hundreds of Western diplomats persona non grata and leaving many embassies short-staffed.

Tracy's 30-year career took her to countries like Pakistan, where she survived an armed attack in 2008. But she says that even under constant physical threat, her posting in Peshawar was, in a sense, easier than Russia.
"There, I still felt that there were things within my control. What made Moscow more difficult were the high levels of uncertainty."
The constant pressure from Russian counterintelligence was the primary source of such uncertainty, she recalls.
Russian diplomats in the West also complain of such unfair treatment. But according to the diplomats who spoke to the BBC, the scope and tactics of Moscow's intelligence services are far greater.
"Expect listening devices, expect cameras in every single room of your house," a former European diplomat says of the warning he received before leaving for Moscow.

Another ex-ambassador says they were forced to dismiss two Russian employees after Moscow's domestic security service, the FSB, tried to recruit them, demanding that they report on everything going on at the diplomatic mission.
The pair told the embassy instead, who let them go - "otherwise, they could have faced some sort of criminal prosecution".

Meanwhile, Russians who would ordinarily build relationships with diplomatic staff - such as those working in academia and culture - are also being intimidated into avoiding contact with Western officials.
One former ambassador says his guests were once "tailed" by FSB agents right up to the doors of the embassy.
Russian officials make little secret of their attitude towards Western diplomats. They have openly accused those from "unfriendly countries" of engaging in "espionage".

Moscow has been particularly critical of those who show an interest in expressions of dissent against the Kremlin and, according to Russian journalist Alexei Venediktov, has effectively banned most Russian officials from speaking to Western embassies.

This has only worsened relations with the West, says Venediktov, who recalls telling Russian officials: "You are being misunderstood precisely because of your own actions - because ambassadors cannot do their jobs."
Today, Moscow has little to no contact with many Western governments, says one ex-European ambassador. "There are no calls, no meetings at ministerial level."
But they say this has made diplomats all the more important, left with the responsibility to communicate their governments' positions to Moscow.
"Generals prove what they can do during a war. The same is true for diplomats. When things get really difficult, every single thing you do actually matters."
Lynne Tracy left Moscow in 2025 feeling she had accomplished her primary mission: the US Embassy had held firm.
But she is also proud of the work she and her team did to maintain connection between Americans and ordinary Russians.
"Because at some point, government-to-government relations will have a chance to improve - and those ties between people will be there to help speed the improvement."

articles.title: Hospitals deliberately targeted by Sudan's RSF fighters, BBC investigation finds
articles.summary: The UN human rights chief Volker Türk says the multiple attacks may amount to war crimes.

blocks.text: A BBC investigation has found evidence that Sudanese paramilitary fighters systematically destroyed el-Fasher's healthcare system during their long siege and subsequent takeover of the city in Darfur a year ago.

UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the findings "deeply disturbing", saying multiple attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on civilian infrastructure, including health facilities, were serious violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes.
The RSF has rejected the BBC's findings.
The paramilitary group's health minister described the allegations as propaganda and a deliberate attempt by the national army and its allies to smear the RSF's reputation.
Using sources who were on the ground in el-Fasher, the BBC has found details of at least 43 separate attacks on hospitals and healthcare sites from May 2024 to October 2025 - some hit multiple times.
Under international law it is illegal to attack health facilities or their staff during conflict.

The investigation also reveals the toll on medical workers in the western city. In the period from April 2023 to October 2025, the BBC's data shows 120 were injured, 55 killed and 10 forcibly "disappeared" or abducted.

"The RSF [were] trying to evacuate the hospitals, to put them out of service because the health system is the cornerstone of any city or any state," says Dr Muhamed Suliman, a surgeon who was based in el-Fasher during the siege and spoke to the BBC.
"The RSF started hitting these areas so citizens have no longer any way to stay there. It was intense. It was deliberate. It was planned."
The investigation comes a year after the fall of el-Fasher, one of the most brutal chapters of the civil war which erupted in April 2023 between the RSF and Sudan's military.
Both sides have been accused of attacks on health facilities.

In March 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the bombing of al-Daein hospital in RSF-held eastern Darfur, which killed dozens and forced the site to close. Sudan's military is believed to have carried out the drone strikes, although it has denied responsibility.
But events in el-Fasher represent "one of the clearest and most severe examples of the wider impact of the conflict on health care in Sudan," the WHO said in response to a BBC query.

UN investigators have reported that the fighting in el-Fasher bore the "hallmarks of genocide", where historical ethnic animosities have seen Arab militias - now the backbone of RSF forces - target non-Arab groups such as those that populate the city.
The BBC's investigation reveals for the first time a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare during the long siege of the city.
Some medical facilities in el-Fasher closed down within weeks of the country's civil war starting in April 2023.
Crucially this included one of the main hospitals - the Teaching Hospital - located in a conflict zone in the middle of the city.
Its operations were moved to el-Fasher's South Hospital. There medical services continued, although increasingly hindered by power cuts and dwindling supplies.
The situation changed dramatically a year later, when the RSF mounted its siege of el-Fasher.
In late May and early June of 2024, the South Hospital was shelled several times as paramilitary fighters pushed forward from their positions in the east of the city.
The first bombing came as a shock, says Dr Suliman.
The area around the hospital that was hit was "very crowded because it was the only working hospital in the city providing surgical services", he says.
On that day medical staff operated on 16 injured patients, he added.

The attacks culminated in an RSF raid on 8 June. Hospital staff were taken by surprise - many of them escaped over the back wall as the RSF fighters entered the building, says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, a pharmaceutical specialist.
But the director general of the hospital, surgeon Izzeldin Ahmed Dawaud Asow, encountered a group of the paramilitaries outside his office.
They did not know he was a doctor, he said, but denounced him with ethnic slurs.
"There are no citizens here. You are Falangi," they said, using a derogatory term implying that non-Arab Sudanese are foreigners.
Dr Asow says he was beaten with rifle butts and lost consciousness at one point. Ultimately, he saved himself by pretending to be dead.
"They put their hand on my chest, and I stopped breathing. And they said: 'Leave him, leave him. The rubbish has died. Leave him.' They left me."

That same day the RSF was driven out by the Sudanese military and its allies and Dr Asow returned to find the bodies of several patients and the surgical equipment in his operating room thoroughly destroyed, he said.
The hospital closed and later fell into RSF hands when the army retreated.
Dr Alaa Eldin Nugud, a prominent Sudanese surgeon who has joined the RSF-backed civilian government as health minister, insisted the South Hospital was being used as a military base.
According to international law, hospitals can lose their protection if they are used by a party to the conflict to commit an "act harmful to the enemy".

In an interview with the BBC, Dr Nugud declared that missile launchers were set up on the grounds and shared a video showing remains of weapons filmed more than a year after the hospital closed, which he said supported his claim.
He also showed us what he called maps of landmines planted around the Teaching Hospital, which is located next to Sudanese military headquarters.
Doctors told us the hospital was not incorporated into the base and said they visited it to pick up medical equipment during the war.
The BBC has found no independent evidence of Dr Nugud's allegations. And the government of the Darfur region categorically rejected the charges.
After the South Hospital shut, its staff and remaining equipment were moved to the Saudi Maternity Hospital in the west of the city, where the army had its main bases.
Within days the pace of attacks on the facility picked up. At this stage the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) sounded the alarm.
"We do not know if hospitals are being intentionally targeted, but… the belligerents are not taking any precautions to spare them," it said in a statement.
However, in the course of our investigation we spoke to six doctors who described a pattern of systematic targeting.
They told us how Saudi Hospital was repeatedly struck - on some days up to 25 times, with a mix of shelling and drones, the latter "intelligent rockets" with precision-guided attacks.
Smaller medical facilities also came under fire. The BBC's timeline records the steady closure of private hospitals and neighbourhood clinics.
Furthermore, when some of these healthcare buildings shifted locations, the alternate venues were also attacked.
The Specialised Children's Hospital, which shut down at the beginning of the war along with the Teaching Hospital, moved to two other locations, both of which were then shelled and forced to close.
Similarly, the main dialysis centre was struck and then attacked again after it relocated.
By the time the RSF seized the city in October 2025, the Saudi Hospital was the only functioning health facility left.
The medical staff there had rallied to try to keep working as conditions worsened.
Doctors described how sandbags were set up to protect the building.

They built underground bunkers out of steel containers and established a number of alternative sites to house and receive patients and conduct surgery as the threat of attacks and the damage to the main structure steadily increased.
Dr Asow said this makeshift surgery was attacked five times in 2025.
In one case, he says, he was operating on a patient's neck when the building was shaken by an explosion - the medical staff ran out in fear, but he stayed.

In another case, health workers had prepared the theatre for an operation, but he told them to move the patient elsewhere because it needed a deep clean given the relentless case load. Shortly afterward the room was destroyed by shells - and the patient survived.
"From that day, some of my staff called me 'Mr Deep Cleaning' because they think that the issue of deep cleaning saved that patient," he said.
Dr Asow also describes how drones tracked the movement of patients.
On 15 March 2025, people carrying the injured from the site of an attack to one of the temporary wards were followed by a hunting drone, he says.
It struck as they reached the gate of the building, killing nine people.
On 17 August of the same year a donkey cart was transferring patients to the alternative operating theatre because all the ambulances had been destroyed, Dr Asow told the BBC.
It was hit by a drone, killing two patients, the driver and the donkey, he says.
The RSF health minister dismissed these accounts as "a continuation of lies" by the military (SAF) and their local allies, known as the Joint Forces.

"Even the medics, and many of the people who were there, because of this conflict, these tribal issues, these racial issues, they are allied with the Joint Forces and with the SAF. That's why you don't depend on that narrative," he said.
Doctors told the BBC they believed RSF fighters deliberately targeted medical facilities because army or allied fighters were among their patients.
The onslaught of shelling and bombing culminated on 25 October 2025 with the RSF storming the hospital amid allegations of a massacre that killed more than 460 patients and their companions.
The RSF has denied a massacre occurred, although the WHO condemned the reported killings and satellite imagery appeared to show clusters of bodies on the blood-soaked grounds of the hospital.
The BBC shared details of its investigation with the UN human rights chief, who said our findings were "deeply disturbing", and consistent with the analysis of his office.

"Our monitoring and documentation shows the RSF repeatedly struck el-Fasher's main hospitals and makeshift health facilities, destroying or seriously damaging them and severely impacting access to health services for thousands of civilians trapped in the city," Türk said.

Healthcare in el-Fasher is now being run by the RSF-backed government. It has released several videos showing the Saudi Hospital and the Teaching Hospital re-opened, cleaned up and seeing some patients.
Dr Nugud says South Hospital is also set to reopen. He denied that doctors were forcibly abducted, telling the BBC that instead they had chosen to stay on to work.

"I have a video in front of the children's hospital when we freed a consultant, a doctor and six of the medical staff who were working with the SAF, and then when el-Fasher got liberated, there was a forgiveness for all of them.
"We liberated them," he said.
The BBC spoke to one of the doctors in the video, Dr Al-Haj Mohamed Ahmed. He told us he had no choice: "I was forced to be there.
"If I spoke out of line, they'd put a bullet through my head."
He was among several medical workers captured while trying to escape the city and sent back, along with Dr Mustafa Ahmed.
They distinguished themselves by bringing a cholera epidemic in a temporary prison at the paediatric hospital under control and were subsequently taken to Saudi Hospital.

"They started to say that you are the people of the city, and we take the city, so we need to work together for the sake of the city," says Dr Mustafa Ahmed, who describes waking up several mornings in a row at the prison to find 50 inmates dead of cholera.
A year on from the fall of el-Fasher, the trauma of this dark period in Sudan's civil war is still painfully sharp.
The front lines have shifted elsewhere with no signs of a resolution to the conflict. And attacks on healthcare continue as part of a wider and devastating humanitarian crisis.
Additional reporting by Peter Mwai
Maps and graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry, Jake Friend and Matt Mitchell-Camp

articles.title: A possible three tornados wallop Arizona, bringing golf-ball sized hail
articles.summary:
Violent storms overnight knocked over utility poles and trees and carried thunder and heavy winds through state

Yet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four…

blocks.text: Yet more severe weather struck Thursday in the US south-west as the Four Corners region surveyed blown-away roofs, trees knocked onto homes and power lines downed from overnight tornadoes that injured one person.

The injuries weren’t life-threatening but rare for an area better known for scalding heat. But this fall has been unusually soggy in the south-west with El Niño conditions that have sent one tropical system after another in from the Pacific, causing the Grand Canyon and surrounding deserts to rage with floods.

Now, golf ball-size hail and tornadoes have joined the mix. National Weather Service meteorologists suspect at least three tornadoes touched down as storms swept across central Arizona late Wednesday.

The nasty weather hit during Lenna Landy’s yoga routine in Overgaard, a community of about 3,000 people 140 miles (225km) north-east of Phoenix. Landy had ignored alerts about a possible tornado, but then the storm struck.
“It was like Zeus-was-angry kind of level, of thunder cracks,” Landy said.
The power went off, her house shook and Landy couldn’t find her glasses.
“If this is my end, I won’t see it coming,” she recalled thinking. “The scariest part was just like, how quickly it came on.”
The storm peeled off nearby roofs, shattered windows and blew a shed into a home, she said. A spruce tree in her yard was split in half.

blocks.caption: A storm dumps heavy rain and hail across Flagstaff, Arizona, on Wednesday. Photograph: Cheyanne Mumphrey/AP

blocks.text: Still more severe weather, including large hail, struck Thursday with much of Arizona under tornado and flood watches. Similar weather soaked New Mexico, while swathes of Utah and Colorado were under flood watches and warnings.

Warm, moist air moving north fuels storms coming in from the California coast. Changing winds can make them spin, creating the conditions for tornadoes, said Ryan Bernhart, a weather service meteorologist in Flagstaff.
“This is very unusual for this area at this time of the year,” Bernhart said.

blocks.caption: Uprooted trees cause damage at an apartment complex after storms hit the area on Wednesday in Mesa, Arizona. Photograph: Ross D Franklin/AP

blocks.text: Tornadoes are somewhat but not exceptionally unusual in Arizona. Notable outbreaks happened in 2019 and 2010.

Strong winds toppled trees in Flagstaff and Mesa, with some landing on walls and carports. A few dozen ponderosa pines more than 30ft (9 meters) tall fell down in the Coconino national forest, north-west of Flagstaff.
“These are not small trees that are down,” Bernhart said. “These are pretty strong trees that had been knocked down.”

articles.title: L'Oreal says weight loss drugs are impacting beauty and skin care sales
articles.summary: The beauty giant's CEO says the use of GLP-1s is "a very important phenomenon for us".

blocks.text: Beauty giant L'Oreal says the rise of weight loss drugs has affected beauty and skin care sales, as it designs products to specifically target some side effects of rapid weight loss.
The company's head Nicolas Hieronimus said the beauty market was proving resilient in a challenging global context, and that the use of GLP-1s was "a very important phenomenon for us".
He told an investor call that the rise in their use was "having an impact on beauty consumption and skin care consumption in particular".
L'Oreal, which owns other popular brands including Maybelline and La Roche-Posay, announced on Thursday that sales in the three months to September rose by 7.7%, above analyst expectations.

The use of GLP-1s has boomed in popularity in recent years, after drugs developed to treat diabetes such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro were found to also lead to significant weight loss because they supress the appetite.
While it is not caused by GLP-1 drugs directly, rapid weight loss can, for some people, come with a side effect of loose skin - including around the face.

Hieronimus said L'Oreal's brands SkinCeuticals and Kiehl's have products "that have been designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 and its side effects on skin sagging" and other effects related to rapid weight loss.
L'Oreal has also moved further into the clinical aesthetic space, increasing its stake in dermatology firm Galderma to 20% last December.
Both companies have been testing products on GLP-1 users worried about loose skin in separate clinical trials, according to Reuters.
Galderma owns popular aesthetic products including Sculptra, an injectable aimed at stimulating collagen production, and Restylane, which is an injectable dermal filler.
Last year the aesthetic firm released a report into the rise of GLP-1 use and related concerns about changes in facial appearance.
Its own survey of weight loss medication users found the vast majority had noticed changes to their facial appearance after using those drugs.
