articles.title: Ombudsman to review impeachment prosecutors' evidence vs. VP Sara
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Thursday said his office will review the evidence that the House prosecution will turn over from the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 11:07pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Thursday said that his office will review the evidence that the House prosecution will turn over from the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

After the House prosecution panel dropped three of the four articles of impeachment against Duterte, lead prosecutor Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville “Jinky” Luistro said that the prosecution team was ready to turn over any evidence to the Ombudsman if needed.
“Probably we will be needing sworn statements. We will evaluate it first. And we will see if we need sworn statements to come with the relay of information,” Remulla said in a press briefing in Cebu.

After presenting three articles of impeachment—Article IV on grave threats, Article I on confidential funds use, and Article II on unexplained wealth—the House prosecution panel withdrew the articles on grave threats and confidential funds. Article III, on bribery, was withdrawn earlier and not presented in court.
Luistro said that the evidence and testimonies presented in arguing these articles will not be wasted.

“As part of our appeal to the public, huwag po tayong manghinayang because these articles are not gone into waste sapagkat tuloy-tuloy po ang ibang ahensya ng ating pamahalaan to pursue criminal action with respect to these articles of impeachment,” Luistro said.

(As part of our appeal to the public, we urge you not to feel dismayed because these articles are not gone into waste as other agencies of the government will continue to pursue criminal action with respect to these articles of impeachment.)
Asked about the National Bureau of Investigation’s (NBI) probe into Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), Remulla said that it needed to be validated first.
“Fact-finding muna yan [Fact-finding first]. So this is a process where we validate the facts that are being presented to us,” Remulla said.
The NBI is also investigating several properties that were linked to Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: 2027 budget has no unconstitutional items, says DBM
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Thursday told senators that the provisions that the Supreme Court (SC) declared unconstitutional in the 2024 and 2025 budgets were no longer in the…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 11:01pm

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Thursday told senators that the provisions that the Supreme Court (SC) declared unconstitutional in the 2024 and 2025 budgets were no longer in the proposed 2027 budget.

In a "24 Oras" report from Mav Gonzales, senators questioned DBM Secretary Kim De Leon about what adjustments needed to be made following the SC order to ensure that there were no constitutional infirmities.

“We don't have SAGIP (Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs) anymore even in 2027 Unprogrammed Appropriations (UA). The Supreme Court has also laid down some guardrails, the four guardrails to make the unprogrammed appropriations constitutional. Among these is that there shouldn’t be any lump sum,” De Leon said.

The SAGIP items in the UA of both the 2024 and 2025 national budgets were deemed illegal by the SC, as it gave the executive branch post-enactment identification or allocative powers — a duty only prescribed to Congress.
The UA is a list of projects that do not have a set allotment of money for them unless government revenues meet or surpass its targets.

In 2024, the executive branch asked Congress for P281 billion in UA funds, but Congress increased it to P731 billion. The following year, Congress again increased the UA from P158 billion to P363 billion.
The 2026 budget also has a UA, but this no longer surpassed what the President asked for.
The proposed 2027 budget still has UA, but this is the lowest since 2019.

“Bottom line… hindi pwede lumampas Kongreso sa proposal ng Presidente both unprogrammed and programmed?” Senate President Win Gatchalian asked. (Bottom line… Congress could not surpass what was proposed by the President both unprogrammed and programmed?)
“That is how we view the decision, your honor,” De Leon replied.
The DBM will also not release funding from Sections 1A and 1B of the 2026 budget if the government does not surpass its revenue targets. Unless the funding is for foreign-assisted projects (FAP),
No UA will also be released from the 2024 budget because this has expired, while the P17.99 billion from the 2025 UA remained untouched.
Senator Imee Marcos said that the obligations for the FAP must be paid.

“We’d like to assure the good senator and the committee na wala pong tatalbog na tseke for foreign-assisted projects, dahil ito ay under a direct financing scheme. Direktang pong binabayaran ng development funders, development institutions, ang ating contractors,” De Leon said.

(We’d like to assure the good senator and the committee that no cheques will bounce for foreign-assisted projects, because this is under a direct financing scheme. We are directly paying the development funders, development institutions, and our contractors.)

Senator Francis Pangilinan said that the previous budgets need not be worried about, and it will only apply moving forward, citing a conversation with SC Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, who penned the decision.
“He actually said that as far as 2024 and 2025 are concerned, the doctrine of post-operative fact will apply,” Pangilinan said.—Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
articles.summary:
‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by…

blocks.text: When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.

But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.

This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.

“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”

The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.

The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.

The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.

Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”

Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.

Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.

“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”

For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.

Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”

The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.

Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.

“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.
“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”
Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.

“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”

During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.
For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.

“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

articles.title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
articles.summary: After two years of student protests, Serbians vote on Sunday in elections that could bring down the ruling party.

blocks.text: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
Image source, Reuters
Young Serbians have been the driving force behind the movement, but none of the candidates are students
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor
Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.
After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.
The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.
Why is this student movement so important?
They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.

At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.
Who is Vučić and how popular is he?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that

blocks.text: Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that
Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.

Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".

Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power.

"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.
How do Serbia's elections work?
Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.
Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.
There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.
Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.
Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.
Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates

blocks.text: Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates
Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.

They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić.
Under an 11-point programme, external, the student movement wants to:

items: eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it
purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime
reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control
stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises

blocks.text: Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
How fair will the vote be?

European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".

Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence, external, and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.
In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".

Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".
Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year, says the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom.

articles.title: How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk?
articles.summary: The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy explains how it happened, and what it means for you.

blocks.text: Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain a massive flaw in internet technology, after AI discovered issues that could be exploited by hackers.

Developers of the PHP platform - which powers more than 70% of websites, including Wikipedia and digital shopping sites - rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.

Cyber-security firm Wiz described the issue as the "most severe" ever detected, while OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
But how did AI discover a massive cyber-security risk in the internet, and what does it mean for you? The BBC's technology correspondent Joe Tidy reports.

articles.title: Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk
articles.summary: As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation…

image.caption: Tetjana, a local resident in Sloviansk, couldn't afford leaving the city even if she wanted toImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: A few days ago, three Russian aerial bombs struck a residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Sloviansk. One hit a five-story apartment building, injuring seven people. Along with neighboring Kramatorsk, Sloviansk is one of the last major towns in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. Since summer, the city has been a combat zone.

In a courtyard surrounded by damaged apartment blocks, a dusty carpet hangs over the metal frame of a swing set. Tetjana, a pensioner who lives in the building across the street, has brought it out of her rubble-strewn apartment to clean it. She was in her kitchen when the bombs struck.
"The bomb hit the second floor, and a woman who lived on the fourth floor was screaming," she tells DW. "They managed to rescue her before that entire section of the building collapsed," she adds.

Despite being offered the opportunity to evacuate, Tetjana has yet to leave Sloviansk. "I don't know where I would go," she says. Rent can cost up to €400 ($449) a month. Tetjana's pension is the equivalent of just €67 ($75) a month. Even with monthly relocation assistance of about €40 ($45), she could not make ends meet. "I couldn't live on that. Nowhere!"

Meanwhile, electricity and water are still available in her neighborhood, but the gas supply has been cut off. "We'll get through this," Tetjana says hopefully. "Everything will be OK. That's what I tell everyone. I want that so much."

blocks.caption: People who want to evacuate are not allowed to bring their pets Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Residents reluctant to evacuate without pets

Days after the attack, the few residents remaining in the damaged buildings were still clearing out their apartments. But another attack hit as they worked. This time, the bombs struck a building housing a state-run emergency assistance center and the Red Cross. While firefighters put out the blaze, rescue workers and volunteers retrieved belongings left inside and cleared away broken glass. Eight people were injured in the attack.

"I was on the balcony when there was a deafening bang. It felt as if someone had hit me over the head," says Natalja, describing one of the recent attacks. The pensioner comes to this part of the city to care for her twin sister. "She can no longer get around. Today, I couldn't bring her bread, only crispbread," she tells DW. Although shops and a few stalls remain at the burned-out market, bread is not available every day.

blocks.caption: Volunteers help clear the debris and retrieve belongings from a resilience center after a Russian bomb struck the building in SlovianskImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "I tried to persuade my sister to leave. I would go to a nursing home and she would go to a hospital. But her dog is sick, and I have one, too," Natalja says, noting that pets are not allowed during evacuations. "I can't leave my sister behind. She is worried and angry with me, as if everything were my fault. I have no strength left."

Natalja slowly sets off for home, "so I can get there before dark." The city center is nearly 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) away. Public transportation has been suspended since 30 people were killed in an attack on two buses in neighboring Kramatorsk.

blocks.caption: Natalja cares for her twin sister who refuses to leave as she would have to leave her dog behindImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "We're used to living under fire"

The center of Sloviansk is heavily damaged. Few people are out on the streets, though a handful of shops remain open. Of the city's 100,000 residents, about 20,000 remain, most of them elderly people who are unable to leave.

Vasyl, a pensioner, is from the village of Mayaky, north of Sloviansk. A neighbor drove him into the city center, where he sat down for lunch in a cafe. "We're used to living under fire by now," he says. "But it's a bad habit. We should have broken it long ago."
Vasyl wants peace for his homeland. But he rejects Russian President Vladimir Putin's demand that the part of the Donetsk region under Ukrainian control be handed over to Moscow.

blocks.caption: Life has almost come to a standstill in Sloviansk and only few shops and market stalls remain openImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Two elderly women talk on a street covered with nets to protect against drones. "I can't remember the last time I slept through the night," says Iryna, a pensioner. "It's terrible, but I have nowhere to go. I'm supposed to leave my two cats behind, but I love them so much. They're all I have."
"We can only hide, trembling, and pray to God that everything will be all right," Iryna continues. "When I have to go to the market, I don't know if I'll make it there alive."
Russian drones attacked the central market several weeks ago, injuring at least three people. Since then, fewer vendors and customers have been coming to the market.

blocks.caption: The constant buzz of drones and the fear of Russian attacks keeps people from sleeping through the nightImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: "We dream of staying here"

Valeriya sells women's underwear. With kindergartens closed, she has to bring her 5-year-old daughter Sofia to work. Their neighborhood in Sloviansk is not yet subject to the mandatory evacuation of families with children.
"We're used to this life by now. We were evacuated in 2022, but later returned. Now we're waiting to be evacuated again," Valeriya says.

Sofia races through the market aisles with her friend Anya, who is a year older. Anya's mother is a soldier defending her hometown. Her grandmother, Tetjana, sits nearby selling men's clothing. She, too, has to look after her granddaughter while working.

blocks.caption: Sofia, 5, and Anya, 6, play at Sloviansk central market as their kindergartens are closed due to the warImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

blocks.text: Tetjana has started shipping her belongings to the Dnipropetrovsk region, where she hopes to start a new life. She is sending them while the post office is still open. "It hurts to see our Ukraine being destroyed," she says, fighting back tears. "Who will rebuild our cities?"

She hopes to return one day. But the fate of Bakhmut weighs on her mind. "Look at Bakhmut. There are no houses left. I'm counting on our boys to hold our cities, even though it's very difficult." Bakhmut, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Sloviansk, fell to Russian forces in 2023 after months of heavy fighting.

The women see little hope for a ceasefire. "Putin won't want one. And our younger generation will ask us what we fought for in the first place," Tetjana says. She believes Russia must withdraw from Ukrainian territory.
Drones buzz overhead as gunfire echoes across the market. "It's hard for our boys to shoot them down," Tetjana says. "But they're doing their best."
Russian strikes hit civilians in Ukraine
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
articles.summary: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz

blocks.text: Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.

Yemeni Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.

Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.
It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.

The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, who also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.

Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.

Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf.

However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.
after newsletter promotion

Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.
In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.

articles.title: At least four dead after storm brings flooding to southern France
articles.summary: The deaths include two women found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

blocks.text: At least four people have died in France, and one other has been injured, after flooding caused by Storm Adam.
The storm triggered widespread flooding across southern France on Tuesday, inundating streets and disrupting transport.
The deaths included two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the Bouches-du-Rhône region.

Corsica was also hit by severe weather. Local media reported that a 4x4 vehicle was swept away by floodwaters on Tuesday - one of the occupants escaped through a window, but another man was found dead. Authorities have not released further details about the fourth death.

In the towns of Mouriès and Saint-Martin-de-Crau, between Montpellier and Marseille, dozens of residents were accommodated in emergency shelters after the floods hit. Officials said one person had been injured in that area.
Roads and train lines ‌in ⁠the area were also disrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot wrote in a post ​on X.
"The water has risen to unprecedented levels," Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the Bouches-du-Rhône department, said in a statement on Wednesday.
Witkowski expressed "a thought for all those who are in distress", adding: "We are mobilised at an exceptional level to resolve several issues."

articles.title: Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter
articles.summary: Journalist Will Murray describes how he and a bystander saved an SUV driver from his vehicle.

blocks.text: A man in a sinking car has been saved by a TV journalist after driving into deep flood water.
Will Murray was at the scene reporting for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Morayfield, Queensland, when he saw a vehicle drive past him into the water.
Murray, and a bystander, rushed to help the driver as the SUV sank.
Murray says when it became clear the car was sinking very fast "there was no thinking involved", because the man might have drowned.
"Better that you jump in and give it a crack", Murray tells BBC News.

articles.title: 'Agent Layla': A sex assault victim went undercover to bring her abuser to justice. Now he's out on parole
articles.summary: A parole board decision to release the man who sexually assaulted her has created a whiplash effect for Vienna Luke, who is simultaneously advocating against Justin Sewell’s release from a halfway…

image.caption: Justin Sewell confessed to sexually assaulting his younger sister-in-law in 2007. (submitted by Shawnessy Luke)

blocks.text: A woman who went undercover to get a confession from the man who sexually assaulted her says she's "fed up" and "retraumatized" by a parole board decision to release him.

The parole board decision comes as Vienna Luke has received support from people across Canada and abroad who have heard her extraordinary story of going undercover as an RCMP agent in the CBC podcast Personally: Agent Layla.
"I feel deflated," said Luke of the decision to release Justin Sewell early. "My story being out there is like, 'Wow, look.' But there's still so much work to be done."
18 years of fighting for justice. 6 months in prison. 7 months in a halfway house.

The parole board made its decision to release Sewell on Oct. 6, citing his low assessed risk to reoffend and his compliance and participation in therapeutic programs during his time in a halfway house.
Justin Sewell (left) was a trusted brother-in-law to Vienna Luke (second from right) and Shawnessy Luke (right). Vienna met him when she was 10 years old. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
As described in the Personally: Agent Layla podcast and in court documents, Sewell drugged, assaulted and photographed Luke in 2007 when she was 20 years old.

After wrestling for years with what really happened the night she was drugged into unconsciousness and assaulted, Luke decided in 2019 to report the assault to police after she and her sister, Shawnessy Luke, recorded a phone conversation with Sewell's ex-lover who said he disclosed putting ketamine in Vienna's drink. In court, Sewell has denied it was ketamine, but a provincial court judge found it was either ketamine or Valium.

RCMP proposed a plan to put Vienna Luke undercover, giving her the code name Agent Layla. They used emails to entice Sewell to meet her face to face at a hotel lounge at the Vancouver International Airport under the premise that him telling the truth might be a path back to family reconciliation.

In the recording from the sting, obtained by CBC and included in Episode 3 of the Agent Layla podcast, Vienna Luke pushes Sewell to describe the specific details of his offence. He admits to drugging and assaulting her, and to watching her through her bedroom window on two separate occasions.
Eventually, Sewell pleaded guilty to sexual assault and two counts of voyeurism.
Sewell was a successful veterinarian in the northern B.C. community of Fort St. John at the time of the assault. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)

After what was described in court as an unusually lengthy sentencing hearing in which Sewell took the stand arguing that a self-diagnosed addiction to pornography was the root cause of his offences, a provincial court judge sentenced Sewell to two years less a day of house arrest in April 2025.
Seven months later, a panel of B.C. Court of Appeal judges overturned that decision and imposed a sentence of 33 months less a day to be served in prison.
After serving about six months in a federal institution, Sewell was granted day parole and transferred to a halfway house in April 2026.

Since then, according to notifications provided to his victims and viewed by CBC News, Sewell has been granted permission to leave the halfway house and travel to his home in Fort St. John or to "recreate" in Grande Prairie, Alta., for 70 days over a period of less than seven months.
Discrepancies in 2 Parole Board of Canada decisions made 6 months apart

The Parole Board first considered Sewell's applications to be granted full parole in an April 2026 face-to-face hearing. His case was up for review again six months later in early October. This time he was subject to a paper review, a parole decision-making process that assesses documents written about the offender's behaviour and programs they have completed, but does not interview the offender.
The two boards came to a few markedly different conclusions.

The parole board members in April 2026 found in their decision that Sewell "engaged in considerable rationalizing and minimizing" of his offences. Instead of addressing the "key issues leading to your violence," the board found he focused on "[his] use of pornography and the problems in [his] marriage, as though solving those particular problems was a solution also for the behavioural issues that led to the sexual assault."
"The Board believes that a day or full parole release to your home community is not adequate to the task of protecting the community from your risk."

With support of her sister Shawnessy Luke (left), Vienna Luke went undercover in her own case and obtained a confession. The sisters continue to work together seeking justice in the case. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

Six months later, despite letters from Vienna and Shawnessy Luke imploring the board to weigh heavily the findings of the April board members who interviewed Sewell and decided against full parole, the October parole board members found Sewell's "compliance, community adjustment, ongoing therapeutic involvement, and low assessed risk" support a reduction in supervision and that release on full parole "will not present an undue risk to society."

That board granted full parole on Oct. 6. Correctional Service Canada confirmed the end of Sewell's sentence is Jan. 1, 2028. For the 14 months that remain, Sewell is required to report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with females, and he is prohibited from accessing pornography.
'How is [he] allowed the freedoms to go on a recreational hunting trip?'

For Vienna Luke, it has been an intense time. On the one hand, she's received messages from podcast listeners commending her for sharing her story of confronting her abuser, which led to a conviction and prison time. On the other hand, she's found herself still advocating behind the scenes for justice in her case.
"I'm a person that chose to report," she said. "You can understand why people are just like, 'I'm going to move on with my life.'"

In the most recent parole board decision, board members cited a letter from the Luke sisters questioning the 70 days Sewell was allowed to leave the halfway house, including his release "for the purposes of a hunting trip."

Justin Sewell in a photo where he is hunting. This image is from before he faced the courts for his assault on Vienna Luke. Sewell is now under a 10-year prohibition on possessing firearms. (Shawnessy Luke/Submitted)
The sisters say that in September they began to suspect that some of Sewell's trips might be to participate in hunting, an activity he described as an important hobby in court.

Concerned he might be violating a 10-year ban on using firearms, the Luke sisters say they called the Fort St. John RCMP non-emergency line to alert the police. They say the officer on the line told them Sewell had been granted permission to go hunting with an "approved associate."
Vienna Luke said she met with Correctional Service Canada and parole board officials to express her concerns.
"As they talked and continued to justify how they were handling him ... and their allowances to him, I started shaking. I was so upset," she said.

The sisters weren't worried for their personal safety. They live in Vancouver, about 800 kilometres from Fort St. John as the crow flies. Their concern was that the decision to grant him time to participate in a hobby was at odds with the seriousness of the crime.
"We had a hunch he was going hunting, but we didn't think he was approved to go hunting," said Vienna Luke.
"We were livid," said Shawnessy Luke.

CBC News reached out to Correctional Service Canada to confirm the details of Sewell's permission to go hunting. In an email, it says the organization cannot provide details of travel permits because of the Privacy Act.

The statement adds that "[w]hile we cannot talk about specifics of this case due to privacy, please note that if, at any time, an offender's risk increases or there is a change in their behaviour ... we take immediate action."

The Luke sisters' concerns were summarized by the parole board, who wrote in the October decision: "It is also concerning that your index offence involved violence and yet you are requesting to engage in an extended activity which involves weapons."
Vienna Luke wants systemic change

Vienna Luke knows the outcome of her case – a conviction in a historic sexual assault – is rare. But throughout the lengthy process since she first reported the assault seven years ago, she has found herself questioning whether the justice system is working for sexual assault survivors.
"You would think that maybe the fact he went to jail, he went to a halfway house, the justice system is telling me that I should feel grateful. Look at what you got," she said.
"I feel ungrateful. What did we do all this work for?"
Vienna Luke told her story in honour of other women who have told their stories of surviving sexual assault. (Vienna Luke/Submitted)

In interviews for the podcast and elsewhere, Vienna has emphasized she is telling her story to honour sexual assault victims who went before her. She told their stories, including their struggles with the justice system, which gave her strength in the hardest times.
Now she's receiving emails from other women telling her she has become a symbol of strength for them.

"I've come so far," she said. "To be in a place where I can speak about what happened to me, what was done to me publicly, and everything I did in this process is unbelievable and really I just feel so proud."

articles.title: Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman – US politics live
articles.summary:
Nancy Mace said: ‘This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season’

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoVivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman

blocks.text: Responding to the ad yesterday, Amy Acton told a group of voters that her mother was not well and Ramaswamy shouldn’t have “exploited her”.
Earlier in the week, her brother had called Ramaswamy’s attack ad a “despicable low” in a statement released by Acton’s campaign:

double quotation markIt’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.

double quotation markAfter he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”
The ad, which had circulated among conservatives on social media, featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, urging Ohioans to not vote for her daughter.
The Ohio gubernatorial campaign between Acton and Ramaswamy is regarded as one of the uglier contests in the 3 November midterm elections.
Acton has refused to debate Ramaswamy, who she has called a “chronic liar” and has also criticized him for airing an ad which features a woman married to a registered sex offender.
Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad for Ohio ‘shameful, disgusting’, says Republican congresswoman
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of US politics. We’re less than two weeks out from the midterm vote and the campaigns are getting even more nasty.

Condemnation continues of Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign in the Ohio governor race after his team put out an attack ad, featuring the estranged mother of his Democrat rival Amy Acton criticising her daughter and calling her a liar.
Acton’s campaign has called it a despicable ad after putting out the clarification that Acton was sexually abused by her stepfather and removed from her mother’s custody at age 12.

Ramaswamy’s team however has dug in behind the ad, and were backed by Veep JD Vance yesterday who condemned Republican criticism. He said Ramaswamy “had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls ​it out like it is”.
However South Carolina congresswoman Nancy Mace joined the chorus of Republican critics saying:
double quotation markThis ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.
She said she was stunned, adding:
double quotation markI just can’t believe that this is what passes for decency in this election.
Stay with us for more developments.

articles.title: Aung San Suu Kyi’s son speaks to detained former Myanmar leader for first time in five years
articles.summary:
Kim Aris says ‘hearing her voice again means more than words can express’ amid loosening of detention restrictions

The son of

blocks.text: The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” the post said. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi, won the 1991 Nobel peace prize, in almost total seclusion for five years after the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing – who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup – was earlier this year installed as civilian president.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

articles.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
articles.summary: Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Which new sectors could revive growth and contain the far-right AfD, whose support has grown…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government set out a high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors, including artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and climate-neutral mobilityImage: NEURA Robotics/pexels.com/@eren-li

blocks.text: Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak.

Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis.

After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, withGerman vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third.
While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years.
The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety.

The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration.
Merz seeks growth via advanced tech

As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics, the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors.
These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility.

Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies."
Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly.
Germany under pressure
Trillions in new investments

A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035.
Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF.

"It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW.
The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment.
He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce.
Investors circle future growth sectors

There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus.
Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting.
US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology.

"The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed.

The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow.

blocks.caption: China has built more than 2,000 economic zones and industrial parksImage: Liu Quanle/VCG/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A case for special economic zones

Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth.
"For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

This, he added, would follow the examples of Silicon Valley and Chinese mega-cities Shenzhen and Shanghai's Pudong district, and echoes the conditions that helped rebuild the German economy after World War II.
In Janszky's view, these zones would help Germany position itself as a first mover in emerging fields rather than remaining tied to older industrial strengths.
"EU regulations may try to prohibit this move, but Germany will have to overcome them so we can grow the economy again," he added.
Defense spending powers tech growth
The sharp rise in Germany's defense spending will also help several of the high-tech sectors now being prioritized.

According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), the defense budget is expected to reach around €120 billion in 2026 — roughly 2.6% of GDP. The government wants this figure to hit 3.5% by 2029.
The resulting procurement will provide a major boost to the production of drones, sensors, communications systems and other dual-use technologies that have both civilian and military applications.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
The cost gap need not be decisive

Yet, with major rival China benefiting from much lower energy and worker costs, along with huge government subsidies, Germany will continue to face similar price disadvantages when exporting its new high-end tech. But it doesn't have to spell failure, said Falck, the ifo expert.
"Take the semiconductor industry as an example. It is probably unrealistic to aim for leadership along the entire value chain. But it is enough to lead at individual choke points," he pointed out.
"And that is exactly where Germany is strong: as a supplier of equipment for state-of-the-art chip fabs and as a supplier to the world's AI gigafactories, with power semiconductors."

In other words, with a first-mover advantage, decades of high-quality production data and a focus on specialized niches, Germany can remain a major force in advanced industrial and engineering technologies.

articles.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker?
articles.summary: The most prestigious individual prize in football will be awarded on Monday, with Bayern Munich's English striker Harry Kane the front runner. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite…

image.caption: Harry Kane is already Bayern Munich's seventh top Bundesliga scorerImage: Carina Johansen/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. But for those with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, he was one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or, in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Stammer, in 1996.
That long drought looks set to end on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, the favorite to pick up the trophy at a ceremony held, as a one off, in his native London.

"It's obviously special for me that the ceremony is taking place in London. "I come from London and lived there for a long time — maybe that's a good omen," Kane told club magazine Säbener51. "The Ballon d'Or would be a massive success for me."

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16 looks to be the main competitor. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title.
Kane career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season make for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 158 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," said Vincent Kompany of his striker last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now – it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

At 33, Kane continues to improve at a point where many footballers start to regress. While he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way, and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions Leagueagainst Arsenal on Wednesday. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance, and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all round game. "The pass was one of my best ones. I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals," Kane said postmatch.
Leading from the front

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after he joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023 that: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care, he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone and that is his mindset and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills. He is a complete package," he said last month as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic.

There are detractors who point to perceived 'stat-padding', scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams, and a lot less money, than in England. While Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

blocks.caption: Harry Kane has missed out on international honors with EnglandImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Should Kane win the award, it will be a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga. Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain would make Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward though. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.
Domestic trophies won but international success eludes
For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023 before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential. He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean… With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggest he could get better still.

articles.title: Bulgaria: Concerns about security in the Black Sea dominate presidential election campaign
articles.summary: Bulgaria's presidential election campaign has been shaped by recent drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea and the government's lack of support for Ukraine, making foreign policy a key factor in the…

image.caption: Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) are the two frontrunners in the race for the presidency in BulgariaImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Six months after Bulgaria's parliamentary election, the country is gearing up to choose its next president.

Although the role of president in Bulgaria is largely ceremonial, the election on October 25 — with a potential runoff on November 1 — will serve as a test for the government of former President Rumen Radev, whose party won a landslide victory in April, securing an unprecedented majority — the first in Bulgaria in almost three decades.

Although there are 27 candidates on the ballot, the race has narrowed to a duel between the incumbent president, Iliana Yotova, who served two terms as Radev's vice president and is backed by the prime minister, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is supported by opposition parties.
The role of the president

According to the Bulgarian Constitution, the Bulgarian president embodies national unity. He or she represents the country at international level (with a few exceptions), is the commander-in-chief of its armed forces, appoints members of the Supreme Judicial Council and various regulatory bodies, including caretaker governments, and has the power to veto legislation.

blocks.caption: Sunday's presidential election will serve as a test for the government of Rumen Radev. Pictured here: newspaper headlines on the morning after Radev's landslide victory in AprilImage: Valentina Petrova/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hristo Panchugov, political scientist at the New Bulgarian University in Sofia, argues that although the president's powers are formally limited, the office is particularly significant in the current context.

"For the first time in Bulgaria's modern democratic history, we have an absolutely uncontested majority that is not held together by any coalition, but rather by a single political party that faces an opposition that is completely falling apart," he told DW.
Panchugov went on to say that it would have been better if the campaign had focused more on "whether the president could serve as a counterbalance."

Opposition candidate Andrey Gyurov reiterated this point in an interview with DW: "We are seeing a concentration of power that always bears the marks of a slide toward autocracy," he said, adding that "a president should know how to say no."

blocks.caption: Iliana Yotova, president of Bulgaria (left), has the backing of Prime Minister and former President Rumen Radev (right)Image: BGNES

blocks.text: Iliana Yotova declined DW's request for an interview.
The impact of the war in Ukraine
Initially, the presidential race was characterized by small rallies, a lack of televised debates and numerous personal attacks on the two leading candidates.
In recent weeks, however, following drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea, the two frontrunners' diverging positions on support for Ukraine have come to the fore.
Bulgaria's government initially declined invitations to join the Coalition of the Willing and NATO's anti-drone initiative but changed its position on the latter after the recent drone attacks.
Yotova advocates for the establishment of a "Coalition of Peace," where she says Bulgaria would have a stronger diplomatic voice in ending Russia's war in Ukraine.

"There are many warmongers in our country; I am not one of them," she said at a campaign rally this month, adding that "as long as I am president — and if you place your trust in me — not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine."

Yotova sought to reassure voters that no Bulgarian troops would be sent to Ukraine, even though this was not part of the public debate and despite a 2025 parliamentary declaration that reaffirmed that the Bulgarian Armed Forces would not participate in hostilities there.
Nevertheless, the recent drone attacks on commercial ships in the Black Sea have put new pressure on both the president and Rumen Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party.
The effect of the Black Sea drone strikes

"The drone strikes in the Black Sea brought the otherwise abstract geopolitical situation right into the daily lives of every Bulgarian," Boriana Dimitrova, managing partner of the Alpha Research market and social research agency, told DW.

blocks.caption: After a second series of drone attacks on ships in waters off the Bulgarian coast, Prime Minister Rumen Radev (center right) summoned the Russian ambassador, Eleonora Mitrofanova (center left), for talksImage: BGNES

blocks.text: Many in Europe, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have laid the blame for the attacks squarely at Russia's door. The fact that Bulgaria's leaders did not clearly attribute blame for the attacks fueled frustration across the country.
After the first drone attack, President Yotova convened the country's Consultative Council on National Security. Its subsequent declaration did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.

A week later, after the second attack, Prime Minister Radev said, "We lack solid, clear evidence to level accusations against any specific party; however logic suggests the outcome works to the advantage of Russia." He then summoned the Russian ambassador for talks.
Opposition to an 'ambiguous' foreign policy stance
The stance of the government and president is having an impact on the race.

"We're seeing a slight decline in support for Iliana Yotova, which is not threatening her first-place position by any means in the first round, but there has been a decline given the ambiguity of some of the positions she has taken," said Boriana Dimitrova.
As the issue of security entered the public debate, some Bulgarians took to the streets in Sofia to protest against what they saw as the government's ambiguous foreign policy stance on this matter.

"I think the drone attacks in the Black Sea and the utterly spineless stance of the president, the prime minister, and everyone acting in unison were the last straw, and I believe that, on the eve of the presidential election, this should serve as a catalyst," Vlada Tzenova, one of the protesters, told DW.

All this is reflected in the preliminary results of the latest opinion poll conducted by Alpha Research. While expected voter turnout is up, the gap between the two frontrunners has narrowed: Yotova is still ahead, leading Gyurov by about 12 percentage points in the first round, but the margin is smaller than it was.
Who could be the kingmaker?
Nevertheless, these recent dynamics do not necessarily mean a shift in the balance of power.

blocks.caption: Protesters gathered in the Bulgarian capital in late September to voice grievances over the direction of state policies and perceived alignment with RussiaImage: Artur Widak/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Political scientist Hristo Panchugov says that Gyurov's campaign has been hampered by his hesitancy to declare his candidacy, a lack of "passion" in his campaign and the fact that he made few comments on current affairs before he joined the race.
Moreover, supporters of the candidate of the pro-Russian nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party, who ranks third in the Alpha Research poll, would be most likely to support Yotova in a second round.

What could decide the outcome of the election is the fact that both GERB and DPS, two of the established parties that attracted the support of more than 660,000 voters in April, did not field a presidential candidate.

According to Alpha Research, half of GERB's supporters do not intend to vote in the first round. The party dominated Bulgaria's political landscape for 17 years but lost power in December following mass anti-corruption protests backed by opposition parties supporting Andrey Gyurov.
Most of the remaining GERB supporters are expected to back Gyurov, as the party has historically opposed Iliana Yotova's political home, the Bulgarian Socialist Party.

At the same time, both Gyurov's campaign and nationalist parties are seeing increased mobilization, with the latter drawing support from voters disappointed by the government's cautious response to the drone attacks.

"We can view these elections as the first test of confidence in the party that recently won the election," Boriana Dimitrova said. "In peaceful times, the center attracts the most attention; in turbulent times, those candidates who take a clearer stance — regardless of the direction — gain greater visibility."
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

articles.title: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use, as experts sound the alarm
articles.summary: The European Union wants to relax rules for pesticides, saying it will be easier for farmers to adopt more environmentally friendly options. But health and environmental experts say the risks are far…

image.caption: In a bid to help farmers, the EU has proposed unlimited, open-ended approval for certain pesticidesImage: Andrii Yalanskyi/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.
Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of maximum 15 years.

The European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities would bear the responsibility, not the industry.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and to help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.
Why does the EU want to deregulate pesticides?
The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states said open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances." But their stance still proposed extending initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.
The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities."

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation." He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the new pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.
How do pesticides affect human health, environment?
Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.
Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

blocks.caption: In January 2020, beekeepers in Berlin protested the continued authorization of glyphosate by leaving unsellable tainted honey at the entrance to the Agriculture MinistryImage: Adam Berry/Getty Images

blocks.text: When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides." However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: a survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation."

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she said regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time. "The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge."
More than 50 substances banned since 2011

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe nongovernmental organization in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"New science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews. That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.
Pesticides banned in Europe linked to bees deaths in Kenya

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby. This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group, Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.
Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the issue.

"The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring new ones to the market," Dorfmann said. Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.
Farmers need 'incentive' to switch to safer pesticides

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.
Can we cut down on pesticide use with 'plant vaccines'?
